body: Ironi Kiryat Shmona have confirmed that an agreement is in place to sell Cristian Martínez to Slovan Bratislava, drawing a line under the Panamanian midfielder's two seasons in the Upper Galilee. The club's confirmation on Sunday was careful in its wording: what exists between the two clubs is a concluded understanding rather than an announced transfer, and Martínez travelled to Slovakia over the weekend to complete the final formalities.

The terms have nonetheless taken shape quickly. Reporting in Israel puts the deal at three years, and the player's registration record now lists him at Slovan with a contract running to June 2029 and an arrival dated 19 July. Neither club has disclosed the fee, which remains unreported.

The timing owes everything to this summer's World Cup. Panama went out at the group stage without a point, yet Martínez emerged with his reputation enhanced: deployed on the flank rather than in his customary central role, he was named Player of the Match in the 1-0 defeat by Croatia.

The interest that followed came from Europe and South America alike. Slovan officials indicated they had tracked the midfielder across several transfer windows and had to see off considerable competition to sign him — a persistence that finally paid off once Panama's tournament ended.

His Kiryat Shmona record explains the demand. The 29-year-old, who has won 69 caps for Panama, arrived on loan in July 2024 and made 33 appearances in his first season before the club made the deal permanent; in 2025-26 he added 31 appearances and four goals from central midfield, establishing himself among the more dependable foreign players in the Israeli top flight.

For Slovan the urgency is straightforward. The Slovak champions open their Champions League second qualifying round tie this week and want their new midfielder registered and available as early in the European campaign as possible.

For Kiryat Shmona, who missed the championship playoff last season, the sale continues a familiar and financially necessary pattern: recruit shrewdly, extract a strong season or two, and sell into Europe. The undisclosed fee will now fund the next iteration of that model — and the search for a successor in the middle of the pitch.

body: Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball have opened an academy with the Hebrew Reali School that will allow teenage players to pursue high-level training alongside their secondary education. The programme is aimed at players from ninth grade and above, giving the city a defined route for girls who want a demanding basketball environment without separating it from their school life.

The partnership brings together a club already operating inside the Israel Basketball Association system and one of Haifa's established schools. Its stated purpose is broader than producing a single team: the academy is designed to support athletic, academic and personal development through one structure rather than asking families to assemble those elements separately.

That distinction matters in youth sport. Training volume normally rises sharply during the teenage years, just as examinations and travel begin to place greater pressure on players. A school-club model can coordinate those demands more deliberately, although the academy has not yet published a complete public timetable, admissions process or coaching roster.

The club's current federation record shows an existing competitive base on which to build. Maccabi Haifa Women's Basketball are registered under team code 2198, with Ilan Beck and Rinat Kahana listed as representatives and the club's home venue recorded at 19 Bikurim Street in Haifa. Its girls' upper-group side completed 14 games with 12 wins and two losses in the most recent table displayed by the association.

The academy therefore extends an active pathway rather than creating one only on paper. Players entering from ninth grade can see a connection between structured development work and a club already competing in the national girls' framework. For northern Israel, that reduces the distance between an introductory youth programme and a serious performance setting.

The opening was presented as a regional first and was attended by Sports Minister Miki Zohar and Haifa mayor Yona Yahav. Their presence gives the launch civic visibility, but the programme's value will ultimately be measured by practical details: coaching quality, training access, academic coordination and the number of players who remain in the sport through the later teenage years.

For Maccabi Haifa, the strategic gain is the chance to identify and retain talent locally. For the Reali School, the academy offers a formal environment for students whose sporting commitments already resemble those of elite athletes. The announcement supplies the framework; the next meaningful evidence will be the published intake, staff and competition plan for its first full season.

body: Tamar Steinberg finished sixth and Sharon Kantor eighth in the women's iQFOiL event at the Long Beach Olympic Classes Regatta, leaving Israel without a podium finish at the final Sailing Grand Slam stop of the season. Steinberg advanced one round further in Thursday's medal series, but neither Israeli reached the four-athlete final that decided the medals on the future Los Angeles 2028 Olympic course.

Steinberg entered the medal series in fourth place and therefore started in the semi-final. A difficult launch from the line cost her the early position required to advance, and sixth became her final classification. Kantor had climbed nine places during the qualifying series to reach eighth, putting her into the quarter-final, where another compromised start ended her attempt to move through the knockout ladder.

Daniela Peleg completed the Israeli women's iQFOiL group in 12th. She finished two places outside the medal-series cut, a narrow margin in a fleet that had already placed Steinberg third and Kantor fifth after the second day. Britain's Emma Wilson converted her position at the front of the event into the overall victory.

The men's iQFOiL campaign ended outside the medal series. Yoav Cohen was the leading Israeli in 21st, Tomer Vardimon placed 27th and Olympic champion Tom Reuveny finished 28th. Those results made the week a development exercise rather than a continuation of Israel's medal production in the class, with the course and the afternoon sea breeze providing the most valuable information to take away.

Israel also fielded two athletes in the women's Formula Kite event. Maya Ashkenazi finished 14th and Gal Zuckerman 15th. That broader entry mattered because Long Beach brought the two Olympic board disciplines together: high-speed kiteboards and foiling windsurfers raced off Belmont Shore on the same waters scheduled to host Olympic sailing in 2028.

The regatta ran from 13 to 16 July and drew more than 100 international competitors across the four iQFOiL and Formula Kite fleets. It was the first of the Los Angeles Olympic-class blocks this summer and the final round of the 2026 Sailing Grand Slam, giving teams an unusually early competitive look at the Olympic venue two years before the Games.

For Israel, the absence of a medal is a meaningful break in a strong women's iQFOiL season, but the more immediate technical lesson came from the elimination races. In a format where advancement can be decided in one short contest, the opening seconds carry disproportionate weight. Steinberg and Kantor had the speed to qualify; Long Beach showed how little recovery time the medal series allows when the start goes wrong.

body: The winners of Sunday's World Cup final will receive championship rings for the first time in FIFA competition history. Argentina or Spain will still lift the trophy and collect the traditional gold medals at New York New Jersey Stadium, but the winning delegation will also be assigned 30 personalised rings modelled on a familiar North American sporting tradition.

The first presentation will take place immediately after the final, when the victorious captain and head coach are due to receive temporary versions during the ceremony. The permanent rings will then be produced to measure and delivered later. Each of the 30 team pieces will be individually numbered and accompanied by a certificate of authenticity.

The design keeps the World Cup at its centre rather than simply importing another sport's jewellery. One side features the tournament trophy; the opposite face will be completed after the final to reflect the identity of the winning nation. That leaves the manufacturer able to personalise the decisive detail only once Argentina or Spain have settled the match.

FIFA has capped the total edition at 2,026 rings, a direct reference to the tournament year. Thirty are reserved for the champions and the remaining 1,996 will be offered worldwide as officially licensed supporter pieces. No public price had been announced when the collection was revealed.

The initiative adds a commercial product to the most protected symbol system in football, but it also changes how this particular winning group will be commemorated. Medals belong to football's established presentation ritual; rings are designed to be worn and displayed as a continuing marker of membership in a championship team.

American leagues have made that idea part of their championship culture, with bespoke rings carrying team colours, records and season references. The 2026 World Cup gives FIFA an obvious setting to adopt the practice: the final is being played in the United States, and the tournament itself has been staged across Canada, Mexico and the US.

What remains unchanged is the sporting order of importance. The ring accompanies the trophy rather than competing with it. For the winner of Argentina against Spain, however, the 2026 title will now produce three distinct keepsakes: the game's most recognised cup, the champion's medal and the first personalised ring awarded by FIFA.

body: Giannis Antetokounmpo used his first formal appearance as a Miami Heat player to define the move in championship terms. Introduced at Kaseya Center on Thursday alongside president Pat Riley and coach Erik Spoelstra, the two-time NBA Most Valuable Player said Miami offered the strongest route to competing for another title. The presentation converted the league’s largest summer trade from transaction news into the opening statement of a new Heat era.

Miami acquired Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis from Milwaukee in a deal approved on 6 July. The official package sent Tyler Herro, Kel’el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kasparas Jakučionis to the Bucks, together with three first-round picks, a 2030 first-round pick swap and a 2033 second-round pick. That cost makes the competitive timeline unmistakable: Miami have exchanged a large portion of their young core and future draft control for immediate contention.

Antetokounmpo will wear No. 7 rather than the No. 34 associated with his entire Milwaukee career. The new number was visible during his introduction and now appears on Miami’s official roster. It is a cosmetic change with symbolic force, marking the separation between a 13-season Bucks career and the first major relocation of his NBA life.

The basketball fit begins with Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo, two elite defenders who can cover unusual amounts of space and attack the rim from different starting points. The opportunity is also Spoelstra’s central tactical problem. Neither star is primarily a high-volume perimeter shooter, so Miami’s spacing, half-court creation and late-game balance will depend on the guards and wings placed around them. The defensive ceiling is obvious; a championship offence still has to be constructed.

Antetokounmpo arrives with the authority to set that standard. He led Milwaukee to the 2021 championship, won consecutive regular-season MVP awards in 2019 and 2020 and was named Finals MVP after the title run. The NBA’s official farewell record credits him with 21,531 points for the Bucks and places him first in franchise history in points, rebounds and assists. Miami are not acquiring the idea of a superstar, but one whose peak has already altered a franchise.

His introduction also carried a clear cultural expectation. Riley and Spoelstra have built Miami’s public identity around conditioning, accountability and postseason ambition; Antetokounmpo’s own reputation rests on physical preparation and sustained competitive intensity. Those reputations make the partnership coherent, but they do not settle the harder questions of health, roster depth or shot creation. Compatibility of standards is a starting advantage, not proof of a title.

The trade formally ended the most successful Bucks era in half a century. Antetokounmpo won the championship that Milwaukee had waited 50 years to reclaim and left as the franchise leader across its three major cumulative categories. His Miami presentation did not erase that history. It established the next test: whether his prime can be converted into another championship window after the Heat paid one of the summer’s largest asset packages to obtain it.

No game has yet been played with Antetokounmpo in a Heat uniform, and Miami’s final rotation remains a preseason question. Thursday’s significance was therefore strategic rather than competitive. The club presented its new centrepiece, the player accepted the pressure of a title objective and both sides made clear that this move will be judged in the postseason. The announcement is complete; the difficult work of building a champion around No. 7 begins now.

body: The NBA is examining the circumstances surrounding Gary Trent Jr.’s new contract with the Milwaukee Bucks, placing a significant free-agent agreement under league scrutiny days after it was reported. A league spokesman confirmed that the NBA was continuing to look into the matter. That is an active review, not a finding that Trent, Milwaukee or his representatives broke a rule.

Milwaukee officially announced Trent’s return on Thursday without disclosing financial terms. The agreement has been reported as four years and $64 million, which would keep the 27-year-old guard with the Bucks through the 2029/30 season. NBA.com also records that Trent declined his player option before returning on the new multi-year deal.

The question being examined concerns possible salary-cap circumvention through a prior understanding. Trent joined Milwaukee in 2024 on a veteran-minimum contract and returned on another short agreement in 2025. The reported concern is whether those lower salaries were connected to a promise of a larger contract once the Bucks had acquired the contractual mechanism to retain him above the cap. No such prior arrangement has been proved.

The unusual jump in salary has drawn attention because Trent’s production declined in 2025/26. He averaged 8.1 points in 21.2 minutes across 65 regular-season appearances, starting 21 games. Both the scoring and playing-time averages were his lowest since his 2018/19 rookie season. He shot 36 percent from three-point range after making 41.6 percent the previous year.

Performance alone cannot establish circumvention. Teams are free to value shooting, continuity and roster fit differently from the public market, and a player’s recent box score does not prove the existence of an undisclosed promise. The league’s task is narrower and more evidential: determine how the sequence of agreements was negotiated and whether any binding commitment predated the point at which Milwaukee was permitted to offer the new deal.

For the Bucks, the timing matters during a wider roster reset. Trent’s contract would create a substantial multi-year commitment to a rotation guard at the same moment Milwaukee are reshaping the team around a younger core. The review does not suspend the agreement, and neither the league nor the club has announced a timetable for a decision or any interim restriction on Trent.

The case also carries significance beyond one player’s salary. The NBA’s cap system depends on clubs competing within shared exceptions and negotiating windows. If a team can secure discounted seasons by promising a later reward, that would undermine the intended balance. Equally, treating every surprising contract as evidence of wrongdoing would interfere with legitimate negotiations, which is why the distinction between suspicion and proof must remain visible throughout the review.

Trent remains a Bucks player while the league gathers information. The verified position is therefore limited but consequential: Milwaukee have re-signed him, the four-year $64 million terms are reported rather than club-disclosed, and the NBA is examining the surrounding circumstances. Any conclusion about a violation, penalty or contract status must wait for the league’s findings.

body: Slavko Vinčić will referee Sunday’s World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at New York New Jersey Stadium. The appointment gives the 46-year-old Slovenian his fourth match of the tournament and places one of European football’s most experienced officials in charge of the game that will decide the world title.

Vinčić will work with Slovenian assistant referees Tomaž Klančnik and Andraž Kovačič. Jordan’s Adham Makhadmeh has been named as the fourth official, with compatriot Mohammed Al-Khalaf serving as reserve assistant referee. The five-man on-field group combines an established Slovenian trio with two Jordanian officials for the final assignment.

This will be Vinčić’s second men’s World Cup. He refereed Argentina’s 2–1 group-stage defeat by Saudi Arabia and Wales’ 2–0 win over Iran in Qatar in 2022. His previous experience with Lionel Messi’s team therefore comes from one of the defining shocks of that tournament, although that historical result supplies context rather than any evidence about how Sunday’s final will be handled.

Vinčić has already taken charge of three games at the 2026 tournament: Brazil’s draw with Morocco, Jordan against Algeria and Mexico’s round-of-32 victory over Ecuador. The last of those included Piero Hincapié’s dismissal. Sunday will be his first appearance since that knockout assignment and his first World Cup final as the referee in the middle.

The scale of the occasion is familiar from club football. Vinčić controlled Real Madrid’s 2–0 win over Borussia Dortmund in the 2024 Champions League final at Wembley. He also refereed the 2022 Europa League final between Eintracht Frankfurt and Rangers in Seville, which Frankfurt won on penalties. UEFA’s official record lists him as an international referee since 2010.

Klančnik and Kovačič were also Vinčić’s assistants at the 2024 Champions League final, giving the Slovenian trio experience together in a comparable one-match showpiece. That continuity is a functional advantage rather than a guarantee of an error-free night: positioning, eye contact and concise radio communication all depend on rehearsed habits when the noise and speed of a final compress decision time.

For Argentina and Spain, the practical significance lies in preparation rather than mythology around past results. Teams use an official’s recent matches to study thresholds for contact, dissent, advantage and time management. Vinčić’s established assistants matter equally: offside decisions and communication across the crew can shape a final long before a major disciplinary call reaches the referee.

Argentina and Spain are scheduled to kick off at 3pm local time on Sunday 19 July. The referee appointment completes another central part of the match operation as both finalists move into their last training days. Vinčić’s task is straightforward to describe and uniquely difficult to execute: keep the world’s largest football match moving, apply the laws consistently and make the officials as secondary to the contest as the contest allows.

body: Spain carried out their World Cup final preparation beneath Canadian wildfire haze in northern New Jersey on Thursday, but the latest outlook points toward improving conditions before Sunday rather than a confirmed disruption to the match. The visible smoke affected the setting around the finalists; it has not produced an official change to the Argentina–Spain schedule.

The Spanish squad trained outdoors in East Hanover, roughly 15 miles from New York New Jersey Stadium, with the sun obscured by the grey layer. The first 15 minutes of the scheduled hour-long session were open to media. Argentina remained at their base in Marietta, Georgia, after reaching the final, so the two teams were not preparing in the same local air conditions at that stage of the week.

Air quality in East Hanover began Thursday in the ‘unhealthy’ range and improved to ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’ by mid-afternoon. The principal concern was fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, carried south by the smoke. Those particles matter around high-intensity outdoor exercise because players move far more air through their lungs than they do at rest, making the training environment a legitimate performance and welfare issue even without a match postponement.

New York State’s official air-quality advisory had covered the New York City metropolitan area and warned that fine-particle levels could exceed an Air Quality Index value of 100. The National Weather Service’s New York office also carried smoke in its short-term discussion through Thursday night. Together, those records support the haze seen at Spain’s session without turning a temporary advisory into a forecast for the final itself.

Argentina and Spain are due to meet at New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday 19 July at 3pm local time. Current projections expect the smoke to clear well before kickoff, with Sunday’s air quality forecast in the ‘moderate’ range. That category is not the same as pristine air, but it represents a clear improvement from the conditions recorded during Spain’s Thursday training.

There has been no official announcement of a relocation, postponement or revised kickoff. The evidence therefore supports a narrower conclusion than the most dramatic reading of the skyline: the smoke complicated part of Spain’s preparation and required monitoring, while the match outlook was improving. Treating the final as already threatened would run ahead of both the forecast and the tournament authorities.

Spain’s staff can adjust exposure and workload if the local readings deteriorate again, but no confirmed programme change has been published. The more immediate competitive asymmetry is geographic. Spain were already working close to the venue under the haze, while Argentina could continue their recovery in Georgia before travelling north. Whether that difference carries any sporting cost cannot be established from the air-quality readings alone.

The next meaningful evidence will come from the weekend forecast and the teams’ final sessions. For now, the responsible position is to distinguish a real training-day problem from a speculative match-day crisis. The air over northern New Jersey looked troubling on Thursday; the verified trajectory before the world-title match was toward relief.

body: Houston’s pressure removed Brooklyn’s preferred rhythm before the game had time to settle, and the Rockets turned a 28–13 first quarter into a 100–83 NBA Summer League win at Cox Pavilion. The result moved Houston to 3–1 and Brooklyn to 2–2, leaving the Nets outside the four-team semi-final field after their four scheduled preliminary games.

The opening period created the decisive separation. Houston made Brooklyn work to initiate possessions, then punished the resulting empty trips with a balanced half-court attack. The teams split the second quarter 21–21, but the Nets still trailed 49–34 at half-time. Houston won the third 29–23 before Brooklyn took the fourth 26–22, a late improvement that reduced the margin without changing the competitive shape of the night.

Ben Saraf played 16 minutes and 26 seconds off the bench and finished with two points, one assist and two steals. He missed all three field-goal attempts, including one from three-point range, and made one of two free throws. Two turnovers and a minus-15 rating completed a difficult offensive line, although the steals reflected the defensive activity he maintained while his shot and creation stalled.

Danny Wolf started at forward and recorded four points, eight rebounds, two assists, one steal and two blocks in 18 minutes and 35 seconds. Six of his eight rebounds came at the defensive end, but five turnovers and five personal fouls limited the value of that work. Wolf made one of three shots from the floor and one of three free throws, ending at minus-15 alongside Saraf.

Brooklyn’s broader shooting problem was more damaging than either Israeli’s individual total. The Nets made 25 of 71 attempts for 35.2 percent and converted only nine of 38 three-pointers, a 23.7 percent return. Houston shot 43.1 percent overall and 45.8 percent from deep, making two more threes on 14 fewer attempts. The Rockets also won the rebounding count 41–32, giving their stronger perimeter efficiency a second-possession cushion.

Bruce Thornton led Houston with 23 points on seven-of-13 shooting, while Tristen Newton added 20 points and six rebounds in 21:32. Egor Dëmin carried Brooklyn with 21 points and five made threes, and Mikel Brown Jr. scored 14. Those returns kept the Nets moving after the opening blow, but they could not overcome a starting group that shot 33.3 percent and produced 53 points across its combined minutes.

Brooklyn did create disruption of its own. The Nets registered 15 steals and eight blocks, both higher than Houston’s totals, and committed two fewer turnovers as a team. The problem was conversion: defensive events did not become enough efficient offence, while Houston repeatedly answered with cleaner shooting. For Saraf and Wolf, the final preliminary game supplied a sharp contrast with Tuesday’s 115–83 win over Sacramento and a clearer measure of the physical and decision-making pressure their next development phase must absorb.

The official game record lists Kastine Evans, Austin Spiker and Monnazjea Finney-Smithy as the three officials. Cox Pavilion in Las Vegas staged the contest; no spectator figure was published. Brooklyn will now move into its final placement game, while Houston’s 3–1 record keeps the Rockets in the wider Summer League qualification picture.

body: Israel's under-20 men removed every trace of relegation anxiety with an 84–59 win over Italy in Ljubljana, securing their place in the top division of the European championship. Oren Aharoni's team took control during the second quarter and kept widening the gap after half-time, producing its most complete response to Wednesday's round-of-16 defeat by Greece.

Italy led 16–15 late in the opening period, but Israel closed the quarter 21–16 and never allowed the game to return to a one-possession contest. The second quarter went 18–16 to Israel for a 39–32 half-time lead. A 20–11 third period then broke the contest open before a 25-point Israeli fourth quarter completed a victory by the night's largest margin of 25.

Yonatan Keller led the scoring with 19 points, while Oren Sahar added 18 and finished with the game's highest efficiency rating at 23. Four Israeli players reached double figures. That spread mattered as much as the leading totals: Italy could not load its defence towards one creator, and Israel maintained pace and pressure through its rotations instead of relying on a single late shot-maker.

The shooting comparison explains why the margin kept moving. Israel made 40 percent of its field-goal attempts against Italy's 31 percent, converted 46.8 percent inside the arc and hit 30 percent from three. Italy managed 37.2 percent on two-pointers and only 16.7 percent from long range. Israel also converted 81.3 percent at the line, protecting the advantage whenever the game stopped.

Control was almost continuous once Israel moved ahead. The official lead tracker records only one lead change, with Israel in front for 37 minutes and 16 seconds and Italy leading for 1:36. Israel's biggest advantage reached 28 points. Those numbers describe a game governed from the front rather than a late escape, a significant distinction after the 79–66 loss to Greece had ended the medal route one night earlier.

The result also settled the tournament's most urgent competitive question. The classification bracket is not cosmetic at this age level: finishing in the bottom positions carries relegation to Division B. By winning the first 9–16 classification game, Israel guaranteed that its next generation will retain access to the highest European level in 2027, while the remaining fixtures will determine its final place from ninth to twelfth.

Arena Stožice II hosted a crowd of 100, with Yener Yilmaz, Lukasz Jankowski and Sinisa Prpa officiating. The modest setting did not reduce the pressure. Israel arrived with less than a day to reset its target, then played with clearer spacing, stronger shot selection and the defensive concentration required to hold Italy to 43 points across the final three quarters. Safety was the minimum objective; the manner of the win restored some authority to the campaign.

body: Maccabi Haifa have reached an agreement with United States striker Andrija Novakovich, adding a proven central-forward profile to Diego Flores's rebuild. The club said the 29-year-old is expected in Israel next week for medical examinations. That condition is decisive: Haifa have an agreement, not a completed registration, and the player should not be described as signed until the medical process is finished.

Novakovich arrives from Italy after a season in Serie B in which he made 33 league appearances and scored five goals. At 1.92 metres, he offers a reference point between centre-backs and a target for deliveries into the penalty area. He has also spent enough of his career working outside the United States to understand the tactical demands of European club football rather than arriving as a development project.

The move changes the shape of Haifa's forward search. Flores has wanted a striker capable of fixing defenders centrally while the wide players attack the spaces around him. Novakovich's frame can help the team play through direct passes when a high press closes the first build-up route, but his value cannot be measured only through aerial duels. Haifa also need clean lay-offs, penalty-area occupation and repeat movement across the front line.

Five goals in 33 league matches is not a guarantee of a high-volume scorer. It is a recent record that requires context. A striker's output depends on minutes, chance quality and role, and Haifa will need to build a service structure that brings him closer to goal. If he spends too much of each match receiving with his back to goal far from the box, the physical profile will solve progression problems without necessarily solving finishing.

The medical requirement deserves more than routine wording. Until the examinations are completed, the club retain the ability to evaluate fitness and the parties have not crossed the final administrative threshold. Presenting the agreement as a finished transfer would erase the exact contingency Haifa placed in their announcement. The next confirmed step is his arrival; a contract announcement should follow only if the checks are satisfactory.

For Haifa, the timing is useful. The domestic cup phase begins later in July, giving the staff a narrow window to integrate a new number nine before the league programme settles. Training work will need to cover pressing triggers as well as attacking patterns. A tall striker can make a team more direct, but Flores will want that outlet connected to the midfield rather than isolated above it.

Novakovich therefore represents a clear roster decision without yet being a completed one. Haifa have selected size, experience and penalty-area presence for the next stage of their reconstruction. The medical will determine whether that plan becomes a signing; the football afterwards will determine whether the team can turn those traits into more reliable chance creation.

title: Israel U20s answered a survival game with grown-up control
dek: The 84–59 score mattered because it preserved Division A status; the way Israel built it showed how quickly a youth team can reset its identity after elimination.

body: Youth tournaments are often narrated through medals and prospects, but their hardest test can arrive after both have moved out of reach. Israel's 84–59 win over Italy was played in that uncomfortable space. The round-of-16 loss to Greece had ended the title route less than 24 hours earlier. The next assignment offered no podium and little glamour, only the institutional consequence of remaining in Division A. Israel responded with the most adult performance of its week.

The first sign was not a spectacular run but the absence of emotional waste. Italy edged ahead during the opening quarter, yet Israel closed it 21–16 without allowing Wednesday's disappointment to become Thursday's tension. The lead grew to seven by half-time, 16 after the third quarter and 25 at the finish. A young team that had lost its primary objective found a secondary one and treated it as non-negotiable.

Control appears in the official data. Israel led for 37 minutes and 16 seconds, Italy for only 1:36, and the lead changed once. The largest margin reached 28. Those numbers do not describe a loose classification game decided by a hot final minute. They describe a side that established where the contest would be played and kept it there through rotations, stoppages and the inevitable periods when the first action failed.

The scoring distribution was equally important. Yonatan Keller produced 19 points, Oren Sahar added 18 and four players finished in double figures. In a survival game, that matters tactically and psychologically. Italy could not solve the attack by taking away one guard, while Israel did not need one player to carry the emotional burden of repairing the tournament. The possession belonged to the group before it belonged to the scorer.

Israel's shot profile gave that collective work a measurable advantage. The team converted 46.8 percent of its two-pointers, 30 percent of its threes and 81.3 percent of its free throws. None of those figures alone is extraordinary. Together they formed an efficient floor: enough pressure near the rim to force decisions, enough perimeter accuracy to punish collapsed coverage, and enough composure at the line to prevent Italy from buying its way back with fouls.

The defensive side created the separation. Italy made 31 percent from the field and only 16.7 percent from beyond the arc. Poor opponent shooting can contain variance, but the quarter pattern suggests more than luck. Italy scored 16 in the first, 16 in the second, 11 in the third and 16 in the fourth. Israel did not merely survive one cold Italian stretch; it kept the champions of 2025 below a functional offensive level across the entire night.

This does not erase the Greece defeat or convert a classification victory into a medal. Good development programmes should resist that kind of emotional accounting. The failure to reach the quarter-finals remains part of the evaluation, including how Israel handled Greece's defensive pace and why its own shooting never found a stable rhythm. The Italy response is valuable precisely because it sits beside that failure rather than pretending to replace it.

Division A status is not a bureaucratic consolation. It preserves the level of opposition available to the next under-20 generation, keeps Israel inside the top championship bracket and protects a pathway that produced consecutive European titles in 2018 and 2019. Relegation would not have destroyed the system, but it would have reduced the competitive environment through which the next group must travel. Thursday's players secured that opportunity for athletes who were not on the floor with them.

Oren Aharoni and his staff should therefore take the result as evidence of a culture under pressure, not a verdict that every basketball problem is solved. The team still has classification games to play and a full tournament to analyse. Yet the response revealed something selection camps and warm-up matches cannot manufacture: how quickly players can accept a changed reality, narrow their focus and execute when the reward is responsibility rather than celebration.

That is the winning touch worth carrying forward. Keller's points and Sahar's efficiency will sit in the box score, but the larger achievement was structural. Israel defended without chasing redemption on every possession, shared the scoring and increased the margin quarter by quarter. A youth side had one night to move from disappointment to duty. It did so with the calm of a team that understood exactly what was at stake.

title: 2018–19: the two summers that changed Israeli youth basketball
dek: Israel's first FIBA title in Chemnitz was followed by a home defence in Tel Aviv, turning a breakthrough generation into the benchmark for every U20 team that followed.

source.name: FIBA
source.originalTitle: Israel claim historic title at FIBA U20 European Championship

verificationSources.label: FIBA official 2018 final report
FIBA official 2019 final report
FIBA official 2019 tournament record and standings
FIBA official record of Israel's 2017 silver medal

body: Israel's under-20 championship story did not begin with gold. In 2017, the team reached the European final in Crete and lost 65–56 to host Greece before a sold-out crowd. Tamir Blatt made the All-Star Five, but the silver medal left a generation with evidence that the summit was reachable and a clear account of the final step it had failed to take.

One year later in Chemnitz, Israel completed that step. The tournament opened with a defeat by host Germany, then turned into a six-game winning run. France were beaten 83–57 in the semi-final, and previously undefeated Croatia waited in the final. Israel led 45–34 at half-time, absorbed the pressure after the break and won 80–66. It was the country's first gold medal in any FIBA competition.

Yovel Zoosman supplied the defining senior performance of the 2018 final: 17 points, 11 rebounds, four assists and four steals. Captain Gil Beni also scored 17, while Miron Ruina added 14 points and 14 rebounds. The spread was important. This was not one prodigy dragging a youth team through a final; it was a connected guard-led group turning defence, rebounding and shared decisions into a title.

Zoosman was named tournament MVP after averaging 14.4 points, 4.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 2.3 steals. Beside him in the All-Star Five was Deni Avdija, only 17 and the youngest player at the tournament. That combination captured the system's immediate strength: players ready to win at their own age and an exceptional younger talent already capable of influencing matches against older opponents.

The defence of the title in 2019 carried a different pressure. Israel hosted the championship, expectations had replaced surprise and Shlomo Arena sold out for the final in five minutes. FIBA recorded 3,500 spectators inside and more than 20,000 people on the waiting list. Spain arrived with the depth and technical quality to test whether the first gold had been a peak or the start of a standard.

The final was tied 42–42 at half-time. Spain opened the third quarter with four consecutive three-pointers, the kind of burst that can turn a home crowd from force into weight. Israel did not fracture. The hosts scored 50 second-half points and won 92–84, becoming only the second team at that time to defend the U20 European title after Serbia's 2007 and 2008 teams.

Avdija and Yam Madar shaped that victory. Avdija finished with 23 points, seven assists, five rebounds and four blocks; Madar added 17 points on 7-of-11 shooting and eight assists. Tomer Porat scored 11, while Raz Adam and Eidan Alber combined for 20. Israel shot 52 percent in the final. The trophy was retained through star quality, but the supporting scores again stopped the opponent from reducing the game to one matchup.

Avdija's tournament numbers explain why the 2019 title became part of a larger basketball story. He averaged 18.4 points, 8.3 rebounds, 5.3 assists, 2.4 blocks and 2.1 steals and was named MVP. Madar joined him in the All-Star Five. Both would move into major professional roles, but the historical achievement belongs to the complete group and to coach Ariel Beit Halahmy's ability to join talent with a coherent tournament team.

Back-to-back titles changed the reference point for Israeli youth basketball. Before Chemnitz, a medal run could be described as an exceptional breakthrough. After Tel Aviv, every strong generation inherited proof that Israel could win at this level, recover inside a final and defend a championship under home expectation. That proof is empowering, but it can also make later teams seem disappointing when development follows a less spectacular route.

The better legacy is not a demand that every under-20 side reproduce gold. It is the pathway those summers made visible: play elite opposition, give young guards responsibility, defend collectively and treat a youth championship as both a competition and an education. The 2026 team's Division A survival win over Italy belongs much lower in the medal hierarchy, yet preserving top-level status protects the environment from which another Zoosman, Avdija or Madar generation might eventually emerge.

body: Hapoel Jerusalem’s attempt to refresh their basketball identity has met immediate resistance, with a supporter petition against changing the club badge reaching about 1,300 signatures. Season-ticket holders received alternative designs during a wider rebranding process, turning what might have remained a marketing exercise into a public argument about who has authority over a club’s most recognisable symbol.

The process has already changed once. A branding company produced an initial design that was expected to form part of a larger presentation of the club’s plans, but that event was postponed and the first proposal did not advance. Revised alternatives were then circulated to season-ticket holders. No replacement badge has been adopted, so the current position is consultation under pressure rather than a completed identity change.

The speed of the response gives the dispute its weight. An initial count put the petition above 1,200 signatures within roughly two hours; a later update placed it at about 1,300. Those figures do not prove that every supporter opposes a redesign, and they should not be presented as a formal referendum. They do show that a substantial organised group considers continuity more important than the club expected.

A badge is unusually difficult brand property because it works in two directions. Management use it across tickets, merchandise, digital products and sponsorship inventory. Supporters carry it across generations, often long before the current owner, executive team or design agency arrives. The legal control may sit with the organisation, but the emotional ownership is distributed through the community.

That tension is sharper because Hapoel have made supporter reconnection a stated strategic goal. In January, chief executive Oren Arieli described returning fans to the Arena, improving transparency and listening more systematically as central parts of the club’s long-term plan. The new 2026/27 season-ticket model was also presented as a supporter-centred project designed to reward loyalty and attract families back.

Rebranding can still serve a legitimate purpose. A clearer mark can work better on small screens, simplify merchandise and give commercial partners a consistent system. But design efficiency is not the only measure of success for a sports badge. If the process weakens trust among the very people the club wants to bring home, a technically stronger logo can become a strategically weaker asset.

Hapoel now have several defensible routes: retain the existing badge, modify one alternative or continue consultation before selecting a new mark. The strongest next step would be to explain the problem the redesign is meant to solve and publish how supporter feedback will affect the decision. Until the club chooses and announces a final badge, the alternatives remain proposals and the petition remains a warning rather than a verdict.

body: Ironi Ness Ziona have signed Paris Lee on a two-year contract, placing one of the Israeli league’s most experienced new guards at the centre of their rebuild. Three reports carry the completed move and contract length, while the 31-year-old arrives directly from a season with UNICS Kazan. This is not a developmental lottery ticket: Ness Ziona are buying decision-making, ball pressure and a large body of elite European work.

EuroLeague’s official record lists Lee as a 1.84-metre guard with 128 appearances across Monaco, Panathinaikos and ASVEL between 2021 and 2025. He started 77 of those games and averaged 9.5 points, 3.7 assists and 1.3 steals. The numbers describe a lead guard who has repeatedly handled possession against switching defences and aggressive pick-and-roll coverage rather than a scorer being asked to learn the position.

His most distinctive strength is at the other end. Lee led the 2023/24 EuroLeague with 1.7 steals per game, an official competition marker that fits Ness Ziona’s need for a guard capable of changing tempo without waiting for a defensive rebound. Steals alone are not a defensive system, but his ability to disrupt the first pass can create the open-floor possessions that make an athletic roster easier to organise.

UNICS provide the immediate career context. The Russian club’s official profile records Lee with the 2025/26 team and identifies him as a VTB United League and WINLINE Basket Cup runner-up. Moving from that environment to Ness Ziona changes both role and expectation: he should receive more control of the offence, but he will also carry greater responsibility for late-clock choices and the development of the guards around him.

The tactical fit begins with pace under control. Lee can advance the ball quickly, attack a high screen and still pull the possession back when the first advantage disappears. Ness Ziona need that judgement as much as his individual production. A roster with new pieces can look fast while actually playing rushed; the point guard’s job is to distinguish an early opportunity from an early mistake.

body: Tiemoko Diarra has signed for Kasımpaşa, closing the route that had appeared set to return him to Israeli football with Hapoel Tel Aviv. The Istanbul club announced the transfer from Stade de Reims and published the signing at its Kemerburgaz facilities. Its statement named chief executive Ceyhun Kazancı as present but did not specify the length of the contract, so no term should be inferred from the announcement.

Hapoel’s failed move was more advanced than casual interest. Three accounts agree that the Tel Aviv club had reached a club-to-club understanding with Reims before the negotiation stalled over the player’s personal terms. Two of those reports put the proposed fee at €1.7 million with a 20 per cent share of a future sale. Those financial details were not announced by either club and therefore remain reported terms, not a published contract.

That distinction explains the apparent reversal. Agreement between buying and selling clubs can open a transfer, but it cannot complete one without the player accepting employment terms and passing the remaining registration steps. Hapoel had a route to Diarra’s rights; it did not have Diarra’s signature. Kasımpaşa now do, and their official post is the decisive record of his destination.

The 23-year-old was an attractive Israeli-market target because his adaptation risk was unusually low. Diarra previously played for Hapoel Haifa, and the two detailed accounts of the current move agree on a return of six goals and four assists in 32 appearances during that spell. He can attack from wide positions, threaten the space behind a full-back and carry the ball through a transition—qualities Hapoel Tel Aviv still need to source elsewhere.

Kasımpaşa offer a different competitive context. The club’s own table records a 13th-place finish in the 2025/26 Turkish top flight. That is not European qualification or a protected elite role, but it keeps Diarra in a strong league and gives him a fresh route to senior minutes after his Reims period. His familiarity with Israeli football may have strengthened Hapoel’s case; it did not outweigh the package he accepted in Istanbul.

For Hapoel, the useful lesson is not simply that a target chose another club. A proposed transfer of this size consumes planning time, an international-player slot and a meaningful part of the recruitment budget before it is completed. When personal terms remain open, the sporting department must keep a parallel shortlist alive rather than treating the club agreement as the finish line.

The collapse also changes the way any replacement should be judged. Matching Diarra’s reputation is less important than replacing the functions the squad expected him to provide: direct running, one-against-one threat and a credible scoring contribution from the flank. A central creator or possession winger would be a different signing even if the market value looked similar.

There is no longer uncertainty about where Diarra will begin the season. Kasımpaşa have made the transfer public and put him under contract. The unresolved question belongs to Hapoel Tel Aviv: whether the work already invested in this deal can be converted quickly into a player who fits the same tactical need, without paying a premium for losing the first choice late in the process.

dek: The 2001 Portuguese champions must vacate their stadium by 31 July after missing a monthly creditor payment, the latest step in a collapse split across club and football company.

body: Boavista have been ordered to cease the activities operated by the insolvent club at the Estádio do Bessa, with the Porto institution required to clear its stadium and adjoining premises by 31 July. The insolvency administrator executed the creditors’ closure decision after a monthly payment of €55,000 was missed, turning a long financial retreat into an operational shutdown.

The order reaches beyond a senior football result or a licensing penalty. It covers the activities run by Boavista Futebol Clube at the Bessa complex, including the club’s other sports and development structures. Staff and teams may use the short period before the handover to remove personal property and wind down operations, but the direction of travel is unambiguous: the facilities are to be delivered free of people and assets at the end of the month.

Legal precision matters because ‘Boavista’ contains more than one insolvent body. The member club and the SAD that ran professional football follow connected but distinct processes. A commercial court ordered the SAD into liquidation in May after its recovery plan was withdrawn from a creditor vote. This week’s instruction concerns the club establishment and its activities at the stadium. It is not, by itself, a single document dissolving every Boavista legal entity on the day of publication.

The separation has not protected either side from the same financial gravity. Public reporting places accumulated debts above €150 million. The club was declared insolvent in 2025 and kept operating only under conditions set by creditors, including recurring payments to cover current costs. Missing the latest instalment activated a mechanism that had been postponed before, rather than creating a new crisis from an otherwise stable position.

That history explains why the shutdown is more consequential than another relegation. Boavista broke Portugal’s three-club title grip by winning the league in 2000/01. Two years later they reached the UEFA Cup semi-finals, drawing 1–1 away to Celtic before Henrik Larsson’s late goal at the Bessa denied them a place in the final. UEFA’s record also shows a European campaign in which Boavista eliminated Málaga and won every home match before that semi-final defeat.

The Bessa was the physical expression of that status. Rebuilt around Euro 2004, it staged Champions League football and housed the club’s administrative, sporting and commercial functions. Its loss therefore removes more than a pitch from the balance sheet. A club can replace a training base or rent a ground; rebuilding the daily network that connects academy teams, other sports, staff and members is a different task, especially when liquidation is already consuming the institution’s assets.

A recovery attempt is still conceptually possible through new investment, creditor agreement or a reconstructed sporting organisation. None should be reported as secured. The current legal act is the closure order, the missed payment and the deadline to surrender the premises. Dissolution and the future ownership of Boavista’s sporting identity remain subsequent questions, not completed facts that can be inferred from the administrator’s instruction.

Portuguese football has seen historic clubs fall through divisions, enter insolvency and reappear in altered form. Boavista’s position is harsher because the member institution, the professional company and the stadium have all become part of overlapping financial failures. The club that once made the Bessa one of Europe’s most difficult away grounds now has two weeks to leave it. Any credible rescue must begin by explaining which Boavista it is saving, what liabilities survive and where its teams would actually play.

body: Israel’s men’s under-20 handball team lost 33–31 to the Faroe Islands in the M20 EHF EURO cross match for places 9–16, surrendering a two-goal halftime lead but keeping their route to the 2027 IHF Men’s Junior World Championship alive. The official tournament record confirms the final score and the 17–15 interval advantage for Israel.

The arithmetic of the two halves describes the reversal without requiring embellishment. Israel scored 17 before the break and 14 after it; the Faroe Islands moved from 15 goals in the first half to 18 in the second. A four-goal swing over 30 minutes turned a controlled position into a narrow defeat, with the match still close enough that neither team was able to build a decisive cushion.

Israel arrived in the placement phase after a volatile preliminary group in Romania. They beat Bosnia and Herzegovina 43–33 but lost 42–33 to Sweden and 39–31 to the hosts. Israel, Romania and Bosnia finished in a three-way tie behind Sweden; Romania advanced to the main round on goal difference, while Israel continued through the intermediate route.

That distinction shaped Thursday’s stakes. The Faroe Islands had reached the main round and were therefore already inside the tournament’s leading group, while Israel entered the 9–16 cross matches from the intermediate phase. The Faroese win moves them toward the places 9–12 games. Israel now enter the places 13–16 path, where the final ranking carries a consequence larger than the position itself.

The IHF set the qualification line for the 2027 Men’s Junior World Championship at 15th place. Twelve European teams secured their tickets by reaching the M20 EURO main round, leaving three places to be settled lower in the ranking bracket. For Israel, one win across the remaining placement sequence would guarantee a finish no lower than 15th and claim one of those last European berths.

That makes the Faroe defeat painful rather than terminal. Israel no longer have margin to treat the next match as another development fixture: a victory would complete the qualification job, while another loss would push the decision into the final contest for 15th. The team have already shown they can produce sustained attacking stretches at this level; Thursday’s second half exposed how quickly a small defensive decline can consume that work.

The broader value of qualification is competitive continuity. This group would move from a demanding European championship directly toward another global age-grade tournament, adding high-level matches at the point when many players begin competing for larger senior roles. The immediate task is much narrower: protect the defensive standard that built the 17–15 lead, find enough second-half scoring to avoid another late squeeze and turn one of the next two opportunities into a World Championship place.

title: World Cup final seats reach $8,680 in Spain's allocation
dek: Official prices expose a dramatic split between a tightly limited $60 supporter tier and the four-figure cost of most federation-allocation seats for Argentina against Spain.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv
source.originalTitle: שחקן נבחרת ספרד ניסה להשיג כרטיס לגמר המונדיאל. התשובה היממה אותו

body: A seat in Spain's official federation allocation for Sunday's World Cup final can cost as much as $8,680. The published table for the Argentina–Spain showpiece sets premium tickets at that figure, standard seats at $5,575 and the value category at $4,185. Those are face values in US dollars, not resale-market mark-ups, and they place even the lowest of the three main categories far beyond an ordinary matchday purchase.

The allocation mechanism makes the price debate more complicated than one extraordinary number. Participating federations receive eight per cent of the net saleable capacity for each of their matches. Spain invited supporters to request knockout tickets before knowing whether the team would reach those rounds, with refunds promised if elimination made a booking unusable. Once a team qualified for a given knockout match, the Spanish federation said there would be no additional opportunity to buy from that allocation.

FIFA later created a sharply different entry point. Its Supporter Entry Tier fixes a limited share of tickets at $60 for every match, including the final. Ten per cent of each participating association's allocation sits in that tier, with the national federation setting its own eligibility and distribution rules. FIFA says another 40 per cent of the association allocation belongs to the Supporter Value Tier, leaving the remaining half divided equally between Standard and Premier categories.

The $60 offer is therefore real, but it does not turn the final into a broadly affordable event. It creates a narrow protected route inside an allocation whose other published prices rise into four figures. Demand determines how many eligible supporters actually secure that route. For everyone outside it, the official price table demonstrates that face value alone can resemble the cost of a major holiday before flights, accommodation and local travel are added.

This structure reflects FIFA's wider pricing policy. The governing body says it can adapt prices between sales phases after reviewing demand and availability, although it distinguishes that process from automatic dynamic pricing. Its stated objectives are to optimise revenue and maximise attendance. At a final with two global teams and extreme demand, those objectives pull against the traditional idea that a meaningful share of the stadium should remain financially accessible to the supporters who followed the teams there.

Argentina and Spain meet at New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday after contrasting semi-finals. The defending champions recovered from Anthony Gordon's goal to beat England 2–1, while Spain controlled France in a 2–0 victory. The final offers Lionel Messi the chance to retain the trophy and Spain the opportunity to win their second men's world title. It is precisely the kind of sporting occasion for which demand will overwhelm any affordable supply.

The central issue is consequently not whether a $60 ticket exists or whether an $8,680 ticket can find a buyer. Both can be true. The question is how much of the stadium is genuinely reachable at each price and how clearly that distribution is communicated. A final presented as a global public event now operates through radically different access lanes: a small protected supporter tier, expensive federation categories and a wider market shaped by scarcity. The football will decide the champion; the ticket map has already decided who can afford to watch from inside.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv have brought RTMI into the football club's senior commercial roster on a two-year agreement. The club confirmed the finance company as a principal sponsor on Thursday, extending a relationship already visible elsewhere in the wider Hapoel sporting family. RTMI's mark will sit on the sleeves of the first team's match shirts and on advertising boards at Bloomfield Stadium.

The placement is important. Sleeve inventory travels with the team in every televised match and survives in photographs long after perimeter advertising has left the frame. It gives RTMI a constant association with Hapoel's playing identity without replacing the club's front-of-shirt position. Bloomfield signage adds a second layer aimed at spectators, hospitality guests and broadcast audiences during home fixtures.

This is not a sponsor entering the Hapoel ecosystem without a working history. RTMI backed the men's basketball club in 2024/25 and renewed that agreement for 2025/26; the basketball club described the extension as worth NIS 1 million for the season. The company also became the principal sponsor of Hapoel Tel Aviv's senior women's basketball team in November 2025. Football therefore represents an expansion of an existing relationship, not a cold acquisition of red-and-white visibility.

That distinction gives the agreement more strategic weight than its physical logo positions alone suggest. Multi-team partnerships can let a sponsor speak to one supporter community across different competitions and seasons, while the clubs gain a partner already familiar with the culture and expectations around the name. The risk is over-commercialisation: Hapoel's value to partners rests heavily on supporter identity, so every additional mark has to feel integrated rather than rented.

RTMI owner Stav Shaham supplies a personal link. He previously owned Hapoel Kfar Saba and has been publicly involved with Hapoel Tel Aviv basketball as a sponsor and board member. In the football club's announcement, Shaham framed the move as the next stage of a longer commitment to Hapoel rather than an isolated campaign. Hapoel chief executive Guy Primor and commercial director Harel Cohen presented the agreement as part of the club's attempt to deepen its business network.

For Hapoel, a two-season term offers more than a one-off injection. Commercial departments can plan activations, hospitality and supporter-facing work across a full cycle instead of renegotiating after a few months. It also gives the club time to judge whether the basketball-to-football crossover produces measurable value rather than only launch-day attention.

The first public test will be ordinary matchday exposure. Supporters will see the new mark on the players' sleeves; television viewers will meet it both there and around the pitch at Bloomfield. Sponsorships are often announced in abstract language, but this one has unusually concrete touchpoints. Its success will depend on whether Hapoel and RTMI turn those visible positions into a partnership that supporters recognise beyond the logo.

body: Maccabi Haifa have made memory part of their 2026/27 uniform. The club unveiled a green-and-white home shirt on Thursday that deliberately returns to the visual language of the 1990/91 team, marking 35 years since Haifa completed the league-and-cup double. It is a heritage reference, but not a reproduction: the new shirt places the old palette and texture inside a contemporary Adidas template.

The design is built around green with white detailing and a patterned surface intended to recall the double-winning strip. That distinction matters. A literal retro remake would belong mainly to the merchandise business; this is supposed to function as the first team's current competitive identity. The launch therefore asks the shirt to do two jobs at once — recognise a formative side in the club's history and remain legible as the uniform of the present squad.

The history is substantial enough to support the choice. Maccabi's official record lists 22 wins, five draws and five defeats across 32 league matches in 1990/91, with 56 goals scored and 28 conceded. The championship was paired with the State Cup to secure the double. Those numbers explain why the season survives as more than a styling reference: it represents a team that combined consistency over a full campaign with success in the knockout competition.

The launch also carries a longer commercial commitment. Maccabi Haifa and Adidas have extended their agreement through 2031, giving the club continuity with its kit supplier well beyond the coming season. The accompanying announcement presents the new home shirt as a bespoke design for Haifa rather than a standard catalogue model. For a club using its own history as the creative brief, that degree of separation is central to the proposition.

The reveal film reinforces the connection between generations. Reuven Atar, one of the figures associated with the double-winning era, appears alongside other former players and members of the current squad. That casting avoids treating 1991 as a museum exhibit. The older team supplies the emotional reference; today's players have to make the shirt recognisable on the pitch rather than only in a campaign.

There is a broader sporting logic behind such launches. A home shirt is one of the few club assets seen simultaneously in the stadium, on broadcasts and across international retail. Maccabi have chosen a design that can be identified with Haifa before a sponsor mark or player name is read. The commercial value lies in that recognition, but it works only when supporters regard the historical connection as credible rather than decorative.

The new strip arrives shortly before competitive football resumes. Maccabi Haifa's official schedule lists a Toto Cup derby against Hapoel Haifa at Sammy Ofer on 25 July as the first fixture of the season. The shirt will then leave the controlled setting of its launch and enter the only test that ultimately fixes a kit in club memory: the matches, players and results attached to it.

title: Sharp scores 12 as Kings fall to Celtics in Summer League
dek: The Israeli guard added two steals without a turnover but shot 4-of-13 in Sacramento's 82–76 loss, two days after scoring 23 against Brooklyn.

body: Emanuel Sharp followed the most productive game of his first NBA Summer League with a more uneven but still instructive performance on Wednesday. The Israeli guard scored 12 points in 19 minutes and 48 seconds, adding two steals and committing no turnovers as the Sacramento Kings lost 82–76 to the Boston Celtics. His defensive activity and ball security survived a difficult shooting night; his jumper did not.

Sharp finished 4-of-13 from the field and 2-of-8 from three-point range. That line matters because Sacramento used him less as a pure spot-up shooter than the box score from his previous appearance might suggest. He had to create against a set defence, attack late-clock space and make decisions after Boston forced the ball away from its initial action. The result was a heavier diet of contested attempts and fewer clean releases.

There was compensation at the other end. Sharp recorded two steals, did not turn the ball over and committed five fouls while trying to disrupt Boston's guards. Summer League is designed to expose precisely these trade-offs: a scorer can miss nine shots and still strengthen his case if the possession quality remains defensible, the next decision is sound and the defensive effort does not disappear with the rhythm of his jumper.

Boston controlled the game through Hugo González, who supplied 24 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in 33 minutes. The Celtics outscored Sacramento by 11 points during his time on the floor. Sharp's minus-10 therefore reflected a stretch in which the Kings struggled to contain the game's most influential player as much as it described his own offensive inefficiency.

The performance also looks different beside what Sharp had done two days earlier. Against Brooklyn he scored 23 points on 7-of-12 shooting, made six three-pointers, collected three rebounds and generated four steals. Repeating that production was always unlikely. The useful development for Sacramento was that the less glamorous parts of his game — pressure, anticipation and care with the ball — remained visible when the shots stopped falling.

Sacramento selected Sharp with the 45th pick in last month's draft after his college career at Houston. That status does not guarantee an immediate rotation role. Second-round guards often have to prove they can defend more than one backcourt position, space the floor without dominating possession and avoid mistakes in short shifts. Sharp's first two Summer League games have already shown both sides of that evaluation: explosive perimeter scoring in one, imperfect shot selection but credible defensive work in the next.

His connection to Israel is not incidental to the story. FIBA lists Sharp as representing Israel and carrying Israeli and American nationality. His route through Houston and into Sacramento gives Israeli basketball another young guard to follow in the NBA development system, but nationality alone will not move him up the depth chart. The Kings will judge whether his shooting travels, whether he can absorb physical switches and whether the zero-turnover line can become a habit rather than a single-night detail.

The Celtics defeat should therefore neither erase the Brooklyn performance nor be disguised as another breakthrough. Sharp missed too many shots, particularly from distance, and Sacramento lost. Yet a prospect's value is revealed by what remains when his strongest skill deserts him. On Wednesday, Sharp still defended aggressively, protected the ball and produced double figures in fewer than 20 minutes. That is not a finished NBA role, but it is credible evidence from which one can be built.

title: Messi's third final would measure reinvention, not just longevity
dek: Cafu's record captures extraordinary durability; Messi's route from 2014 creator to 2022 scorer and 2026 playmaker explains why Argentina can still build around him at 39.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: בדרך לשיא הבלתי אפשרי: מסי יכול להשתוות לקאפו
source.author: ONE editorial team

verificationSources.label: FIFA official record of Cafu's three World Cup final appearances
Independent confirmation of the 2026 Argentina–Spain final
Independent record of Messi's two semi-final assists

body: If Lionel Messi starts Sunday's World Cup final against Spain, he will join Cafu as only the second man to play in three men's finals. That is the clean historical fact. The more interesting story is what the comparison cannot show. Cafu's record describes an elite body and mentality surviving across three Brazilian teams; Messi's prospective equaliser describes a footballer repeatedly redesigning his influence as the speed available to him changed.

Cafu's sequence remains singular. He replaced the injured Jorginho during the 1994 final against Italy, started the 1998 defeat by France and captained Brazil to victory over Germany in 2002. The role evolved from understudy to established full-back to leader, but the essential proposition remained recognisable: relentless width, recovery running and the capacity to repeat high-intensity actions along the same touchline.

Messi's three versions are less alike. In 2014 he was still the devastating carrier around whom Argentina compressed its attack, reaching the final before Germany won in extra time. In 2022 his game contained fewer long accelerations but more control over when a match accelerated. He scored twice in the final, converted in the shootout and finally won the trophy after the 3–3 draw with France.

The 2026 version has moved further towards selection and timing. Messi enters the final with eight goals, yet the semi-final against England turned on his passing. With Argentina trailing late, he created Enzo Fernández's equaliser after a short corner and then supplied the cross from which Lautaro Martínez headed the winner. Those were his third and fourth assists of the tournament, enough to move him ahead of Kylian Mbappé on the Golden Boot tiebreak without taking a shot that changed the score.

Three final appearances can look like a single continuous achievement when presented in a record book. In reality, the intervals are the point. Twelve years separate Maracanã in 2014 from East Rutherford in 2026, long enough for opponents to replace entire generations and for the sport's pressing structures to change around him. Messi has not merely held a place while the scenery changed. He has had to find a different answer to the same question: where can his first touch still damage the best team left in the tournament?

This is where longevity becomes too passive a word. Remaining present at 39 is an achievement; remaining structurally useful is the greater one. Argentina no longer ask Messi to dominate every metre between halfway and the penalty area. They need him to recognise the five seconds when a defensive block loses shape, receive in the right lane and choose a pass before the space closes. The burden has narrowed, but its value has not.

The England comeback also showed the protection around that model. Fernández could finish from distance, Martínez could arrive from the bench to attack the decisive cross, and Argentina could survive long stretches without Messi constantly manufacturing progression. That is not evidence that he has become incidental. It is evidence that the holders have built a team capable of preserving his decisive actions rather than exhausting them.

There is a cost to that accommodation, and pretending otherwise turns analysis into tribute. Argentina must decide when Messi joins the press and when the rest of the side closes the space for him. They must create width without asking him to make repeated recovery runs, and they must still progress the ball when opponents deny the central pocket he prefers. The bargain works only while ten other roles remain coherent. England nearly broke it for 84 minutes before Argentina found two moments of clarity.

Spain will make the distinction severe. The European champions reached the final by beating France 2–0 and have the technical confidence to keep Argentina away from the ball. Messi cannot solve that problem through reputation or record accumulation. He will need teammates to recover possession, carry the game through pressure and place him where one action can matter. A third final appearance would therefore belong to the whole architecture around him as much as to the number on his back.

Cafu's three finals should not be reduced to a rung on somebody else's greatness ladder, and Messi's possible third should not become another automatic verdict in an argument that never ends. The better reading is about adaptability. Cafu made repetition historic; Messi is approaching the same landmark through transformation. Argentina's reward is not simply that their greatest player lasted. It is that he learned how to remain decisive after the game stopped allowing him to be the player he once was.

dek: The Belgian Grand Prix begins on Friday with Mercedes' drivers separated by 25 points and Ferrari arriving after winning two of the last three races.

body: Formula 1 reaches Spa-Francorchamps on Friday with a championship that suddenly looks less settled. Kimi Antonelli still leads the drivers' standings, but George Russell has reduced the gap between the Mercedes team-mates to 25 points. The Belgian Grand Prix is therefore more than the tenth round of the season: it is the first full test of how Antonelli responds after his Silverstone retirement turned a comfortable advantage into a live intra-team contest.

Silverstone altered the tone without overturning the order. Charles Leclerc won for Ferrari, Russell finished second and Lewis Hamilton completed the podium, while Antonelli failed to reach the flag. Russell did not need to beat his team-mate wheel to wheel to make the title race tighter; reliability did the work for him. Spa now asks Mercedes to manage two competing interests — maximising another strong car and allowing both drivers to pursue the same championship.

The scale of Mercedes' control remains easy to underestimate. The team won seven of the opening nine Grands Prix: Russell took Australia and Austria, while Antonelli won in China, Japan, Miami, Canada and Monaco. Ferrari interrupted that run through Hamilton in Spain and Leclerc in Britain. Two victories in the last three rounds do not erase Mercedes' advantage, but they do mean its drivers can no longer treat every strategic decision as a private duel.

Spa is a particularly revealing place to test that balance. At 7.004 kilometres it is the longest circuit on the calendar, combining the flat-out climb through Eau Rouge and Raidillon with a technical middle sector and an extended run back towards the Bus Stop chicane. Teams need enough straight-line efficiency to attack or defend on the Kemmel Straight without leaving the car exposed through the faster corners. The Ardennes weather adds another variable because conditions can differ across a lap that takes cars through several kilometres of forest.

The official programme gives teams three conventional practice sessions rather than a compressed sprint weekend. First practice starts at 11:30 local time on Friday, qualifying is scheduled for 14:00 on Saturday and the 44-lap race begins at 13:00 on Sunday. For viewers in Israel, those sessions begin one hour later: 12:30, 15:00 and 14:00 respectively. The full race distance is 308.052 kilometres.

Ferrari's recent progress changes the strategic geometry. Leclerc's Silverstone victory was his first since 2024, and Hamilton's third place put both red cars on the podium. If that pace carries into Belgium, Mercedes cannot simply separate Antonelli and Russell with conservative tyre calls and collect the largest points total available. A credible Ferrari challenge creates undercut risks, forces quicker decisions and makes any preference between the two title contenders more visible.

Antonelli remains in the stronger position because 25 points is the value of a Grand Prix victory. Russell, however, arrives with momentum and the knowledge that one retirement has already transformed the standings. Spa will not decide a championship with twelve rounds still to follow after Sunday, but it can reveal something just as important: whether Mercedes' season is still being controlled from the front, or has become a fight its two drivers must now manage in public.

title: Messi takes Golden Boot lead without scoring after two-assist semi-final
dek: Argentina's captain and Kylian Mbappé remain level on eight goals, but Messi's four assists now give him the first tiebreak with one match left for each player.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: מבלי לכבוש: למה מסי עלה לפסגת נעל הזהב?
source.author: Sport5 editorial team
