body: Lionel Messi moved ahead of Kylian Mbappé in the 2026 World Cup Golden Boot race without adding to his eight goals. The change came through creation rather than finishing: Messi supplied both Argentina goals in the 2–1 semi-final comeback against England, lifting his tournament total to four assists and giving him the first tiebreak over Mbappé, who has three.

The award is decided first by goals. Only when players finish level does the assist count separate them, which is why the leadership changed even though neither contender scored in his semi-final. Messi and Mbappé remain tied on eight goals; the relevant difference is now four assists to three. It is a lead, not a secured trophy, because both have one match left.

Messi's first decisive pass arrived in the 85th minute after Argentina worked a quick corner. He carried the ball in from the right and found Enzo Fernández outside the area, from where the midfielder beat Jordan Pickford. Seven minutes later Messi delivered from the right again, this time crossing for substitute Lautaro Martínez to head the winner.

Those two actions changed three competitions at once. They overturned England's lead, placed Argentina in Sunday's final against Spain and moved Messi above the defending Golden Boot winner. The sequence also illustrates the peculiarity of an individual scoring award that can turn on passing: the player at the top did not score, yet directly created both goals that kept his team alive.

Mbappé still has a route back. France face England in Saturday's third-place match in Miami Gardens, and goals in that fixture count towards the tournament totals. If Mbappé scores and Messi does not in the final, the French captain would move ahead on goals. If they add the same number of goals, Messi's current assist advantage remains relevant unless Mbappé also changes that column.

Messi's opportunity comes a day later against Spain in East Rutherford. Argentina do not need him to chase the award at the expense of the match: another assist is as useful to the team as a goal and would also strengthen his tiebreak position. That alignment matters in a final, where forcing low-percentage shots for an individual prize would be tactically self-defeating.

Mbappé won the 2022 Golden Boot with eight goals, one more than Messi, after scoring a hat-trick in the final. Four years later both have already reached Mbappé's winning total from Qatar. The expanded tournament has created more matches and more scoring opportunities, but the last decision still rests on two elite attackers producing under the very different pressure of a placement match and a final.

For now, the table says Messi leads: eight goals, four assists, one final remaining. Mbappé follows with eight goals, three assists and the third-place game still to play. The simple headline is that Messi went top without scoring. The more useful explanation is that his passing altered the semifinal so decisively that it also altered the tournament's leading-scorer race. The final weekend will decide whether that narrow edge survives.

body: Britain has asked FIFA to investigate the political banner displayed by Argentina's players after their 2–1 World Cup semi-final victory over England. The intervention moves the episode beyond a provocative celebration: the governing body now faces a formal call to decide whether the message breached its prohibition on political and ideological messaging inside stadiums.

The banner read 'Las Malvinas son Argentinas' — 'The Malvinas are Argentine' — and appeared on the field in Atlanta after Lautaro Martínez's added-time winner had sent the defending champions into Sunday's final against Spain. Giovanni Lo Celso was among the group holding it. The players therefore attached a territorial claim directly to the victory image from one of the tournament's most watched matches.

Prime Minister Keir Starmer's office backed the request for FIFA scrutiny. The British government restated its position that the future of the islands, known in Britain as the Falklands and in Argentina as the Islas Malvinas, rests with the islanders. Business Secretary Peter Kyle described the players' conduct as inappropriate. FIFA had not announced a disciplinary finding when this report was updated, so an investigation or sanction should not be treated as complete.

Argentina's president, Javier Milei, supported the sentiment while drawing a line between the players' emotions and state policy. He described the display as understandable and the sovereignty claim as valid from Argentina's perspective, but said football should be separated from the diplomatic route. Milei also acknowledged that the team could face a fine. His response gives the banner political endorsement without presenting it as a new diplomatic initiative.

The underlying dispute remains unresolved. The United Nations lists the islands as a Non-Self-Governing Territory administered by the United Kingdom and records a sovereignty dispute between the British and Argentine governments. Its decolonisation committee has continued to call for a peaceful negotiated solution. Argentina maintains its claim; Britain rejects it and supports the islanders' stated wish to remain a British Overseas Territory.

Those positions are shaped by war and democratic argument. Argentina invaded the islands in April 1982 and British forces retook them after a 74-day conflict in which hundreds of Argentine and British service personnel, as well as three islanders, were killed. In a March 2013 referendum, 1,513 voters — 99.8 per cent of valid votes — chose to retain British Overseas Territory status on a reported turnout of 92 per cent. Argentina does not accept that vote as settling sovereignty.

FIFA has sanctioned political messaging before, including an Argentine team display about the islands in 2014. That history makes disciplinary action plausible, but it does not predetermine the present case. The relevant questions are what FIFA's current code covers, whether the players' on-field display falls within it and what proportional response the governing body chooses after reviewing the circumstances.

The sporting timetable keeps moving while those questions remain open. Argentina are preparing to face Spain and attempt to become the first men's team since Brazil in 1962 to retain the World Cup. The banner now follows them to East Rutherford as both an international political dispute and a possible disciplinary matter — a consequence created after the semi-final rather than by anything that happened during it.

dek: The EuroLeague rebounding specialist returns to Spain's title race after a trophy-laden finish in Milan, carrying a game shaped by his breakthrough seasons in Israel.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: שכרו בפנים: ג'וש ניבו חתם רשמית בבארסה
source.author: Sport5 editorial team

verificationSources.label: FC Barcelona official signing announcement
Olimpia Milano official departure announcement

body: Barcelona have signed Josh Nebo until 30 June 2029, giving their frontcourt a proven EuroLeague rebounder whose route to the Palau Blaugrana ran through two influential stops in Israel. The 2.06-metre centre completed his medical before the club announced a three-season agreement, one day after Olimpia Milano confirmed the end of his two-year spell in Italy.

The move is less about manufacturing offence than improving the possessions around it. Nebo is an explosive finisher rather than a post-up hub: he creates value as a screen-setter, lob target and relentless pursuer of missed shots. Barcelona's own career summary credits him with averages of 9.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and a 13.7 performance index rating across 136 EuroLeague appearances for Žalgiris, Maccabi Tel Aviv and Milan.

His European rise began in Eilat. Arriving from the American college game in 2020, Nebo averaged 13.6 points and a league-leading 10 rebounds across 26 Israeli league games, according to the figures published with his signing. That season established the combination that has carried him upward ever since: vertical range at the rim, quick second jumps and enough mobility to defend away from the basket.

A season with Žalgiris brought his EuroLeague debut before Maccabi took him back to Israel in 2022. He won consecutive domestic championships in yellow and finished the 2023/24 EuroLeague campaign at 11.1 points and 7.1 rebounds per game, leading the competition in rebounding. Those numbers mattered, but so did the tactical reliability behind them. Nebo could play above the rim in pick-and-roll actions without demanding touches that belonged to the guards.

Milan was a more complicated chapter physically, yet it ended with silverware. Nebo helped Olimpia complete what the Italian club described as a historic treble, including the 2025/26 league and cup. Barcelona report that he averaged 10.1 points and 5.4 rebounds in his final EuroLeague season there. Olimpia's farewell also emphasised his professionalism and role within the group, useful context for a player joining another dressing room with immediate title pressure.

For Barcelona, the basketball logic is clear. Nebo supplies rim running, offensive rebounding and defensive energy without needing an offence redesigned around him. His limitations are equally legible: he is not being recruited to stretch the floor or create from the elbow. The value of the signing will depend on the spacing around him and the guards' ability to turn his screens and rolls into advantages before a half-court defence is set.

There is also a strong Israeli reference point for judging the deal. Nebo left the league as a more complete and more expensive player than the raw athlete who arrived in Eilat, then used Maccabi's EuroLeague stage to prove that his rebounding and finishing translated against elite size. Barcelona are buying that developed version on a long contract. The next question is whether he can convert specialist excellence into the week-to-week durability required by Spain's domestic schedule and a full EuroLeague campaign.

title: Israel adopts restart countdowns, treatment waits and wider VAR
dek: The domestic game now has immediate sporting penalties for slow restarts and substitutions, a one-minute treatment wait and a narrow expansion of video review.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: שינויי החוקה שיכנסו לתוקף בישראל ממחר
source.author: Sport5 editorial team

verificationSources.label: IFAB official 2026/27 law changes
IFAB announcement on match-flow and VAR changes
IFAB official 2026/27 Laws of the Game
Israeli referees briefing on the domestic rollout
Independent account of the Israeli implementation

body: Israeli football enters the 2026/27 season under a law book designed to make delay more expensive and certain video-officiating errors easier to correct. The Referees Association has now set out the domestic application of changes that took effect internationally on 1 July. They alter who receives the next restart when a team wastes time, restrict the benefit of slow substitutions and treatment stoppages, and extend VAR into a small number of disciplinary and identity decisions that previously sat outside its reach.

The most visible intervention concerns throw-ins. A referee who judges that the team taking the throw is delaying unfairly can whistle, signal for the restart and begin a raised-hand countdown from five. If the ball is still not in play when the count expires, possession changes: the opposition take the throw from the same position. This is not an automatic five-second clock after every ball crosses the touchline; it begins when the referee identifies deliberate or unfair delay.

Goal kicks now carry a more severe territorial consequence. The same whistle, signal and visual countdown can be used when the restart is being delayed. Failure to put the ball into play by the end of the count gives the opponents a corner on the nearest side. A yellow card is not automatic at that point because the lost restart is already the punishment; a caution is reserved for excessive delay after the decision has been reversed.

That distinction should change the calculation for teams protecting a lead. A slow throw-in once risked little beyond a warning or booking. It can now surrender the ball immediately. Delaying a goal kick is costlier still because it converts a protected restart deep in a team’s own territory into an attacking set piece for the opposition. Coaches will need replacement balls, clear restart options and players who recognise the referee’s signal before five seconds disappear.

Substitutions receive their own clock. Once the board is shown, the departing player generally has ten seconds to leave the field. Missing that deadline does not cancel the change, but it does prevent the replacement from entering immediately: play restarts with the team temporarily reduced, and the substitute must wait until the first stoppage after one running minute has elapsed. The sanction targets the competitive reward for a slow walk rather than treating every delayed exit as an automatic booking.

Treatment stoppages carry a parallel cost. A player assessed on the field, or whose injury causes play to be stopped, must ordinarily leave and remain outside for one minute after the restart. The law retains defined exceptions, including goalkeepers and players hurt by a physical offence for which an opponent is cautioned or sent off. That distinction is important: the rule is designed to deter tactical stoppages without punishing a player whose opponent has committed a serious or reckless offence.

VAR’s remit also expands, although within defined limits. A red card produced by a clearly incorrect second yellow can now be reviewed. The video official is not being invited to revisit every caution; the intervention concerns the dismissal created by the second booking and still requires a clear error. The change addresses the previous anomaly in which a direct red card could be corrected but an equally damaging dismissal caused by a plainly wrong second caution generally could not.

Mistaken identity has been widened as well. Video officials may assist when the referee shows a yellow or red card to the wrong player even if the actual offender belongs to the other team. Competitions can also choose to permit immediate review of a clearly incorrect corner award, but only when the decision can be corrected before the restart and without manufacturing a new delay.

The optional language matters in Israel. Competitions without VAR cannot use a video protocol they do not operate, and competition organisers must decide whether to adopt the corner-review option. The universal law changes and the optional protocols should therefore not be collapsed into a promise that every match, division or stadium will be officiated in precisely the same way.

Supporters should notice the restart countdown first because it produces an unmistakable visual cue and an immediate sporting penalty. Coaches may feel the substitution and treatment rules more sharply because both can leave a side playing with ten for a controlled period. The broader test will be consistency. If referees reserve the sanctions for the circumstances defined in the law and communicate them clearly, the changes can remove dead time without turning ordinary stoppages into theatre. If application varies sharply between matches, the argument will shift from the purpose of the rules to the threshold for using them.
facts: The IFAB Laws of the Game 2026/27 took effect on 1 July 2026.
A deliberately delayed throw-in can trigger a visual five-second countdown and be awarded to the opposing team if time expires.
A deliberately delayed goal kick can trigger the same countdown and become a corner for the opposition.
A player who takes more than ten seconds to leave during a substitution can force the replacement to wait until the first stoppage after one running minute.
A player treated or assessed on the field must ordinarily remain outside for one minute after play restarts, subject to defined exceptions.
A clearly incorrect second yellow that produces a red card is now within the VAR review protocol.
VAR mistaken-identity review can apply when the actual offender belongs to the other team.
Competitions may choose immediate VAR review of a clearly incorrect corner award when it will not delay the restart.

title: Argentina stun England with two late goals to reach World Cup final
dek: Enzo Fernández cancelled out Anthony Gordon’s opener before Lautaro Martínez headed a 92nd-minute winner, sending the holders into Sunday’s final against Spain.

source.name: Associated Press
source.originalTitle: Defending champion Argentina reaches World Cup final by beating England 2-1
source.author: James Robson

verificationSources.label: Independent full-time match report
Confirmed live chronology and final score

FIFA semi-final and tournament context

body: Argentina reached the 2026 World Cup final by overturning England’s lead with two goals inside the final eight minutes of a 2–1 semi-final victory in Atlanta. Enzo Fernández equalised in the 85th minute and substitute Lautaro Martínez headed the winner in the second minute of added time, denying England the extra time that had appeared inevitable.

England had moved in front after 55 minutes through Anthony Gordon. Declan Rice’s quick pass released Morgan Rogers, whose low delivery travelled across the face of goal. Gordon arrived at close range and directed it beyond Emiliano Martínez, turning a tense, physical contest into one England could try to control without chasing a second goal recklessly.

For half an hour, that calculation worked. England could defend the centre, ask Argentina to build around the block and preserve energy for the transitions that had produced the opening goal. The danger was that a one-goal margin left no allowance for a single failed clearance or a moment of quality from Messi. England never found the second goal that would have changed that arithmetic.

Their control finally broke when Messi found Fernández outside the penalty area and the midfielder drove the equaliser beyond Jordan Pickford with five minutes of regulation time remaining. The goal changed more than the score. England could no longer protect a narrow advantage, while Argentina attacked again before their opponents had recovered their distances or their composure.

Martínez supplied the decisive touch from the bench. His added-time header completed the comeback and removed the need for another 30 minutes, a brutally sharp conclusion after a match that had spent long periods in midfield duels and confrontations. Argentina had trailed from the 55th minute until the 85th; seven minutes later, they were finalists.

The holders will now face Spain in Sunday’s final in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Spain secured the first place in the showpiece by beating France 2–0 in Dallas. Argentina are one win from retaining the trophy they lifted in Qatar, a feat no men’s national team has achieved since Brazil won consecutive World Cups in 1958 and 1962.

England’s opportunity to reach a first men’s World Cup final since 1966 disappeared with the match almost complete. The result will be judged not only by the two goals conceded, but by the inability to slow Argentina’s momentum after Fernández levelled. Thomas Tuchel’s side now move to the third-place match against France, while the tournament’s final becomes a meeting between Messi’s defending champions and Spain’s emerging generation.

title: July 16, 2001: the Maccabiah that opened against the odds
dek: Security fears, a reduced field and the memory of the 1997 bridge disaster shadowed the 16th Maccabiah, yet more than 2,000 athletes still marched into Teddy Stadium.

source.name: Maccabiah
source.originalTitle: The 16th Maccabiah

verificationSources.label: Official Maccabiah history: 16th Games
Contemporary opening-night report filed from Jerusalem
Contemporary pre-Games participation and security report
Contemporary closing report and seven-day Games record

body: The 16th Maccabiah opened at Jerusalem’s Teddy Stadium on 16 July 2001 after coming close to postponement. A deteriorating security situation had reduced expected participation and forced organizers to reconsider whether the Games could proceed. The eventual opening was therefore more than a ceremonial start: it was the point at which months of uncertainty became an actual competition.

The Maccabiah’s later official history records an emergency meeting in June and government assurances of exceptional security measures. That retrospective explains the institutional decision. Contemporary reporting shows what it looked like on the ground: athletes were assigned protection in transit, entry checks were extensive and the opening-day account counted more than 1,000 security personnel around the stadium.

Even under those conditions, the ceremony had scale. A report filed from Jerusalem that night recorded more than 2,000 athletes representing 45 countries and an estimated 20,000 local spectators. Delegations entered to applause before the Israeli team received the largest response. Fireworks, acrobats, dancers and mass performance turned the field into a stage without disguising the tension outside it.

The two athletes entrusted with the flame gave that spectacle a sharper sporting meaning. European pole-vault champion Alex Averbukh carried the torch into Teddy Stadium, and Keren Leibovitch, who had won three swimming gold medals at the Sydney Paralympics the previous year, lit it. Their roles joined elite Israeli achievement across Olympic and Paralympic sport at the exact moment the organisers were asking the Games to stand for continuity.

Teddy Stadium carried its own significance. The official Maccabiah record identifies the 2001 ceremony as the first opening in the movement’s history to be held there. Moving the event to Jerusalem placed the Games in a venue surrounded by the political and security pressures of the moment, rather than insulating the ceremony from them.

There was another memory the organizers could not set aside. Four members of the Australian delegation had died after the bridge collapse at the 1997 Maccabiah opening in Ramat Gan. The 2001 ceremony included a memorial for those athletes, while the Australian team had gathered at the collapse site the previous day. The new Games were opening while responsibility, grief and trust from the previous edition remained unresolved parts of the event’s history.

The program was shortened from the usual ten days to seven and the field was smaller than at a normal Maccabiah. Contemporary coverage before the opening expected roughly 2,000 athletes from around 40 countries, compared with about 5,000 participants in a typical edition. Those forecasts and the opening-night count differ slightly because one was written before final arrivals; together they describe the same reality of a reduced but still international Games.

Competition still produced an emphatic sporting record. Israel finished far ahead in the medal table with 96 golds, 74 silvers and 74 bronzes; the United States followed with 21 golds, 23 silvers and 30 bronzes. Olympic champion Lenny Krayzelburg was the leading name in the pool, while Olympic gold medallists Maria Mazina and Sergei Charikov strengthened the fencing programme. The figures matter because they prevent the event from being remembered only as a security operation with an opening ceremony attached.

Later recollection often treats the 2001 Maccabiah as a statement of resilience. The contemporary evidence supports that reading, but it also makes the achievement less abstract. Athletes made individual decisions to travel, organizers accepted a compressed event, security personnel transformed how everyone moved, and Jerusalem spectators filled Teddy Stadium anyway. The enduring fact is not that fear disappeared on July 16. It is that a Jewish international sporting event began in full public view while that fear was still present.

dek: The 34-year-old centre returns to Lithuanian club basketball for the first time since 2012, giving the EuroLeague side an imposing low-post and rebounding anchor.

body: Žalgiris Kaunas have signed Jonas Valančiūnas, bringing Lithuania’s senior centre back to domestic club basketball after 14 NBA seasons. The move gives the EuroLeague side one of the continent’s most recognisable interior players, but its value is more specific than reputation: Žalgiris have acquired a half-court reference who can create efficient possessions without needing the offence to be built around perimeter isolation.

The homecoming label contains an important rivalry. Valančiūnas developed with Perlas and Lietuvos Rytas before leaving for Toronto in 2012; he has not returned to his former club. His last EuroLeague season came with Rytas in 2010/11, followed by a EuroCup campaign in which he averaged 10.8 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.6 blocks. Wearing Žalgiris green therefore reconnects him with Lithuanian basketball while placing him on the opposite side of its most charged domestic divide.

Valančiūnas entered the NBA after Toronto selected him fifth in the 2011 draft. His career then ran through Memphis, New Orleans, Washington, Sacramento and Denver, a six-team sequence that required him to move from long-term starter to situational veteran without losing the core of his game. He has been asked to score on the block, screen for higher-usage creators, control the defensive glass and accept changing minutes as lineups became smaller and faster.

His final Denver regular season illustrates that last transition. Valančiūnas appeared in 65 games, started six and averaged 8.7 points, 5.1 rebounds and 1.2 assists in 13.4 minutes behind Nikola Jokić. The modest playing time should not be confused with an empty role. Denver needed concentrated physical production in short stretches; Žalgiris can give the same skills more possessions and a clearer place in the hierarchy.

Offensively, the attraction begins with geometry. A centre who establishes deep position forces the defence to choose between conceding single coverage and sending help from a shooter. His screens can create separation before he touches the ball, while offensive rebounds turn defended possessions into second chances. For those advantages to survive at EuroLeague speed, Žalgiris must keep enough shooting around him that the lane does not become a crowd of extra defenders.

The defensive calculation is less forgiving. Valančiūnas remains a major rebounder and a deterrent near the rim, but opponents will try to involve him repeatedly in pick-and-roll actions and pull him into space. Žalgiris can protect that area through conservative coverage, disciplined weak-side rotations and lineups with mobile defenders at the other positions. The signing supplies size; the coaching challenge is preventing opponents from turning that size into a target.

His recent international work argues that meaningful high-level production remains available. At EuroBasket 2025 he averaged 15.7 points and 6.7 rebounds for Lithuania across seven games and converted 64.7 per cent of his two-point attempts. A national-team tournament is shorter than a EuroLeague season, but it demonstrated that a larger offensive responsibility can still produce efficient scoring rather than merely ceremonial veteran minutes.

Žalgiris are therefore making two bets at once. The emotional bet is that Lithuania’s most established active centre can deepen the bond between the team and its basketball public. The competitive bet is that a defined European role will extract more from Valančiūnas than the reduced assignment he held in Denver. Neither is guaranteed by the name on the shirt, but both are grounded in a skill set—screening, post scoring and rebounding—that remains immediately legible.

body: Israeli midfielder Orian Goren has trained with Barcelona’s first team during the opening phase of the club’s 2026/27 preseason. The 17-year-old was among the academy players included when Hansi Flick’s senior group returned to work at the Ciutat Esportiva Joan Gamper, placing him inside a high-level evaluation environment before the full first-team squad reassembles.

Barcelona listed Goren among 15 Barça Atlètic and youth players who completed medical and fitness testing on Monday, July 13. Ten established first-team players were present for those checks. The club then named Goren again among the academy contingent involved in Tuesday’s first pitch session, when nine senior players trained and many World Cup participants remained away.

The distinction matters. Participation in preseason work is not the same as a permanent promotion, a squad registration or a guarantee of competitive minutes. It does, however, allow Flick and his staff to assess how an academy midfielder handles the senior team’s speed of play, positional demands and physical intensity while the usual roster is incomplete.

Goren is registered by UEFA as an Israeli midfielder born on March 15, 2009. Barcelona’s own 2025/26 U19A roster also lists him in midfield, while UEFA records his involvement with Israel at under-19 level. Those records establish the relevant pathway: an Israeli youth international progressing through Barcelona’s academy structure and now receiving direct exposure to first-team preparation.

For Goren, the useful measure is not simply that he appeared in training photographs. Preseason opportunities become meaningful when a young player absorbs tactical information quickly, keeps the ball under senior pressure and makes reliable decisions as the tempo rises. The environment is the test; a photograph is only evidence that the test began.

The invitation is nevertheless significant for Israeli football. Few Israeli teenagers are assessed inside an elite European first-team programme, and Goren entered that setting at 17 while remaining part of Barcelona’s youth structure. It is a credible step in his development, neither a ceremonial appearance nor proof that the senior transition is complete.

The next evidence will be harder and more revealing: further invitations after the World Cup players return, minutes in a senior friendly or inclusion in a competitive matchday group. Each would survive the shrinking of preseason places. Until one arrives, the accurate conclusion is that Goren has earned a closer first-team look, not a permanent first-team role.

title: England protected a lead until they stopped protecting the game
dek: Gordon’s goal rewarded Tuchel’s shape, but retreat invited Argentina to keep returning. Fernández and Martínez exposed the difference between managing a score and controlling a match.

source.name: FIFA
source.originalTitle: England v Argentina: Live stream, team news, tickets and more

verificationSources.label: Independent full-time match report
Confirmed match chronology and final score
FIFA semi-final context and confirmed venue
FIFA tournament final schedule

body: England’s semi-final plan worked long enough to create the most dangerous illusion in tournament football: that a narrow lead and control are the same thing. Anthony Gordon’s 55th-minute goal vindicated the attacking structure Thomas Tuchel had chosen. Declan Rice moved the ball early, Morgan Rogers attacked beyond Argentina’s compact midfield and Gordon arrived on the far side of the defence. It was a coherent sequence, not a lucky break, and it gave England a position from which a place in the final should at least have been manageable.

The distinction between a sound plan and a complete one emerged immediately afterwards. England had shown how they could progress through Argentina’s pressure when their midfield received with a forward picture and a runner threatened the last line. Once ahead, however, those same forward connections became intermittent. Possession ceased to be a means of altering the geography of the match and became something England were prepared to surrender in exchange for numbers behind the ball.

There is nothing inherently timid about defending deeper against Lionel Messi. A compact block can close the central lanes he uses to combine, restrict passes into the penalty area and invite lower-value circulation in front of the defence. But depth creates its own bill. Clearances travel to opponents rather than team-mates, the centre-forward becomes isolated, and the defending side must execute another sequence without the relief of making the opponent retreat. England accepted that bill for half an hour and never found a reliable way to stop it accumulating.

Argentina did not require Messi to dominate every possession. His value was also gravitational: England had to preserve enough cover around him that other players could approach the edge of the area without the defensive line stepping out recklessly. When Messi supplied Enzo Fernández in the 85th minute, Fernández still needed an exceptional finish from outside the box. Yet the opportunity belonged to the broader pattern. Argentina were repeatedly established in England’s half, close enough to recover second balls and begin another attack before the block could breathe.

The equaliser should have changed the tactical calculation. At 1–1, England no longer had a lead to protect, so the benefits of extreme caution had disappeared while its costs remained. The required intervention did not have to be dramatic. A controlled spell on the ball, one midfielder receiving beyond the first press or a forward winning a foul higher up the pitch would have forced Argentina to reorganise. Instead, the match retained the same direction and England continued to defend the same territory under greater emotional pressure.

Lionel Scaloni’s use of Lautaro Martínez sharpened that pressure. The substitute supplied a different reference point inside the penalty area and headed the winner in the second minute of added time. Substitutions are often assessed as isolated acts of inspiration, but this one worked because Argentina had already arranged the conditions around it: territory, repeated entries and enough players near the box to sustain attacks. Martínez changed the target; England did not change the location from which Argentina could aim at him.

Game management is consequently a more demanding idea than adding a defender or lowering the block. It is the management of risk across every phase. The team in front still needs an outlet who can secure the first pass, a midfielder willing to receive under pressure and at least one route that makes the chasing side turn towards its own goal. Without those elements, extra defensive numbers may protect the penalty area while simultaneously increasing the volume of attacks it must absorb.

None of this means Argentina’s comeback was predetermined. Fernández’s strike required rare execution and a late header can always be decided by a small positional error or an individual duel. Tactical analysis becomes dishonest when it removes contingency from football. The relevant question is not whether England could have guaranteed survival, but whether their choices improved or worsened the probability of seeing the match out. By steadily reducing their own attacking threat, they gave Argentina more attempts to find the exceptional action they needed.

The chronology is unforgiving: England led from the 55th minute until the 85th and then conceded again before extra time could begin. The two goals had different finishers and different final actions, but they grew from the same sustained territorial advantage. Tuchel solved the opening problem of how to damage Argentina’s shape. He did not solve the closing problem of how to keep Argentina’s shape occupied while England were ahead. That is why this defeat belongs less to the language of collapse than to the finer, more useful distinction between defending a score and controlling a game.

body: Israel’s men’s under-20 team did not merely lose a knockout game to Greece; it crossed into a different tournament. The 79–66 round-of-16 defeat at Arena Stožice II ended any route to the quarter-finals and placed Oren Aharoni’s side in the classification bracket for ninth to 16th. The opponent is now fixed: Italy, in Ljubljana on Thursday, with the winner moving towards places nine to 12 and the loser dropping into the group where relegation is decided.

Greece created the separation that Israel could not recover. Oren Sahar scored 20 points and Rany Belaga added 19, meaning two players supplied 39 of Israel’s 66. That concentration did not make defeat inevitable, but it left too small a margin when other possessions failed to produce. In youth tournament basketball, where scouting time is short and physical condition changes quickly, a team still needs a third scoring route once its first two options are carrying almost three-fifths of the total.

The disappointment is sharper because Israel had built a credible group phase. A 78–68 win over Romania was followed by a 90–77 defeat to host Slovenia, before an 87–73 victory over Czechia completed a 2–1 record. Across those three games Israel averaged 80.7 points. Greece held the team nearly 15 points below that level, turning what had been a functioning offence into a narrower contest around Sahar and Belaga.

The competition system offers no protection for that winning record. All 16 teams entered the round of 16, so group performance determined the pairing but did not provide a bye or a second route to the title bracket. One defeat was enough to remove Israel from the top half. The same format now gives the team another immediate assignment, only with survival rather than a medal path shaping the consequences.

Italy arrive in the same position after an 86–63 loss to Serbia. Their tournament has also been uneven, but the classification meeting is not an invitation to read either round-of-16 margin as a forecast. Both teams have had less than a day to reset. The more relevant contest will be over control: which side can establish its half-court offence without allowing the earlier defeat to accelerate decisions or turn missed shots into hurried defensive transitions.

For Israel, the rotation must create support without asking Sahar and Belaga to become less aggressive. A third ball-handler reaching the paint, an extra shooter converting the first clean kick-out or a frontcourt player generating second possessions would change the geometry of the attack. The objective is not statistical balance for its own sake. It is to prevent Italy from loading its defence towards the two players who carried the scoring against Greece.

The relegation arithmetic is unforgiving but not yet terminal. The eight round-of-16 losers play through the nine-to-16 classification bracket, and the teams placed 14th, 15th and 16th fall from Division A. Beating Italy would guarantee Israel a finish in the nine-to-12 range and remove that danger immediately. Losing would send Aharoni’s team into the 13-to-16 bracket, where only one of four final positions is safe.

That is why the response matters beyond this squad’s final ranking in Ljubljana. Division A preserves annual exposure to Europe’s leading under-20 programmes and keeps the next age group inside the continent’s highest competitive tier. Israel no longer has the tournament it wanted after the group phase, but it still controls whether this becomes a contained knockout disappointment or a structural setback. Italy is the first and cleanest opportunity to settle that distinction.

body: The Recanati family have completed the acquisition of the Federman family’s 29% holding in Maccabi Tel Aviv Basketball Club, increasing their own stake from 29% to 58%. The transfer of funds closed the transaction on Wednesday evening. Its value has been reported at approximately $50 million, although the private completion documents have not been published.

That arithmetic changes the balance of ownership immediately. Two families no longer hold matching blocks; one shareholder now owns a majority of the club’s equity. For an institution whose governance has long depended on several established ownership groups, the concentration itself is the central development.

The route to completion was not direct. Earlier financial reporting described an agreement under which Rapyd founder Arik Shtilman would acquire the Federman stake. The Recanati family subsequently exercised a right of first refusal, allowing them to match the path to the same 29% holding. Wednesday’s payment therefore did more than confirm an intention: it ended the competing transaction process and transferred the shares.

There is also a historical separation inside the deal. The Federman family’s involvement covered decades in which Maccabi occupied the commanding position in Israeli basketball and remained a durable EuroLeague institution. Their exit removes one of the names most closely associated with that era. The Recanati family, already embedded in the club, are not arriving as outside owners; they are consolidating control from within the existing structure.

A 58% equity holding, however, does not disclose the whole system of authority. Public reporting has not set out the post-transaction board, the voting threshold for reserved decisions or the protections retained by the remaining shareholders. Majority ownership may provide decisive influence over ordinary matters, but it should not be translated automatically into unilateral control over every strategic or financial choice.

The reported purchase price requires a similar distinction. Roughly $50 million values the stake that changed hands; it is not a new player budget and does not flow by definition into basketball operations. Recruitment, coaching resources and EuroLeague expenditure depend on separate operating decisions. Treating the acquisition value as available sporting cash would confuse the price of ownership with the financing of the team.

The consequential disclosures will therefore be practical rather than ceremonial: who sits on the board, how responsibilities are divided, whether the shareholders approve a different multi-year budget and which executives carry the resulting mandate. Those details will show whether concentrated ownership produces faster decisions, larger investment or simply a new distribution of the same obligations.

For now, the confirmed boundary is clear. The Federman family’s 29% stake has changed hands, the Recanati holding has reached 58% and Maccabi Tel Aviv have entered a majority-owner phase. The transaction is complete; its sporting meaning will be determined by governance and capital decisions that have yet to be made public.

title: Pogačar breaks open the Tour on Bastille Day as lead reaches 3:36
dek: A decisive attack on the Col de Pertus carried the yellow jersey to a third stage win of the 2026 Tour and put Jonas Vingegaard more than three and a half minutes behind.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: מרסק הטור: פוגצ'אר ניצח גם ביום הבסטיליה
source.author: Sport5 desk

verificationSources.label: Tour de France official stage 10 report

body: Tadej Pogačar did more than win the Tour de France’s Bastille Day mountain stage. His attack on the Col de Pertus split the general-classification group, erased the last survivor of the breakaway and converted a difficult but still compressed race into one governed by a lead of three minutes and 36 seconds. By Le Lioran, the yellow jersey had taken his third victory of this Tour and forced every rival team to reconsider what a successful final fortnight could still look like.

Stage 10 was built to expose weak management after the rest day: 166.6 kilometres from Aurillac, roughly 3,800 metres of climbing and seven categorised ascents. A 31-rider break formed only after repeated attacks, yet UAE Emirates-XRG never let its advantage grow beyond 1:25. That control made the front group expend energy without allowing it to become a strategic threat. The stage was being prepared for the favourites long before Pogačar made his move visible.

Javier Romo spent 36 kilometres alone before being caught at the foot of Puy Mary. Richard Carapaz then took over, driving his advantage to a minute by the base of the first-category Col de Pertus. Carapaz’s attack had enough quality to win a stage under different race conditions; here, it became the target against which the yellow jersey could measure his own acceleration.

Visma-Lease a Bike increased the pace through Davide Piganzoli, but Pogačar attacked one kilometre from the Pertus summit and crossed the gap to Carapaz almost immediately. He was 20 seconds clear of the Vingegaard-Evenepoel-Seixas group over the top, then kept pressing across the final ascent of the Col de Font de Cère. The important detail was not simply that nobody followed the first acceleration. The gap continued to grow after the terrain became less selective, evidence that the damage extended beyond one explosive minute.

Pogačar finished 32 seconds ahead of Remco Evenepoel, while Paul Seixas took third. Jonas Vingegaard reached the line in seventh place, 44 seconds behind the winner. In the overall standings, Vingegaard now trails by 3:36 and Evenepoel sits third at 4:06. Those are no longer gaps that can be recovered through bonuses, positioning or one opportunistic descent; they demand a sustained failure from the leader or a mountain offensive capable of producing minutes.

The stage also rearranged the contest behind the two principal favourites. Isaac del Toro lost 1:31 and fell to seventh overall. Evenepoel moved onto the podium, Seixas entered the top five and Juan Ayuso climbed ahead of both younger riders. UAE therefore gained time through Pogačar while losing a second high overall position, a trade that simplifies leadership but reduces the number of cards the team can play against long-range attacks.

The victory was Pogačar’s 24th Tour stage win and made him the first rider to win three stages held on 14 July. That record carries symbolism, but the sporting achievement is sharper: three victories in the opening ten stages while wearing the burden of outright favourite. He has been able to contest stages without allowing the daily race for wins to weaken his control of the overall classification.

Control now changes sides. UAE can judge breaks by composition, defend selectively and make Visma spend riders before Vingegaard attacks. Vingegaard cannot wait for Pogačar to volunteer a bad day; his team must create repeated pressure, isolate the race leader and accept the counter-attacking risk that accompanies any move large enough to recover three and a half minutes. Stage 10 did not settle the Tour, but it rewrote its economy: Pogačar owns time, and everyone else must spend energy to buy it back.

body: John Otomewo has completed a €1.6 million move from Hapoel Jerusalem to Stade de Reims, converting one of Israeli football’s fastest development stories into the largest sale in Hapoel’s history. The 19-year-old defensive midfielder has signed a five-year contract with the French Ligue 2 club after completing the medical process that took him to France earlier this week.

The transfer is remarkable for its compression. Otomewo arrived in Jerusalem in the summer of 2025 after Hapoel identified him at a talent tournament in Nigeria. He entered through the youth team, trained with the senior group and made his first-team debut in the Jerusalem derby. Within a single season he had moved from discovery project to regular starter and then to a substantial European sale.

Hapoel’s official player record credits him with 21 senior appearances in 2025/26 and one Israel State Cup goal. The club’s own assessment emphasises ball-winning, aggression and the ability to circulate possession in tight areas. Those are not ornamental qualities for a holding midfielder: they explain how a teenager could become trusted during a relegation fight, when mistakes in central areas carry immediate consequences.

The €1.6 million return matters beyond the headline record. Hapoel Jerusalem operate as a supporter-owned club, so transfer income is one of the few ways to create capital at a scale that ordinary matchday and commercial revenue rarely produce. Otomewo’s sale validates a recruitment route built on finding players before better-funded markets have completed their evaluations, then giving them meaningful senior minutes rather than storing them behind established names.

That model only works if the sporting pathway remains credible. A club cannot sell the promise of development indefinitely; players and representatives need evidence that strong performances lead to responsibility and, when the right offer arrives, mobility. Otomewo now provides that evidence. He was not merely scouted cheaply and traded. Hapoel placed him in Premier League matches, absorbed the risk of his learning curve and received a record fee after the football justified the projection.

Reims are buying a different kind of risk. A five-year contract gives the French club time to develop Otomewo and protects potential resale value, but it does not remove the jump in difficulty. He must adapt to a new language, a more physically demanding weekly environment and a team whose immediate objective is to compete near the top of Ligue 2. The fee creates expectation; the length of the agreement provides patience.

His cleanest route into the side will begin with the work that accelerated his rise in Jerusalem: covering space in front of the centre-backs, winning contact without losing positional discipline and moving the first pass quickly enough to let more creative players receive facing forward. Reims may eventually ask for a broader passing range or greater penalty-area contribution, but the transfer does not require him to become a different player on arrival.

For Hapoel, the transaction closes with both sporting loss and strategic proof. Replacing a starting midfielder will cost time and money, and the success of one sale cannot guarantee the next. Yet the club have turned a Nigerian scouting initiative, a youth-team place and 21 senior appearances into €1.6 million in a year. For Otomewo, the same sequence has produced five seasons in French football. That is not merely a record deal; it is a development pathway made commercially real.

body: Ten-man Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Hapoel Be’er Sheva 3–1 at Turner Stadium on Thursday night to win the Israel Super Cup. Saied Abu Farchi scored twice and Sagiv Yehezkel supplied all three Maccabi goals, turning the season’s first domestic showpiece into a forceful statement by the State Cup holders.

Dor Peretz restored Maccabi’s lead in the 58th minute from Yehezkel’s delivery before Roy Revivo received a second yellow card in the 66th. Maccabi refused to protect a one-goal margin passively: they attacked the space behind Be’er Sheva’s advancing shape, and another Yehezkel cross allowed Abu Farchi to complete his brace and settle the final at 3–1.

Yehezkel was briefly shown a second yellow of his own during a late substitution after turning back from the nearest touchline when cups were thrown towards him. Referee Aviv Klein reviewed the incident and cancelled the caution. The intervention was permitted by the 2026/27 law change that allows VAR to review a clearly incorrect second yellow when it immediately produces a red card; the substitution law also permits a different exit point for safety or security.

The second-half goal rewarded Maccabi for finding Peretz between Be’er Sheva’s midfield and defensive line. Yehezkel carried the move to the left side and supplied the final ball; Peretz did not need maximum power, placing his finish accurately enough to beat Ofir Marciano. It also gave him a goal that stood after an earlier effort had been ruled out for offside in the build-up.

Maccabi’s goal punished a serious error in Be’er Sheva’s defensive build-up and gave Abu Farchi a direct route to the finish. Be’er Sheva’s reply was more inventive: Kangwa completed the move with a backheel, restoring parity before Maccabi could settle into protecting the lead. The two goals immediately changed the match from a cautious first competitive outing into a test of how quickly either side could regain control after losing it.

The opening exchange also exposed the tactical burden carried by both midfields. Maccabi’s five-man unit is designed to place bodies around the ball and release Dor Peretz or Sagiv Yehezkel in support of Abu Farchi. Be’er Sheva need Lucas Ventura and Eliel Peretz to protect transitions while allowing Kangwa to move into scoring positions. Both mechanisms produced an early reward; neither initially gave its defence sustained protection.

Be’er Sheva started Ofir Marciano, not new signing Marco Wolff, in goal. Guy Mizrahi, Miguel Vítor, Matan Baltaxa and Ofir Davidzada formed the back line, with Roy Levy and Amir Ganah supporting Igor Zlatanović. Maccabi selected Ofek Melika behind Itay Ben Hamo, Mohamed Ali Camara, Raz Shlomo and Roy Revivo, with Abu Farchi ahead of Yehezkel, Itamar Noy, Issouf Sissokho, Ido Shahar and Peretz.

The football began after a significant security operation around Turner. Four people were detained close to the stadium after police found several clubs during a vehicle search. Be’er Sheva station officers transferred the occupants for further questioning while the South District deployed additional personnel in the area before kick-off.

No charge, supporter affiliation or attempt to enter the stadium was specified in the pre-match police account, and no injury was reported in connection with the stop. The established facts are the intervention, seizure and detentions. They do not support a conclusion about criminal responsibility or a link to either club without further official information.

The fixture was a direct rematch of the two showpieces that framed last season. Be’er Sheva won the previous Super Cup 2–1 despite playing most of the match with ten men, then secured the league title. Maccabi responded in May by beating Be’er Sheva 2–1 in the State Cup final. Thursday’s win reversed the previous Super Cup result and added a second consecutive trophy against the champions.

The European calendar gives the performance value beyond the silverware. Be’er Sheva move into Champions League qualifying against Víkingur Reykjavík, while Maccabi begin their Europa League programme later in July. Maccabi’s transition threat and response to the red card provide a strong platform; both teams must still reduce the moments when one lost pass exposes an entire defensive structure.

title: Zach LeDay signing raises Hapoel Tel Aviv’s frontcourt ceiling
dek: The EuroLeague forward has signed a two-year deal and returns to the country where his professional career began, bringing Hapoel another high-level scoring option.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv have signed Zach LeDay through the end of the 2027/28 season, adding a proven EuroLeague scorer to a frontcourt that can now be assembled in several different ways. The attraction is not merely his résumé. LeDay gives Hapoel a forward who can create an advantage without requiring the offence to change shape around him on every possession.

The move also closes a circle. LeDay began his professional career with Hapoel Gilboa Galil in 2017/18, then built his European standing with Olympiacos, Žalgiris Kaunas, Olimpia Milano and Partizan before a second spell in Milan. He returns to Israel at 32 with extensive knowledge of the competition Hapoel are trying to navigate rather than as a newcomer learning its tactical and physical demands.

At 202 centimetres, LeDay sits between traditional frontcourt definitions. He is strong enough to establish position against many power forwards, mobile enough to attack a closeout and credible enough from distance that a defender cannot simply retreat into the paint. Against a switch, he can take a smaller opponent to the block; against a slow big, he can face the basket and make the first defensive rotation arrive early.

That inside-out range is the organising value of the signing. A conventional centre often dictates where the other four attackers must stand. LeDay can instead occupy the elbow, screen and pop, slip into space or finish a possession as the nominal five. The variety should help Hapoel avoid possessions in which their spacing announces the intended action before the ball has crossed half court.

His recent numbers support the tactical case. EuroLeague's official record lists 12.2 points and 3.8 rebounds across 18 appearances in 2025/26. The sample was shortened, but the scoring level still matters: Hapoel are acquiring a player who handled meaningful usage for Milan, not relying on a distant peak or a reputation detached from current production.

There are trade-offs to manage. A smaller frontcourt can concede size on the defensive glass, while line-ups that use LeDay beside another scoring big will need perimeter defenders capable of containing the first action. His presence creates options; it does not remove the need to choose among them. The most revealing pre-season decision will be how often Hapoel trust him at centre against elite EuroLeague opponents.

The two-year term makes that fit more consequential than a short rental. Hapoel can build combinations around LeDay across more than one campaign, but they are also committing roster space to a veteran whose value depends on precision rather than raw athletic dominance. Guards must deliver the ball to his preferred spots, and the surrounding shooters must punish the help he draws.

This is why the signing changes Hapoel's possibilities more than it changes a depth chart. LeDay can be a scorer, screener or spacing device within the same quarter. If those roles are connected coherently, he will make several teammates easier to use. If they are not, even a distinguished name can become one more talented player waiting for his turn.

body: Anan Khalaili’s proposed transfer from Union Saint-Gilloise to Inter has fallen through after the Israeli international did not receive the sporting-fitness approval required for registration in Italy. Sport5 reports that the collapse ended a deal that had been moving towards completion and would have represented an exceptional transfer for an Israeli-developed player.

The distinction between a club medical and the Italian fitness ruling is important. Inter president Giuseppe Marotta said the refusal came through the Italian Olympic Committee process rather than Inter’s medical staff. ANSA had previously reported that the authority requested additional tests before reaching its decision. No diagnosis has been made public, and privacy prevents responsible reporting from going further than the documented ruling.

Luciano Buonfiglio, president of the Italian Olympic Committee, subsequently said Italy’s more rigorous controls are designed to protect athletes and stressed that life takes priority over earnings. His remarks explain the governing principle behind the decision; they do not identify Khalaili’s medical information or establish how another country’s registration process would assess him.

The fitness outcome changes the status of every earlier transfer report. Travel, agreed personal terms and advanced club negotiations do not equal a completed move; registration and the relevant medical approval remain essential. Khalaili is therefore still a Union Saint-Gilloise player unless and until another club completes its own process and announces a deal.

According to Sport5, Ipswich Town are now expected to intensify talks with Union. The English club had already made a formal approach in May, the report says, and is considered capable of operating in the financial range previously discussed with Inter. Interest is not the same as an accepted offer, however, and neither club had announced a transfer at the time of the report.

Sport5 also describes optimism in Khalaili’s camp that a move to England can be completed during the current window. That confidence is attributed to the people around the player and should be read as their assessment, not as independent medical evidence or a guarantee that a future examination will produce a different conclusion.

Walla Sport later carried an outside cardiologist’s view that Khalaili could be approved under a different medical assessment, while Sport1 reported that his camp still prefers an English move. Neither follow-up overturns Inter’s decision or completes a new transfer; they add context to the same event and are consolidated here rather than published as duplicate stories.

From a football perspective, Ipswich would present a different development question from Inter. Khalaili’s acceleration, direct running and ability to cover the right flank are attractive in an intense English game, but the decisive issue would be the role offered to him and the club’s plan for managing whatever concern stopped the Inter transaction.

The next credible milestones are clear: a formal offer accepted by Union, permission for a medical, completion of the receiving country’s fitness process and official club confirmation. Until those steps occur, the accurate headline is not that Khalaili is joining Ipswich, but that one major move has collapsed and a previously interested English club is reported to be exploring the opening.

Union Saint-Gilloise have since indicated how the next phase will run. Head coach David Hubert, quoted in Israeli reports on 18 July, said Khalaili is expected back in training next week after time with his family in Israel, and confirmed the club will conduct its own medical examinations in Belgium on his return, so it can hold a complete, independent picture of his condition to share with interested clubs. Hubert said he speaks to the 21-year-old almost daily, called the collapse hard to digest 'both sportingly and humanly', and said Union are prepared for either outcome — a stay or a sale. Those around the deal are further reported to expect a 'big and beautiful move' to be completed this summer; that is the camp's stated confidence, not an agreed transfer.

body: The dispute surrounding the Ironi Tiberias investigation has escalated from evidential objections into a procedural challenge. The club have submitted a petition to the Israel Football Association’s supreme judicial body seeking to halt or disqualify parts of the process, according to a report detailing the requested remedies.

The petition reportedly asks for the investigator to be removed, for any prospective indictment built on the disputed inquiry to be cancelled and for the association to disclose the material collected in the case. Those are applications made by the club, not rulings already granted by the federation, and the distinction matters while the case remains open.

Ironi Tiberias are also reported to have filed a police complaint concerning the investigator and to be pursuing NIS 500,000 in a separate civil claim. A federation petition, a police complaint and a damages action operate on different legal tracks; the existence of one does not establish the merits of another.

The new challenge follows earlier reporting that identified difficulties in the evidence and suggested five players could be cleared because the available material might not meet the disciplinary threshold. That possibility has direct sporting weight, but it remains provisional until the competent football authority issues a decision.

The club’s lawyers had previously asked the association to examine allegations concerning the investigator, including claims touching other teams and betting. Those allegations remain allegations. They should not be converted into findings, nor should the club’s confidence about the case be confused with an acquittal.

The immediate competitive issue is player eligibility. Anyone formally cleared can return to normal activity, while any remaining disciplinary exposure for players or staff will depend on the evidence admitted and the decisions issued through the association’s judicial structure.

A subsequent report says the national anti-doping agency has opened plea-arrangement discussions with some of the players in an effort to resolve part of the case more quickly. Talks are not completed agreements, and any proposed sanction would still have to satisfy the standards applied under the World Anti-Doping Code. The development therefore changes the procedural route, not the current eligibility verdict.

The positions in those discussions have now become more specific. The agency is reported to be seeking a one-year suspension for coach Eliran Hodeda, four months for Chen Sol and terms of between three and five months for the players involved. The parties are described as far apart, so those periods are demands in an unresolved negotiation rather than sanctions imposed by a tribunal.

Until the petition itself and a federation response are available in a claim-specific public record, the defensible position is narrow: Ironi Tiberias have mounted a reported legal challenge, the underlying evidence is contested and the outcome is not yet settled.

body: Spain are through to the World Cup final after beating France 2–0 in a semi-final decided by one moment of penalty-area pressure and one emphatic second-half finish. Mikel Oyarzabal converted a 22nd-minute penalty before Pedro Porro doubled the lead in the 58th minute, rewarding a performance built on territorial control and disciplined protection behind the ball.

The opening goal gave Spain the kind of control that matters more than possession figures in a knockout match: France now had to chase without allowing the spaces that Spain’s wide players are built to exploit. Oyarzabal accepted the responsibility from the spot and put his side ahead. It was his fifth goal of the tournament, drawing him level with Spain’s record for goals in a single men’s World Cup.

France’s task became more difficult when centre-back William Saliba went down and was replaced by Maxence Lacroix in the 30th minute, eight minutes after the opening goal. The enforced change interrupted an already stressed defensive unit, but no authoritative post-match diagnosis had established the nature or severity of Saliba’s problem. It should therefore be treated as a confirmed in-game injury substitution, not as evidence of a specific condition or recovery timetable.

Porro’s goal after the interval changed the risk calculation completely. At 1–0, France still needed only one clean attack to reset the semi-final; at 2–0, every forward run carried the possibility of leaving another transition behind it. Spain protected the advantage and kept France scoreless, turning a high-profile meeting of attacking talent into a controlled passage to the final.

The result also settles the historical angle that framed the build-up. France arrived with an exceptional modern record in World Cup knockout matches. Spain did not need to defeat that history in the abstract. They scored first, added the insurance goal and managed the match in front of them.

Didier Deschamps questioned the refereeing after the match, particularly the sequence that produced Spain’s penalty, but he also acknowledged the central football verdict: Spain controlled the contest and France operated below the level required for a semi-final. That distinction matters. One decision can shape the game state without explaining France’s failure to disrupt Spain once they were behind.

Lucas Digne later accepted personal responsibility for the challenge on Lamine Yamal that produced the penalty, saying in his first public response that he was disappointed in himself. His message also thanked France’s supporters and looked towards the remaining tournament commitment. That accountability adds human context without changing the wider analysis: the foul opened the scoring, but France’s collective response never forced Spain out of control.

Spain’s defensive record gives the final a second tactical theme. Unai Simón has recorded six clean sheets while conceding only once in seven tournament appearances. The back line have not simply survived pressure inside their own penalty area; Spain’s possession structure and counter-press have repeatedly reduced the number of open transitions their opponents can create.

This is Spain’s second men’s World Cup final. Their first ended with the title in 2010. The identity of the 2026 opponent will be decided by the other semi-final, so any tactical projection for the final must wait until that fixture is complete.

Spain now move from the problem of breaking France down to preparing for a different opponent and a different type of final. Their semi-final supplied the cleanest possible foundation: a lead taken before the interval, a second goal before the hour and a night without conceding.

title: Five tactical questions that will shape the next sporting week
dek: From Be’er Sheva’s European rest defence to Gloukh’s occupation of Ajax’s half-spaces, these are the details that will decide more than the next headline.

source.name: Israel Sports Pulse
source.originalTitle: Israel Sports Pulse weekly tactical briefing

verificationSources.label: UEFA: Champions League second qualifying round
Ajax: Oscar Gloukh player profile
EuroLeague: Tomáš Satoranský profile
FIFA World Cup tournament centre
Tour de France: official stage 10 report

body: A useful preview of a sporting week should do more than list fixtures and attach predictions. The serious task is to identify the mechanisms through which those events can change. Five current stories present five distinct problems: control after losing the ball, occupation of attacking space, roster construction, knockout-game management and the tactical consequences of a substantial time advantage. They belong to different sports, yet each is ultimately a test of how a team distributes risk.

That framing matters because outcomes alone can conceal the quality of a decision. A football side may survive several dangerous transitions and still have protected the ball poorly. A basketball roster may add the most recognisable available guard without solving the combinations around him. A cycling leader can finish safely in the bunch while his rivals have nonetheless increased the future cost of defending the jersey. The score records what happened; structure helps explain whether it can happen again.

Hapoel Be’er Sheva’s Champions League tie with Víkingur Reykjavík begins with rest defence. Víkingur advanced 3–2 on aggregate against Győr and scored twice away in Hungary, evidence that they can damage a tie when space opens beyond an opponent’s first attacking line. Be’er Sheva therefore need sufficient protection behind the ball when their full-backs advance. An uncontrolled turnover can convert a patient attack into the away transition that defines a two-legged contest, and an opening assignment in Iceland increases the value of controlling game state rather than forcing an early breakthrough.

For Oscar Gloukh, the more revealing question at Ajax is where and when he receives, not simply how many goals and assists he accumulates. A permanent central role requires him to appear between the opposition midfield and defence without depriving Ajax’s build-up of an accessible first pass. Look for receptions on the half-turn, progressive actions after central touches and the speed with which he counter-presses after losing possession. Those details will show whether Gloukh is becoming part of the team’s organising structure or remains a gifted specialist inserted for particular attacking situations.

Tomáš Satoranský presents Hapoel Tel Aviv with a roster problem rather than a simple recruitment question. At 2.01 metres, he can see and pass over smaller guards, defend a wider range of match-ups and share the court with another ball-handler without sacrificing backcourt size. His possible classification as a local player has strategic value because registration status affects how import places can be allocated elsewhere. The decisive issue is therefore not whether he would be named the starting point guard, but which five-man units his size, secondary creation and administrative status would make available.

Spain’s 2–0 semi-final victory over France offers a different lesson in knockout control. Mikel Oyarzabal’s penalty established the favourable game state and Pedro Porro’s 58th-minute goal forced France to commit greater numbers. The clean sheet should not be reduced to last-ditch defending around the box. Spain also limited the frequency with which their own possession losses became open-field French attacks. Reproducing that protection behind wide advances will matter in the final, when chasing an extra attack could be less valuable than denying the opponent one clean transition.

At the Tour de France, Tadej Pogačar’s advantage of three minutes and 36 seconds over Jonas Vingegaard changes the burden of initiative. Pogačar’s team can monitor the composition of breaks, choose which climbs require a direct response and make rivals spend energy merely to create uncertainty. Vingegaard’s side needs situations capable of recovering minutes rather than seconds. That points towards cumulative pressure: increasing fatigue before the decisive ascent, separating the leader from team-mates and accepting the possibility that an ambitious move also creates losses. Time is a strategic asset for one team and an active opponent for the other.

The five cases also show why ‘aggression’ and ‘caution’ are inadequate analytical labels. Be’er Sheva can attack with numbers while remaining conservative about the spaces they leave. Gloukh can play between the lines without abandoning the build-up. Hapoel can make an ambitious signing whose greatest value is flexibility rather than usage. Spain can dominate possession while treating transition prevention as an attacking responsibility. Visma can race aggressively long before Vingegaard launches a visible attack. The location and timing of risk are more informative than the emotional language attached to it.

Each proposition is observable. Watch Be’er Sheva’s spacing behind their attacks, Gloukh’s reception zones, Hapoel’s guard combinations, Spain’s protection when wide moves break down and the point at which Visma-Lease a Bike begin spending riders to destabilise the Tour. Those details will not make the week predictable. They will, however, separate explanations from reactions — and reveal which teams understood the problem they were trying to solve before the result supplied its own, often misleading, story.

body: A grenade was thrown at the Japanika restaurant in Rosh Pina on Wednesday morning, extending the violent series directed at branches of the chain owned by Beitar Jerusalem chairman Barak Abramov. Police arrived after a reported explosion and opened an investigation. No casualties were reported in the Rosh Pina incident.

The attack came after several explosions and an attempted arson had been recorded within a short period. Police accounts cited in independent reporting described two grenade explosions, a pipe-bomb attack and an attempted arson overnight on Tuesday, three of them directed at Japanika locations. The Rosh Pina explosion therefore belongs to an evolving criminal investigation rather than an isolated property-damage incident.

Four people had already been arrested in connection with the wider series by the time of the latest attack. Police identified one of those detained as Yossi Musli and later announced three further arrests. Arrest and remand proceedings are investigative measures, not findings of guilt; responsibility for the individual incidents and any eventual charges remain matters for police and the courts.

The most important line to preserve is the boundary between Abramov's businesses and the football club he owns. The attacks concern private commercial properties. Beitar Jerusalem have not been accused of involvement, and nothing in the latest police account turns the investigation into a case against the club, its players or its supporters.

Abramov's dual role nevertheless explains why the story carries sporting significance. A sustained campaign against businesses controlled by the owner of one of Israel's most prominent clubs can affect his security, attention and commercial environment even when the football operation is legally separate. That connection justifies careful coverage; it does not justify importing unproven criminal claims into reporting about Beitar.

The next authoritative developments will be court decisions on detention, any police attribution of suspected roles and a charging decision if prosecutors believe the evidence supports one. Until then, the established facts are limited: another Japanika branch was attacked, no casualty was reported there, an investigation is open and four people have been arrested in connection with the wider sequence.
