body: Beitar Jerusalem’s recruitment plan has moved beyond a simple search for depth. The club are considering additions at holding midfield and centre-back, but the number and profile of those signings depend on a registration question that has not yet been settled: whether Muaid Aseka receives temporary-resident status. Until that process is complete, Beitar cannot treat the extra foreign-player flexibility as available.

That administrative detail shapes the football decision. A foreign holding midfielder would give the team another specialist capable of protecting the space ahead of the centre-backs, slowing counterattacks and allowing the more adventurous midfielders to play higher. A new centre-back would answer a different need by adding cover in a position where injuries, suspensions and fixture congestion can expose a shallow rotation. The club may want both; registration and budget will decide whether both are realistic.

The need is not being assessed in isolation from the current squad. Work on the training ground has changed the internal view of at least one player who was not initially central to the plan. That is a useful reminder that summer recruitment is not a fixed shopping list. A strong camp can remove a position from immediate priority, just as a departure or a poor physical assessment can create a new one.

Several players are nevertheless outside the professional plans. Uri Dahan, Ravid Abergel and Ilay Hagag have been told they are not expected to form part of the coming-season group. Their situations matter beyond the individual decisions: moving players out can release salary room, simplify the matchday hierarchy and create minutes for a more deliberately balanced squad.

Ismaila Soro Tavares is the most consequential possible exit. Dinamo Bucharest have improved their proposal for the midfielder, but no agreement has been completed. Beitar therefore have to plan for two versions of the midfield at once—one with Tavares retained and another in which his departure creates both a tactical vacancy and additional room for recruitment.

The club’s challenge is sequencing. Committing early to a foreign centre-back could limit the options available if Tavares leaves; waiting too long could allow suitable targets to move elsewhere. The most efficient order is to establish Aseka’s registration status, clarify the Tavares negotiation and only then allocate the remaining foreign-player places. Each choice changes the value of the next one.

For now, this remains a squad-construction story rather than a transfer announcement. Beitar are exploring two positions, three players have been placed outside the plans and Dinamo’s interest in Tavares has strengthened, but none of those strands constitutes a completed incoming deal. The eventual shape of the squad will reveal whether the club prioritised immediate defensive security or preserved flexibility for a later market opportunity.

body: Beitar Jerusalem’s traditional open training session produced a serious safety concern when Omer Atzili and Yarden Cohen were burned by flares at the club’s Beit Vagan complex. Sport5 reports that roughly 5,000 supporters attended and that a large number of flares and firecrackers were set off while the players trained. The report does not give a medical classification for either player’s injury, so their condition should not be described more precisely until the club provides one.

The problem extended beyond two isolated contacts with pyrotechnics. According to Sport5, firefighters were called after a fire spread inside the training complex. That turns the episode from familiar pre-season theatre into a question of crowd management and player safety. The photographs and atmosphere surrounding an open session can be powerful for a club, but the sporting value disappears quickly when players, staff or supporters are placed in danger.

ONE separately reported that thousands of supporters filled the session with songs, flares and players being carried on shoulders. Its coverage framed the turnout as evidence of belief around Beitar after the club’s strong season-ticket sales. That enthusiasm is real and commercially significant, but it also makes the distinction between celebration and control more important. A large crowd inside a working training facility needs routes, boundaries and enforcement suited to the number of people present.

The timing raises the immediate football question. Beitar are preparing for domestic opposition and the Conference League qualifying programme, and Atzili remains one of the side’s most influential attacking players. Cohen is also an important first-team option. Until examinations or an official club update are available, it would be wrong to claim either player will miss a match; it is equally wrong to treat burns sustained during training as a harmless detail.

The next responsible update should answer three concrete points: the severity of both injuries, whether either player’s training load changes, and what operational review follows the fire. The incident should not be inflated with unverified medical language, but it should not be reduced to colourful footage either. Sport5’s report establishes that two players were hurt and emergency personnel attended the complex.

Beitar’s support can be one of the club’s largest competitive and financial assets. Protecting that atmosphere requires the club and relevant authorities to make sure the next open event can retain its intensity without asking players or spectators to absorb avoidable risk. For now, the injuries—not the spectacle—are the part of the session that demands follow-up.

title: Israel U20 handball beat Poland by eight to keep world route open
dek: Needing a seven-goal win, Israel delivered a 39–31 victory to finish the group on top and move into the 9th–16th classification phase with World Championship qualification still available.

source.originalTitle: סיימה בראש: העתודה גברה 31:39 על פולין

body: Israel’s men’s U20 handball side turned a demanding qualification equation into a 39–31 victory over Poland. Sport5 reports that Israel entered the match needing to win by seven goals. An eight-goal margin took the team to the top of the group and into the 9th–16th classification matches, from which a place at the World Championship remains available.

The result was not a routine recovery. Israel had lost to Romania and Czechia, leaving little room for another incomplete performance. The coaching staff accepted that the required margin called for risk, including extended phases without a goalkeeper. That approach exposed space when possession changed, but it also helped Israel create the pace and volume of attacks needed to chase the target rather than merely the win.

A 19–14 half-time lead supplied belief without completing the job. Poland reduced the gap to three early in the second half and kept the match between two and four goals for a long stretch. Israel therefore had to produce a second surge after the initial momentum had disappeared. The decisive sequence came late, when the lead grew beyond the seven-goal threshold and the team protected it through the closing possessions.

Asaf Sharon scored 13 goals and Tal Eckstein added eight, according to Sport5. Sharon’s Latin spelling and national-team record are also documented by the European Handball Federation. Goalkeeper Yonatan Ben-Shitrit made seven saves in the first half, while Eitan Elbaz contributed five later in the match. Those interventions mattered because the attacking gamble could only work if Israel found enough defensive stops to turn pressure into transition opportunities.

The victory changes the tournament but does not complete the qualification task. Israel now enter the classification stage with access to the World Championship route, not a guaranteed ticket. The distinction is important: the Poland performance created another opportunity after the earlier defeats, and the next fixtures will determine whether the comeback has a larger consequence.

For Israeli handball, the most encouraging part is the response to a precise competitive demand. The players knew the margin, lost control of it temporarily, and still found the final run required. That combination of tactical courage and late execution gives the next phase genuine weight rather than turning it into a consolation bracket.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv have resolved the most important internal decision of their summer: Dor Peretz will remain captain and lead the team into Kenny Miller’s first full season. The club’s own record confirms that Peretz signed a new contract, ending a period in which he and his family considered the professional and personal case for moving abroad.

That choice is more consequential than retaining one experienced midfielder. Peretz is the bridge between a dressing room accustomed to title expectations and a coach still installing his authority. He offers penalty-box running, leadership and an understanding of the club’s competitive temperature; just as importantly, his decision prevents Maccabi from having to replace a captain while simultaneously rebuilding other areas of the side.

Miller’s influence formed part of the calculation. Appointed head coach for 2026/27 after helping stabilise the end of last season, he inherited a team that recovered sufficiently to win the State Cup but still conceded too freely. Peretz believes the Scot restored standards and direction. The new campaign will test whether those standards can become a repeatable structure rather than an emotional late-season response.

The tactical demand is clearest without the ball. Miller wants fewer goals conceded and longer periods of controlled intensity, which requires more than centre-backs winning duels. The distance between the midfield and defence must shrink after possession is lost, wide players must recover quickly enough to protect the full-backs, and Peretz must judge when his trademark forward runs are worth vacating central cover.

The Super Cup exposes the problem before the squad is complete. Kristijan Belic, Elad Madmon, Tyrese Asante and Kervin Andrade were reported suspended for the meeting with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, while Helio Varela had not returned from his post-World Cup break at the time of the pre-match briefing. Dan Glazer is the confirmed summer addition available to re-enter the side, but one familiar midfielder does not solve every structural absence.

Recruitment therefore matters in two different ways. Maccabi need quality, but Miller also needs players whose arrival dates leave enough time for tactical integration. A late signing can lift the theoretical ceiling of the squad while offering little immediate help with pressing triggers, rest-defence positions or set-piece assignments. The coach expects additions, yet only a named and completed registration should alter the published squad picture.

The calendar removes any comfortable bedding-in period. Maccabi open with a trophy match at Turner and move into Europa League qualifying the following Thursday. Those fixtures demand different forms of control—surviving the emotional and physical pressure of an away domestic final, then managing a two-leg European tie in which a loose transition or poorly defended restart can reshape the month.

Peretz’s contract settles the leadership question, not the football argument. Maccabi now know who will carry Miller’s message onto the pitch. Whether the team can defend with the discipline its coach demands will depend on the captain’s positional choices, the readiness of the current group and the speed with which the club turns recruitment intentions into players Miller can actually use.

Ajax official Oscar Gloukh transfer announcement

body: Oscar Gloukh has chosen continuity over another summer transfer chase. The Israel midfielder says he is focused on Ajax unless the club decides otherwise, and has defined his second-season objective with unusual clarity: become a regular starter. It is a more demanding ambition than simply staying, because it places the argument about his future inside the team rather than in the rumour market.

Ajax’s official record makes the scale of that commitment plain. Gloukh joined from RB Salzburg in August 2025 for a guaranteed €14.75 million, with variables capable of lifting the fee to €17.25 million. He signed for five seasons, wears No. 10 and remains under contract until June 2030. Neither the investment nor the shirt guarantees selection, but both explain why a quick exit would amount to abandoning the project before its shape has settled.

His first campaign contained enough production to resist any easy verdict. Gloukh’s account of the season gives him nine goals and six assists in 38 appearances across all competitions. Those numbers show that he affected games. They do not show that Ajax found him a permanent tactical home, particularly during a year in which he worked under three coaches with different ideas and selection priorities.

The position question is therefore central. Gloukh sees his best work coming as a central midfielder or from the left with licence to move inside. A fixed touchline role gives him fewer chances to receive between the lines, turn toward goal and combine around the penalty area. The challenge for Ajax is to create those access points without leaving the team narrow or asking the full-back to defend an entire flank alone.

The challenge for Gloukh runs in the other direction. The current work has placed greater emphasis on forward defending, rapid recovery after losing the ball and collective pressing. A creative player becomes automatic at this level when the staff trust the moments between his touches: the angle of his press, his reaction to a turnover and his discipline when another midfielder advances. Technical authority gets him into the conversation; repeatable off-ball decisions keep him in the XI.

That is why the coaching instability matters without becoming an excuse. Ajax’s official record confirms the June departure of Oscar García after a brief first-team spell, another change in a season already marked by movement on the bench. Each reset altered the language used to judge the same player. Gloukh now needs a stable reference point quickly, because a second year cannot be evaluated forever through the disruption of the first.

Eran Zahavi’s earlier warning to his former Maccabi Tel Aviv team-mate fits the moment. Dutch football offered attacking possibility, but the historic image of Ajax could not simply be assumed to match the institution Gloukh was joining. That advice reads less like pessimism than a demand for realism: reputation supplies opportunity, while the daily structure determines whether a gifted midfielder actually develops.

For Israel, the best outcome is not a move for movement’s sake. It is a Gloukh who earns a defined role, plays through difficult weeks and becomes responsible for more than highlights. His public position removes one source of noise. Pre-season usage, pressing assignments and the first competitive team sheets will now reveal whether Ajax see their No. 10 as a specialist option or as part of the side’s permanent spine.

title: Israeli basketball coaches demand freeze on registration overhaul
dek: The coaches’ organisation has given the Basketball Association 14 days to explain a proposed fee increase and the removal of continuing-education requirements before considering legal and regulatory action.

source.name: Sport5
source.originalTitle: המכתב של ארגון המאמנים נגד איגוד הכדורסל

body: Israel’s basketball coaches’ organisation has asked the national association to suspend changes to coach registration and licence renewal for the 2026/27 season. Sport5 reports that the organisation’s legal adviser, Amir Cohen, sent a formal letter to the association with copies to culture and sports minister Miki Zohar and a Ministry of Sport representative.

The first disputed measure is financial. The letter says that from 1 October the cost of renewing a coaching certificate after the deadline would rise from NIS 90 to NIS 200. That is an increase of more than 120 per cent. The coaches’ organisation argues that a change of that scale requires a documented economic and professional explanation rather than a simple administrative notice.

The second measure concerns continuing education. According to Sport5, the association decided to remove a requirement for professional-development hours. The coaches’ organisation says members previously invested money and time to meet that standard and that abandoning it without consultation or explanation disregards both that investment and the professional rationale behind the earlier rule.

The letter frames the argument as a governance issue, not only a disagreement over price. It contends that the Basketball Association performs a public function and therefore carries heightened duties of transparency and reasoned decision-making. That is the coaches’ legal position as reported by Sport5; it is not yet a court finding, and the association’s complete response was not included in the report.

Three demands have been set with a 14-day deadline: the full minutes of the meetings in which the changes were adopted, a written explanation of their economic and professional basis, and a structured process for coaches to present their position. If those demands are not met, the organisation says it may seek regulatory intervention, freedom-of-information material or legal proceedings.

The practical significance extends through the basketball pyramid. Registration rules affect senior, youth and development coaches, while continuing education is part of the system that establishes common professional standards. The useful next update will be the association’s reasoning and whether implementation is paused; until then, the accurate description is a formal challenge and ultimatum, not a completed legal victory for either side.

body: Hapoel Tel Aviv have completed the signing of Tomáš Satoranský on a one-year contract, turning the previous agreement in principle into one of the club’s most significant moves of the summer. Sport5 reports that the transfer was formally announced on Wednesday, while Walla Sport also records a one-season deal. The 34-year-old Czech guard joins after the expiry of his Barcelona contract and will work under Dimitris Itoudis.

The announcement matters because it removes the principal uncertainty surrounding the transaction: Satoranský is now a Hapoel player, rather than a target with agreed terms. Walla Sport reports that Satoranský described the move as a challenge he had been anticipating and that Itoudis stressed the guard’s experience and team-first approach. Those remarks point towards a defined leadership role, even though Hapoel have not yet disclosed every registration detail attached to the deal.

Barcelona’s official departure record provides the scale of the experience Hapoel are acquiring. Satoranský’s contract ended on 30 June after a four-season second spell with the Catalan club. He made 315 appearances during that return and 465 across his two Barcelona periods, winning seven trophies. Barcelona also credits him with a club-record 888 EuroLeague assists in 207 games, a measure of both his longevity and his capacity to organise half-court offence at the highest European level.

The most recent EuroLeague numbers describe a facilitator rather than a high-volume scorer. In 25 games in 2025/26, all of them starts, the competition’s official profile lists Satoranský at 7.2 points, 3.6 rebounds and 4.4 assists in 24 minutes 59 seconds per game. He shot 45.8 per cent from three-point range, converting 33 of 72 attempts. That combination of efficient spot-up shooting and passing gives Itoudis flexibility when another guard initiates the possession.

Tactically, Satoranský’s 2.01-metre frame is central to the fit. He can see and pass over smaller defenders, defend more than one perimeter position and operate as either the primary ball-handler or the connective guard in a two-creator lineup. His official NBA profile records seven seasons in the league, adding a different level of experience to a player whose European résumé already includes long spells in Barcelona and elite international competition with Czechia.

One issue remains separate from the completed transfer. According to Sport5, Hapoel are examining whether Satoranský could qualify for Israeli citizenship through family ancestry and, eventually, local-player registration. That process has not been confirmed as complete. Until the relevant civil and league decisions are made, he must be treated in roster analysis as a foreign player; the signing itself does not determine his registration category.

For Hapoel, the immediate gain is control. Satoranský is not being recruited to dominate possession on every trip but to improve the quality of decisions around the first action: entering sets cleanly, exploiting size mismatches and keeping the ball moving after an advantage is created. The contract is official; the next meaningful questions concern how Itoudis distributes creation duties and whether the separate local-status process changes Hapoel’s options elsewhere on the roster.

body: Bnei Eilat have taken the most recognisable step yet in their attempt to climb out of Liga Bet, signing Gil Itzhak to a three-year contract. The 33-year-old forward moves from the National League environment into Israel’s fourth tier, a drop large enough to make the deal relevant beyond ordinary lower-division recruitment. It is a declaration that Eilat expect to compete for promotion now, not merely develop toward it.

The Israel Football Association’s player record confirms the spelling Gil Itzhak and separates the verified identity from the scale of the surrounding claims. His value to this project begins with senior experience and penalty-area judgement: knowing when to hold a centre-back, when to attack the near post and how to remain involved during matches in which a favoured side meets a deep defensive block.

The reported financial package underlines the ambition. It has been put at NIS 450,000 net per season, alongside housing, a car and a promotion bonus. Those terms have not been published by the club and should not be treated as an official salary disclosure. Even as reported figures, however, they describe a commitment far beyond the usual profile of a fourth-tier signing.

Itzhak is also one piece of a broader construction rather than a solitary marquee name. Kobi Refua is directing the sporting project, while Gidi Kanyuk, Ofek Fishler and Ben Yehezkel are among the experienced arrivals attached to the rebuild. The recruitment logic is clear: reduce the uncertainty of a promotion chase by placing players accustomed to higher levels in the decisive central positions.

That logic still has to survive the football. A forward can provide a focal point, but he cannot manufacture a coherent attack by himself. Eilat need runners close enough to feed on second balls, full-backs capable of supplying width and midfielders who can move possession quickly before opponents settle into two compact lines. If those connections fail, Itzhak’s reputation may make him easier to isolate rather than harder to defend.

Liga Bet brings its own demands. Pitch conditions, long journeys, physical duels and uneven match rhythms can punish a squad built around what players achieved elsewhere. Eilat will often carry the burden of expectation and may face opponents prepared to surrender possession for long periods. Patience, set-piece quality and availability across the season will matter as much as the names on the team sheet.

The three-year term changes the meaning of the signing too. This is not a short promotional appearance designed only to create summer attention. It gives the club continuity if promotion requires more than one attempt, while also making squad planning and financial discipline more important. An ambitious package is useful only when it fits a budget that can support the entire group through the length of the agreement.

For the wider Israeli game, the move pulls attention toward a division that rarely receives national coverage. body: Manchester United have signed Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa on a contract running to June 2031, subject to registration. The agreement gives United five seasons of control over a 29-year-old midfielder whose value is rooted less in projection than in repeatable Premier League production: he arrives as Belgium’s captain, a recent European trophy winner and a player already accustomed to carrying possession through crowded central areas.

The price requires more care than the contract. A £35 million fee has been widely reported, but United did not publish a figure in their announcement, so the number should not be treated as a club-confirmed term. What can be stated without qualification is the length of the commitment. This is not a short bridge deal for an experienced player; United have invested in Tielemans as part of the midfield’s medium-term structure.

His final season at Villa supplies the obvious sporting case. Tielemans recorded seven Premier League assists, then helped Villa win the Europa League and scored the opening goal in the final against Freiburg. He followed that campaign by captaining Belgium to the 2026 World Cup quarter-finals. United list him on 90 senior international appearances, a body of work that sharply reduces the uncertainty around temperament, workload and elite-match exposure.

The more interesting question is what type of control United believe they have bought. Tielemans is not simply a high-volume creator who must be stationed close to the penalty area. His more valuable interventions often come earlier: receiving with pressure arriving, opening a passing lane with his first touch and accelerating an attack without forcing a low-percentage ball. In a team that wants cleaner progression, those decisions can be as important as the final assist.

That does not make him a one-man solution. A midfielder asked to dictate from deep needs protection behind the ball and runners ahead of it; a No. 8 given licence to advance needs a partner capable of holding the centre when possession turns over. Tielemans can perform parts of both roles, but flexibility is useful only when the surrounding responsibilities are clear. United’s task is to build a midfield relationship, not merely insert a famous name into an empty square on a team sheet.

The contract also frames the risk. Tielemans enters at 29, an age at which United should expect immediate authority rather than a lengthy adaptation project. Five years protects continuity and, in theory, avoids returning to the market too soon, but it also carries the physical and financial exposure that accompanies any long agreement with an established player. The deal will be judged by the quality of his prime seasons, not simply by whether he remains available at its end.

Tielemans described the move as the culmination of years of work and pointed to United’s ambition to compete for major trophies. Director of football Jason Wilcox emphasised his consistency, technique and mentality. Those qualities fit the logic of the recruitment: after a season in which he influenced league matches and a European final, United are paying for a player expected to stabilise important phases immediately rather than one who may eventually learn how to do so.

Registration and pre-season integration now come before the tactical verdict. Tielemans could become the controlling passer in a pair, the forward-moving member of a three or a hybrid midfielder whose starting position changes with the opponent. The most convincing version will not ask him to perform every central-midfield function at once. United have secured an experienced organiser through 2031; the decisive work is to give that organiser a coherent platform.

title: Paris, 1993: the night Israel turned 2–1 into history
dek: France were preparing to celebrate World Cup qualification. Israel, bottom of the group and without a competitive win, scored twice in the final eleven minutes to leave the Parc des Princes in disbelief.

source.name: FIFA
source.originalTitle: Cinq matches mémorables | Qualifications UEFA | Mondial 2026

body: The scoreboard at the Parc des Princes said 2–1 to France and the clock had entered its final eleven minutes. For the hosts, this was supposed to be the night a place at the 1994 World Cup became official. For Israel, sitting at the bottom of Group 6 and still searching for a first win of the campaign, there was no qualification prize left to chase. That imbalance is what makes the ending endure: one team had the ticket almost in its hand; the other played as if the match itself was enough.

Ronen Harazi had given Israel a 20th-minute lead. France responded with the authority expected of a side containing Eric Cantona, Didier Deschamps, Jean-Pierre Papin, Laurent Blanc and Marcel Desailly. Franck Sauzée equalised in the 28th minute and David Ginola made it 2–1 in the 39th. The Israel Football Association’s official record confirms that score at half-time, a familiar shape for a favourite briefly inconvenienced before control is restored.

Control never became comfort. Shlomo Scharf’s Israel stayed close enough for one moment to matter. In the 64th minute, Eyal Berkovic replaced Avi Nimni. With eight minutes of normal time remaining, the substitute scored the equaliser. The IFA records it in the 82nd minute; FIFA’s retrospective places it at 82 minutes. Either way, the effect was immediate: France had gone from celebration to calculation, and the stadium was waiting for the whistle rather than a party.

Then came the goal that fixed the match in Israeli sporting memory. In the second minute of added time, Reuven Atar scored to make it 3–2. The official records agree on the scorer and the final result. UEFA later quoted Atar describing it as the greatest moment of his career. It was also his first goal for the senior national team, delivered in Paris against a side that believed its evening had already been written.

The result did not send Israel to the World Cup. The IFA campaign record shows a team that finished sixth with one win, three draws and six defeats; the victory in Paris was that lone win. Its meaning came from a different place. Israel had lost the reverse fixture 4–0 and had conceded heavily elsewhere in the group. The Parc des Princes offered no broader redemption, only proof that one match can break entirely from the season around it.

For France, the shock became the first half of a national sporting trauma. They still had one home qualifier left and needed a draw against Bulgaria. A month later, Emil Kostadinov’s late winner made it France 1–2 Bulgaria and took the visitors to the World Cup instead. FIFA’s histories connect the two Paris defeats, but the Israeli victory deserves to stand on its own: it created the danger before Bulgaria delivered the final consequence.

More than three decades later, the game remains powerful because its facts resist embellishment. Israel trailed at half-time. Berkovic entered from the bench and equalised. Atar scored in added time. A team with nothing left in the table found something permanent in the record: the precise sequence is why people still tell the story.

title: Mexico, 1970: the goal that put Israel on the World Cup map
dek: Three minutes after Sweden took the lead in Toluca, Mordechai Spiegler answered from distance and created a moment that still stands alone in Israeli football history.

source.name: FIFA
source.originalTitle: Israel celebrate Mexico 70 milestone

verificationSources.label: Israel Football Association: Sweden 1–1 Israel
Israel Football Association: Italy 0–0 Israel
Israel Football Association: 1970 World Cup campaign
FIFA+: Israel at the FIFA World Cup

body: Israel arrived in Mexico in 1970 as World Cup debutants, a team entering a tournament whose scale had previously been experienced from far away. Qualification had been secured against Australia, and the opening group match brought a 2–0 defeat by Uruguay. That left Emanuel Sheffer’s side needing a response against Sweden in Toluca, not for symbolism, but to remain alive in the competition.

The official campaign record gives the pressure a simple shape. Israel had only three group matches and no protective route into a second phase after a slow start. With two points awarded for a victory at the time, another defeat would have left the final fixture against Italy with almost no competitive leverage. Sweden was therefore the point at which participation had to become resistance.

The first half on 7 June ended goalless. Sweden then broke through in the 56th minute through Tom Turesson, according to the Israel Football Association’s official match record. For a debutant already behind in the group, the goal could have made the tournament feel suddenly brief. Instead, Israel answered almost immediately.

Mordechai Spiegler equalised in the 59th minute. FIFA’s retrospective describes a strike from around 20 metres; the IFA record confirms the scorer and the 1–1 final score. The distance matters because the goal was not the end of a slow passing sequence inside the six-yard box. It was a decision taken early enough and struck cleanly enough to change the match before Sweden could settle into its lead.

The goal remains unique. The IFA’s campaign record shows that Israel scored once across its three matches in Mexico, making Spiegler the country’s only men’s World Cup goalscorer. That distinction can sound like a museum label when separated from the game. In its real setting, it was an equaliser three minutes after falling behind, scored under the pressure of possible elimination.

Its timing also changed the tactical problem. Sweden had no opportunity to protect the lead through a long spell of slower possession or deeper defending; Israel removed that game state before it could settle. The remaining half-hour became a contest for the next goal rather than an attempt to escape a controlled Swedish advantage. Holding the draw was active match management, not simply survival after a late consolation.

Israel’s team was built around collective discipline rather than the promise of one star carrying every phase. The official line-up against Sweden included goalkeeper Itzhak Vissoker, captain David Primo, Itzhak Shum, Giora Spiegel and Spiegler. FIFA later recalled the group’s club-like cohesion: preparation, shared responsibility and the removal of ego were central to how the players believed they could compete.

Four days later, Israel drew 0–0 with Italy in the same city. The IFA record lists an Italian side containing Luigi Riva and Gianni Rivera, yet Israel completed the match without conceding. Combined with the Sweden draw, it meant the debutants left Mexico with two points under the scoring system then in use and only three goals allowed in three matches.

Israel have not returned to the men’s World Cup since 1970. That absence increases the weight placed on every surviving photograph and replay, but the achievement does not need romantic inflation. The sequence is strong enough: a first tournament, a defeat, an immediate response against Sweden, a clean sheet against Italy and one goal that still accounts for the country’s entire World Cup scoring record.

body: Kawhi Leonard’s proposed return to Toronto remains on hold, and NBA commissioner Adam Silver has now placed the league’s clearest broad timeframe around the case: he hopes the external investigation affecting the transaction will be completed this summer. Silver also separated the league’s role from the commercial decision, saying the NBA did not order the trade to stop and that the two teams chose not to complete it while the investigation remains open.

That distinction matters because the agreement is unusually large even by NBA offseason standards. The proposed package sends Leonard to Toronto, with Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick moving to Los Angeles alongside unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033, second-round picks in 2030 and 2033, and a 2027 first-round pick swap. It was agreed in principle on 30 June but remains listed as on hold rather than completed.

Toronto explained its position on 9 July. The club said it had been informed that acquiring Leonard would also mean assuming the risk of any outcome from the investigation that might affect the player. The Raptors therefore elected to wait for the process to finish, while stressing that they still want to bring Leonard back. The pause is not a renegotiation of the basketball package on the public record; it is a response to uncertainty over the status of the contract and player.

The underlying review concerns whether a reported $28 million endorsement agreement between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC breached NBA salary-cap rules. The league opened the investigation in September 2025 and appointed outside counsel to conduct it. No violation has been established, and the existence of an investigation should not be treated as a finding against Leonard, the Clippers or any individual involved.

Silver’s latest intervention narrows one point but does not resolve the central problem. The commissioner said the external inquiry must run its course and maintained a summer target rather than giving a fixed completion date. For Toronto, that leaves a major part of its 2026–27 roster plan suspended: the club cannot build with certainty around Leonard while the players and draft assets in the proposed exchange remain attached to an uncompleted transaction.

The sporting stakes are significant. Leonard is coming off a season in which he averaged 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds and 3.6 assists across 65 games. Toronto, meanwhile, improved by 16 wins, finished fifth in defensive efficiency and took Cleveland to seven games in the first round. Adding an elite half-court scorer and defender would change the Raptors’ ceiling, but the cost—two rotation players and control of multiple future draft assets—also makes the unresolved risk impossible to dismiss as paperwork.

Los Angeles are waiting on the other side of the same transaction. The Clippers have already moved toward a younger roster, and the proposed return of Ingram, Dick and long-range draft capital would accelerate that reset. Until the investigation is concluded and the trade is formally processed, however, neither franchise can treat its intended return as settled inventory.

The accurate position is therefore narrower than the most dramatic versions of the story. Leonard has not completed a move to Toronto; the agreed framework has not been cancelled; and the NBA has not announced a sanction. Silver has expressed an expectation that the review will finish this summer, but the calendar remains open. The next decisive event will be the investigation’s conclusion—not another round of trade speculation.

title: World Cup final halftime reportedly set to stretch towards 30 minutes
dek: The planned 11-minute performance would require a substantially longer interval than the 15-minute maximum in Law 7, although FIFA has not publicly confirmed the final restart timetable.

source.originalTitle: חריגה מהחוקה: מחצית גמר המונדיאל תוארך מאוד

verificationSources.label: IFAB Law 7: duration of the match and half-time limit

body: The World Cup final’s half-time interval is reportedly being prepared to last between 25 and 30 minutes, roughly twice the conventional break, so that the tournament’s first final halftime show can be staged at New York New Jersey Stadium. The longer timetable has not been publicly confirmed by FIFA. It should therefore be treated as a reported operational plan, not a settled amendment to the match schedule.

The technical conflict is straightforward. Law 7 of the Laws of the Game says players are entitled to a half-time interval not exceeding 15 minutes. Competition rules must state the duration, and the interval can be altered only with the referee’s permission, but the published law still sets 15 minutes as the ceiling. A 25–30-minute pause would not be a small scheduling adjustment; it would require a clear explanation of how the match authorities intend to apply that provision.

FIFA has confirmed the entertainment component. The governing body describes an 11-minute live broadcast featuring Madonna, Shakira, BTS and Justin Bieber, with Burna Boy, Gustavo Dudamel and the PS22 Chorus featuring Coldplay also listed. The final takes place on Sunday, 19 July. What remains unannounced is the full interval window needed to move production equipment and performers onto the field, deliver the show and clear the playing surface for the second-half restart.

That distinction between performance time and interval time is crucial. An 11-minute show cannot simply occupy an ordinary 15-minute break: players and staff also need time to leave the pitch, receive tactical and medical instructions, return through the tunnel and complete any permitted re-warm-up. Production crews would need to install and remove staging around those football operations. The reported 25–30-minute figure reflects the total logistical window rather than the duration of the music alone.

From a performance perspective, the concern is not that an extra quarter-hour automatically produces an injury. The issue is a break in routine at the highest-intensity point of the tournament. Players normally manage hydration, treatment and tactical adjustment against a predictable restart. A substantially longer pause could require revised warm-up procedures, especially for substitutes and for starters whose muscle temperature drops while they remain indoors.

The referee’s role also needs precision. Law 7 allows the referee to approve an alteration to the interval, but that is different from improvising an event schedule on matchday. Teams, match officials and broadcasters would need one documented restart plan before kick-off, including the warning sequence for players to leave the dressing room and the point at which the field returns to sporting control after the production has cleared it.

For now, three facts can be separated cleanly. The final and its 11-minute show are official; the Laws of the Game retain a 15-minute half-time maximum; and a 25–30-minute interval is being reported without a matching public FIFA timetable. Until that final operational notice appears, the scale of the extension—and the mechanism used to authorise it—remains the important unresolved part of the story.

His college route was already a lesson in adaptation. Sibande moved from Miami University in Ohio to Pittsburgh and was named the Atlantic Coast Conference’s Sixth Man of the Year in 2023. That award describes a player who learned to influence games without requiring every possession to be organised around him, a useful foundation for an import entering an Israeli rotation with established domestic guards.

The professional journey has been broader still. Sibande began with Kataja in Finland, then played for Maroussi and Merkezefendi before reaching Spain with Girona. Darüşşafaka and Chemnitz added two more tactical environments, so Kiryat Ata are not asking a first-year professional to solve the ordinary problems of travel, scouting adjustments and changing roles at the same time as he learns the league.

The ACB’s official record lists 25 league appearances for Girona in 2024–25. That season matters less as a headline number than as evidence of the level he has already had to process: Liga Endesa demands quick reads in pick-and-roll coverage, disciplined off-ball positioning and the ability to create a usable possession late in the shot clock. Kiryat Ata are buying into that accumulated experience as much as any single scoring average.

Tactically, Sibande’s value begins with pressure. A guard of his size can attack a switching defender, rebound down to start transition and absorb contact when the first action does not create a clean lane. Kiryat Ata will still need to establish how much primary creation he carries and how the shooting is distributed around him, but the signing increases the number of line-ups in which the team can defend with comparable size across three perimeter positions.

The next stage is integration rather than reputation. body: Ronen Hanzis is returning to competitive football with Ironi Beit Dagan after two seasons away from the senior game. The 24-year-old left-sided attacker joins a club in Liga Bet South A, Israel’s fourth tier, at a point when the prestige of his development years matters far less than his capacity to train, recover and contribute every week.

The pedigree remains unusual for this level. Hanzis moved from Maccabi Petah Tikva into Maccabi Tel Aviv’s youth system in 2019, reached the senior side the following year and made his first-team debut in the 2020 Super Cup. He later came off the bench in Maccabi’s Champions League play-off against Salzburg, an appearance that placed him one tie from the group stage while still a teenager.

His clearest early evidence of sustained senior production came during a loan at Beitar Tel Aviv Bat Yam. Maccabi’s official career record credits him with six goals in 22 appearances there. The same record lists 33 youth-international appearances and six goals for Israel, showing how regularly he was selected within the national pathway before his club momentum slowed.

None of those numbers can substitute for current match fitness. Hanzis last appeared in the 2023/24 season, so Beit Dagan are not receiving a player whose recent output can be projected neatly from one campaign to the next. They are receiving a footballer with high-level references and a long competitive interruption. That combination creates upside, but it also makes patience and workload management central to the signing.

Beit Dagan’s setting changes the terms of his career. At Maccabi, a young winger had to win isolated minutes inside a squad built to chase titles and European qualification. In Liga Bet, Hanzis can pursue continuity and a larger share of attacking responsibility. The opportunity is greater; the entitlement is not. His place must still be earned against teammates who already understand the division’s tempo and physical demands.

The useful performance markers go beyond goals. Beit Dagan need to see whether Hanzis can repeat high-speed runs, receive under contact and recover quickly enough to press again after an attack breaks down. His movement without the ball and the quality of his final action will reveal more than a single sprint or an eye-catching dribble. A returning winger has to reconnect the sequence between anticipation, acceleration and decision.

Liga Bet is not a controlled rehabilitation environment. Matches can become direct, second balls carry disproportionate value and surfaces or game states do not always favour a technically accomplished wide player. That should not diminish Hanzis’s advantages; it should sharpen the test. If he can impose his timing and touch without withdrawing from the physical work, his background ought to become visible in repeatable actions rather than in reputation alone.

This is a reset with a measurable first objective: remain available and accumulate a serious run of matches. Goals, assists and a possible route back up the pyramid can follow, but they are downstream of continuity. Hanzis has already been close to elite football and has already spent a long period outside the competitive rhythm. Beit Dagan now offer him something more valuable than a nostalgic label—the chance to make his present-day game the subject again.

title: Wærenskjold wins the fastest stage in Tour de France history
dek: The Uno-X rider took the Nevers sprint after 161.3 kilometres at an average 50.91 km/h, eclipsing a record that had stood since Mario Cipollini’s 1999 victory.

source.name: Sport5

body: Søren Wærenskjold won stage 11 of the Tour de France in Nevers and reached the finish with two achievements compressed into the same 3hr 10min 06sec. The Uno-X Mobility rider secured his first Tour stage victory over the 161.3 kilometres from Vichy, while the peloton’s average of 50.91 km/h made this the fastest road stage in the race’s history.

The finish did not resemble a perfectly controlled sprint assembled around one dominant train. Wærenskjold launched early in a broken sequence, held his speed and denied Olav Kooij the space needed to come past. Jasper Philipsen was classified third after the finish review. The Norwegian’s advantage came from recognising the moment before the established sprinters had imposed their preferred order, then committing without waiting for reassurance.

That distinction matters because raw speed alone does not explain this result. Wærenskjold is a powerful classics rider who can survive demanding terrain and produce a heavy acceleration, rather than a pure sprinter whose entire programme is organised around the final 200 metres. In Nevers, those broader attributes became sprint weapons: stability in a disordered approach, enough strength to open early and the resistance to prevent his effort from collapsing before the line.

The stage record gives the day a second layer. Mario Cipollini’s 1999 victory between Laval and Blois had set the previous road-stage benchmark at 50.355 km/h. Wærenskjold’s stage exceeded it by more than half a kilometre per hour despite two fourth-category climbs and an advertised 1,400 metres of elevation gain. The short route and sustained tailwind helped, but neither factor could produce the number without a race that refused to settle.

Nelson Oliveira, Mathis Le Berre and Anthon Charmig kept the breakaway alive until 5.5 kilometres remained, obliging the teams interested in the sprint to maintain the chase. Julian Alaphilippe had already lost contact. That prolonged contest prevented the lull that can arrive when a break is caught early and the peloton begins negotiating position rather than speed; the pursuit fed directly into the frantic final approach.

Uno-X then converted the collective tempo into a specific opportunity. Moving Wærenskjold forward before the narrowed run to Nevers did not deliver the kind of long, uninterrupted lead-out that removes decisions from a sprinter. It gave him something more suitable to his profile: contact with the front and permission to choose the launch himself. His early move was a tactical response to uncertainty, not a desperate substitute for pace.

The general classification remained intact. Tadej Pogačar finished safely in the main group and retained a 3min 36sec lead over Jonas Vingegaard, with Remco Evenepoel third at 4min 06sec. Yet a day without time gaps was not necessarily a day without cost. After the Massif Central, the contenders and their support riders were denied the lower-intensity transition that the stage profile might have suggested.

For Uno-X Mobility, the victory is the team’s second at the Tour after Jonas Abrahamsen’s breakthrough in 2025. For Wærenskjold, it changes the way rivals must calculate fast finishes: he does not need a conventional sprint to become dangerous, and disorder may improve his chances rather than diminish them. Nevers will remain in the record book for 50.91 km/h, but the winning lesson was less mechanical—the rider who understood the finish first was still strong enough to make that understanding decisive.

body: Hapoel Eilat have appointed Rani Cohen as chief executive as the club prepares to return to Israel’s top basketball division. The timing makes the role more than a routine administrative change. Eilat are moving from a dominant National League campaign into a competition with different licensing demands, salary pressures and roster risk, and Cohen arrives with experience inside both a major club and the league’s central administration.

The promotion was earned emphatically. Eilat secured their place in April with an 84–70 win in Ashkelon and completed the National League regular season with 29 victories from 30 games. The Israel Basketball Association’s final club record lists a scoring average of 94.2 points and 78.1 conceded, a margin that confirms the scale of their superiority rather than reducing the season to one decisive result.

Cohen previously served as acting chief executive of the Basketball Super League during the disrupted 2023–24 season. The league’s own records credit him with managing the organisation through that period before David Bason’s appointment. Earlier, Cohen held a senior administrative role at Hapoel Jerusalem, giving him direct experience of the commercial and operational standards expected around a club competing at the top of the domestic game.

His immediate brief in Eilat is structurally different from winning promotion. The first clock is administrative: licensing, registrations, budget controls and commercial commitments must all be ready for a division that applies more financial and operational pressure. Decisions made in separate departments during a National League season now have to run through one top-flight plan.

The second clock is sporting. A roster built to control a long second-division campaign must now survive weekly match-up disadvantages without accepting contracts that damage the club beyond one year. Foreign-player balance, domestic depth and the relationship between coaching priorities and the available budget become connected decisions rather than isolated recruitment choices.

Eilat’s geography adds another layer. The club must recruit players and staff to Israel’s southernmost top-level market, manage travel and training logistics, and convert the momentum of a 29–1 season into a stable local audience. None of those tasks is solved by the promotion record itself. Cohen’s value will be measured by whether the club can build repeatable systems around those constraints rather than relying on the emotional lift of returning to the league.

No contract length or detailed executive structure has been made public. The verified position is that Cohen takes charge of a promoted club with an unusually strong statistical base and a compressed transition window. title: The final is not Messi against Yamal. It is a contest over where risk lives
dek: Argentina can make Spain’s possession uncomfortable; Spain can make Argentina defend choices rather than players. Sunday’s final will be decided by the spaces around its two headline names.

source.name: Associated Press
source.originalTitle: The World Cup final is set, with Messi and Argentina facing Yamal and Spain for the title on Sunday

verificationSources.label: Confirmed finalists and current championship context
FIFA final date, venue and competition schedule
FIFA historical context for an Argentina–Spain final

body: The temptation is to market Sunday’s World Cup final as a private appointment between Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal. It is an irresistible image: the defining player of one generation opposite the young attacker already being asked to carry the next. It is also a poor tactical description. Messi and Yamal will influence the final most profoundly through the decisions they force from players who are nowhere near them. The trophy will be decided by which team can move that risk into an area it is prepared to defend.

The competitive frame is unusually rich. Argentina reached New York New Jersey by recovering from a 55th-minute deficit to beat England 2–1; Spain arrived through a controlled 2–0 victory over France. FIFA’s schedule places the final on Sunday, 19 July. It will be the first World Cup final between the reigning world champions and the reigning European champions. Argentina can become the first side since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy, while Spain are seeking the second world title in their history. The coaches also share unusual history: Luis de la Fuente taught Lionel Scaloni during his coaching education in Spain, and both have spoken publicly about their friendship. Familiarity will sharpen the contest, but it does not remove the need to solve what the other team has become.

Spain’s central question is how aggressively to use the width that has helped them dictate territory. Yamal can receive outside the opposing block, carry a defender towards him and open an inside lane for a midfielder or overlapping runner. The value of that pattern is not the isolation alone; it is the chain reaction. Argentina must decide whether the nearest midfielder moves across, whether the full-back steps out and which player then protects the pass released behind that pressure. Spain want the defending side to make several connected choices at speed.

Argentina’s answer cannot simply be to assign more bodies to Yamal. Every additional defender pulled towards Spain’s right side increases the space available elsewhere, particularly if the first clearance is not secured. Lionel Scaloni’s team need the near-side pressure to be forceful enough to delay the attack and the far side compact enough to contest the next pass. That is a problem of distances rather than bravery. If those distances expand, Spain can keep the attack alive without requiring Yamal to beat two players himself.

Messi poses the inverse problem. He does not need to remain fixed in one lane, so Spain cannot solve him with a permanent marker without damaging their own midfield geometry. If a centre-back follows him away from the line, Argentina gain depth for a runner. If a midfielder drops too early, Spain lose pressure on the next Argentine pass. If nobody follows, Messi can receive facing forward. Spain must therefore defend the handover: the moment responsibility for him passes from midfield to defence without either line losing its shape.

That makes possession after possession loss the final’s most consequential phase. Spain can spend long periods advancing with structure, but the players positioned behind an attack must be ready for Argentina’s first forward pass. Messi’s threat is magnified when he receives before the Spanish block has reset and a runner can attack the space beyond him. Spain do not have to eliminate every turnover. They must prevent a turnover from becoming a clean, central transition in which Argentina can choose the timing of the final pass.

Argentina face a related burden when their own attacks end. Their comeback against England was built through sustained territory late in the match, but Spain are more comfortable using the ball as a defensive instrument. An Argentine press that arrives in separate waves would allow Spain to pass around the first challenge and force the defending midfield to cover too much ground. The champions need a clear trigger—an awkward reception, a backwards pass or a player facing his own goal—rather than spending energy on pressure that Spain can see coming.

The midfield contest will consequently be less about raw possession than the quality of each side’s next action. Spain can dominate the ball and still be tactically vulnerable if their circulation leaves no protection for the loss. Argentina can accept less of the ball and still control important moments if their first recovery pass escapes pressure. Both sides must resist the easy interpretation that patience belongs to Spain and disruption to Argentina. Each will need both, often within the same sequence.

Spain’s first New Jersey session added a small but relevant availability question. Yamal and Pedro Porro worked separately from the main group, and the Spanish federation described the decision as precautionary workload management. Porro has been managing a minor hamstring problem, while Yamal has aches and bruising from the France semi-final; both are expected to be available on Sunday. Tactically, the distinction matters because Spain can protect Yamal’s training volume without redesigning the right side, while Porro’s condition affects the depth available behind it.

The venue places another kind of load on both structures. The final is scheduled for 15:00 local time in an outdoor stadium, and Spain have three days to adjust to New Jersey’s heat and humidity. FIFA says the final pitch was installed in May after years of research and was hybrid-stitched to pursue consistency across the tournament, although players and teams have still criticised how the surface has felt in matches. If the day becomes physically draining or the ball moves less cleanly than either side expects, compact distances and controlled accelerations will become more valuable than continuous pressure.

The bench may become decisive because the match offers sharply different game states. Argentina’s late semi-final winner came from substitute Lautaro Martínez, evidence of how a new penalty-area reference can alter the value of territory already established. Spain’s challenge is different: their replacements must preserve the spacing and counter-pressure that make their possession coherent, not merely add fresh dribbling. A final that remains level will reward control of fatigue; an early goal will test whether the leading side can continue to make the opponent defend.

Messi and Yamal deserve the billing because they can execute actions unavailable to almost everyone else. The more revealing contest, however, lies in the architecture built around that talent. Spain must decide how much structure they are willing to place ahead of the ball. Argentina must decide how much territory they can concede without losing access to the next attack. The iconic photograph will probably contain one of the two stars. The winning mechanism is more likely to be found a few metres away, in the player who recognised where the risk had moved before the rest of the stadium did.

title: Stiles inquest finds heading-linked CTE contributed to his death
dek: A coroner found the England champion had severe dementia caused by Alzheimer’s disease and CTE, with repeated heading responsible for the CTE.

source.name: Sport1 / Maariv

source.author: Sport1 desk

verificationSources.label: Independent report of the Stockport inquest findings

body: A coroner has concluded that a brain condition caused by repeated heading contributed to the death of England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles. Senior coroner Alison Mutch reached the finding at an inquest in Stockport, almost six years after Stiles died in October 2020 at the age of 78. The ruling is deliberately more precise than the claim that football alone caused his death: it identifies a specific disease process, its cause in his case and its contribution to the final medical picture.

Postmortem examination showed severe dementia associated with both Alzheimer’s disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. Neuropathologist Daniel Du Plessis attributed the CTE to Stiles’s repeated heading during his career. The inquest heard an estimate of roughly 140,000 headers across his playing life. That number describes the scale of the exposure presented to the court; it does not mean medicine can assign equal damage to every header or calculate an individual player’s future risk from a simple total.

The distinction between Alzheimer’s disease and CTE is important. They are different neurodegenerative conditions, although both can contribute to cognitive decline, and CTE is established through characteristic changes found in brain tissue after death. The inquest’s conclusion concerns Stiles as an individual, based on his medical evidence and exposure history. It adds a powerful legal finding to football’s brain-health debate without turning one case into a universal diagnosis for former players.

Stiles’s stature gives the ruling unusual resonance. The Football Association’s official record shows that he played every minute of England’s victorious 1966 World Cup campaign, won 28 international caps and spent 11 years in Manchester United’s first team. He helped United win two league titles and the 1968 European Cup. The image of his Wembley victory dance—with the Jules Rimet Trophy in one hand and his false teeth in the other—became part of English football’s visual memory.

The wider evidence already points to an elevated burden of neurodegenerative disease among former professionals, while leaving the exact mechanism under investigation. The 2019 FIELD study compared 7,676 former Scottish professional players with 23,028 matched controls. Neurodegenerative disease was recorded as the primary cause of death in 1.7% of former players and 0.5% of controls, an adjusted rate about three and a half times higher. Crucially, that study did not establish whether heading, concussion, another feature of the sport or a combination explained the difference.

Football has nevertheless changed its practice on a precautionary basis. Professional guidance in England recommends no more than ten higher-force headers in a training week, focusing on actions such as meeting long passes, crosses and set pieces. At grassroots level, the phased removal of deliberate heading from younger age groups has expanded over successive seasons. Those policies acknowledge a potential cumulative risk while research continues; they should not be misrepresented as proof that every form of heading carries the same danger.

The Stiles finding will intensify scrutiny of the game’s historic duty of care and its support for former players living with dementia. His family is among those pursuing separate civil claims against football authorities. An inquest determines the medical cause and circumstances of a death; it does not decide negligence or damages. The coroner’s conclusion is therefore highly significant evidence, but the broader questions of legal responsibility remain for a different process.

For the sport, the responsible response is neither denial nor an exaggerated promise that the science is complete. Stiles’s case establishes that repeated heading caused his CTE and that the resulting brain condition contributed to his death. The population research shows a wider association between professional football and neurodegenerative mortality but cannot yet apportion the cause. Holding both truths at once is the basis for better rules, better long-term care and a more honest account of the physical cost carried by an earlier generation.

title: Israeli football records fewer racism convictions and pitch pyrotechnics
dek: New figures point to a meaningful improvement after tougher anti-racism rules, although unequal reporting periods and missing match-level denominators limit the headline percentages.

source.author: ONE

Israel Football Association: official anti-racism rule amendment

body: Israeli football has reported substantial reductions in two of its most persistent stadium problems: racist chanting and pyrotechnic devices thrown onto the pitch. The newly released totals are encouraging, especially because they follow a deliberate change in disciplinary policy. They are not yet a complete measure of supporter behaviour, however. The available figures count convictions or identified incidents, not every occurrence, and they do not provide a per-match or per-attendance denominator.

The racism comparison behind the headline decline is 19 club convictions during the first six months of the 2025/26 season, before the amended rules took effect, against five during the following four months. Five is 74% lower than 19 as a raw count. Because the periods are unequal, that is not the same as a 74% fall in the monthly rate: the averages move from about 3.2 convictions a month to 1.25, a reduction of roughly 61%. Both calculations show improvement; only one adjusts for time.

The rule change was approved by the Israel Football Association in December and became effective on 1 February 2026. Its official notice expanded the disciplinary response to racism and discrimination, including higher escalating fines, restrictions on away-ticket sales and the possibility for clubs to submit structured prevention programmes. The design attempts to change incentives before an offence occurs, rather than treating punishment after the match as the entire policy.

That domestic trend must also be read alongside a separate FIFA decision. In March, world football’s governing body found multiple breaches of the disciplinary provisions covering offensive behaviour and discrimination, fined the IFA CHF150,000, issued a warning and ordered a prevention plan. The new conviction totals do not cancel that ruling; nor does the ruling prove the later measures failed. They address different periods and different institutional questions.

The pyrotechnics comparison is broader in time. Fifteen cases of devices being thrown onto the playing surface were recorded in 2022/23, compared with eight in 2025/26—close to a 50% reduction. That is a safety-relevant distinction: a flare in a stand and an object landing on the field are not the same risk. Yet the published totals again lack the number of fixtures monitored, the competitions included and a consistent account of detection, so they should be treated as an indicator rather than a final incidence rate.

Policy can influence those numbers through more than severity. A sanction that targets away access or competitive consequences gives organised supporter groups a direct reason to police behaviour within their own section, while club prevention plans can address education, reporting and stewarding. The danger is that a lower disciplinary total may also reflect under-reporting or different enforcement. Public confidence will therefore depend on transparent definitions and season-by-season data, not isolated percentages.

The most responsible conclusion is positive but provisional. Racism convictions fell sharply after the February amendment, even when the unequal time periods are corrected, and pitch-throwing pyrotechnic incidents are well below the 2022/23 total. The next step is to publish match-normalised figures, distinguish allegations from convictions and show whether the improvement survives a full season under the new rules. If it does, Israeli football will have evidence of behavioural change rather than only a favourable snapshot.

title: Kunin doubles up as Mazkeret Batya retain national artistic-swimming cup
dek: A two-point club contest and Katy Kunin’s solo-duet double gave Israel’s summer championships a finish defined by both collective depth and senior quality.

body: A.L.E. Mazkeret Batya have retained Israel’s senior artistic-swimming cup after a championship decided by only two points. The club finished the combined winter-and-summer standings on 103, with Maccabi Tel Aviv on 101 and Hapoel Jerusalem third on 88. The national federation lists the summer meet at the Wingate Institute from 12 to 14 July, bringing the domestic senior season to a close at the country’s principal aquatic venue.

The narrow margin is the most revealing part of the club result. Mazkeret Batya had won the previous edition by 31 points; this time Maccabi Tel Aviv remained within a single routine’s reach. Retaining the cup therefore required depth across the programme rather than one dominant performance. Jerusalem’s 88-point total also kept three clubs meaningfully involved, a healthier competitive shape than a runaway table would have produced.

Katy Kunin delivered the strongest individual performance. The Hapoel Jerusalem swimmer won the senior solo with 231.2763 points, ahead of Yogev Dagan of Mazkeret Batya on 195.0625 and Maccabi Tel Aviv’s Noya Tzarfati on 190.2950. Kunin’s winning margin exceeded 36 points, separating the event’s established international-level performer from a podium that also reflected the discipline’s widening domestic base.

Kunin then completed a double alongside Noga Levi. Their duet scored 240.4263, with Aya Mazor and Shia Shar Shalom Nechmad second on 207.3038 and Noa Kagan and Tzarfati third on 190.7254. Kunin and Mazor form Israel’s current senior duet internationally, so the domestic event placed regular national-team partners on opposing sides of a title race before they return to shared international work.

Mazkeret Batya’s clearest event victory came in the acrobatic team routine. Its 164.9625 total established a large gap over Maccabi Tel Aviv’s 110.1466 and Artswim’s 104.8472. Maccabi Tel Aviv answered by winning the separate team event with 146.0160, an important contribution to the club’s late pressure in the overall cup standings.

The results also show why domestic championships matter beyond medals. Artistic swimming is built from several competitive units—solo, duet, mixed work, team routines and acrobatics—and national-team depth depends on athletes being tested across those demands. A close club table creates more meaningful selection evidence than isolated training scores, while Dagan’s senior podium adds visibility for men in a discipline whose international programme has expanded mixed opportunities.

Mazkeret Batya leave Wingate with the cup, but not with uncontested control of the field. Maccabi Tel Aviv reduced a 31-point deficit from the previous edition to two, Jerusalem supplied the outstanding individual champion and several national-team combinations were separated rather than grouped together. The trophy stayed in the same hands; the competitive balance around it changed substantially.

body: Hapoel Holon have signed American guard Claudell Harris Jr for the 2026/27 season, turning an agreement reached earlier in the week into a completed addition. Harris arrives at 23 after his first professional campaign in Europe with Promitheas Patras. The move is less a purchase of finished production than a calculated bet that a young scorer can translate flashes from Greece into a steadier role in Israel.

FIBA lists Harris at 190 centimetres and records averages of 9.2 points, 1.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists across five Basketball Champions League appearances for Promitheas. In the Greek league he produced 10.1 points and 2.6 rebounds per game while shooting 36% from the field. Those numbers describe an adaptable rotation guard, not yet a primary offensive engine.

His best European nights show the upside Holon are buying. Harris scored 21 points away to Heidelberg and later supplied 17 points with seven assists in Promitheas’s double-overtime victory over Rytas Vilnius. The contrast between those peaks and his overall averages is central to the evaluation: he has already created and scored at continental level, but now needs to repeat it over a longer sequence.

Head coach Predrag Krunić has identified Harris’s ability to cover multiple perimeter roles, create his own shot and operate within the team’s offence. New sporting director Daniel Ravitz has framed the signing in similar terms, emphasising youth, athleticism and versatility. That shared language suggests Holon are building for pace and interchangeable backcourt assignments rather than recruiting a guard for one narrow function.

There is still a clear developmental risk. A 36% overall field-goal rate in Greece leaves room for improvement in shot selection and finishing, while the Champions League sample comprises only five games. Holon will need to distinguish productive aggression from difficult volume, especially when Harris is asked to initiate possessions rather than attack a defence already moved by somebody else.

The fit could nevertheless be valuable in the Israeli league. A bigger guard who can shift between on-ball creation and secondary scoring gives a coach more options against switches and pressure. If Harris can defend both backcourt positions, his versatility will extend beyond lineup notation and allow Holon to preserve pace without surrendering size. That defensive part of the role remains to be demonstrated in the new environment.

Holon’s expectation is that the second professional season produces a substantial step. The evidence supports the possibility, not the guarantee: Harris has age, length for the position and two high-level scoring examples, but he also arrives with modest efficiency and limited European experience. The signing will succeed if Holon turn the isolated peaks into dependable possessions rather than asking a developing guard to become the entire offence immediately.

title: Fenerbahçe turn Marcus Bingham’s breakout year into a two-season bet

body: Fenerbahçe have signed Marcus Bingham Jr on a two-season contract, giving the 26-year-old centre his first EuroLeague assignment after the most productive year of his professional career. The move also completes a steep climb that passed through three Israeli clubs: Bingham played for Hapoel Haifa, Hapoel Holon and Hapoel Tel Aviv before moving to UNICS Kazan and establishing himself as far more than a situational rim protector.

The official VTB United League record explains why a reigning European champion would commit two years. Bingham appeared in 54 games for UNICS in 2025/26 and averaged 15.6 points, 7.1 rebounds, 1.4 steals and 1.8 blocks. At 2.13 metres, he offered unusual activity away from the basket as well as conventional size around the rim. Those steals and blocks matter together: they describe a defender capable of affecting possessions at different heights and in different spaces.

His offensive development was equally important. Bingham left Israel with a reputation built primarily on reach, vertical finishing and shot deterrence; in Kazan he carried a much larger scoring load over a full domestic and playoff programme. Fenerbahçe are not recruiting him on one tournament burst or a short sequence of favourable match-ups. Fifty-four appearances provide a substantial sample, and the VTB League selected him in its team of the semi-finals.

The next level will still ask different questions. EuroLeague offences repeatedly pull centres into screening actions, force them to defend a second and third decision and punish a late rotation with an open corner three. Fenerbahçe can use Bingham’s mobility to play more aggressively at the point of the screen, but that value depends on the back line rotating with him. Length alone does not solve the spacing and speed of an elite possession.

There is also a clear role question on offence. Bingham’s Kazan production does not mean he will receive the same number of touches in Istanbul. His most transferable work will be running hard after defensive rebounds, creating pressure as a lob target, screening with precision and turning offensive rebounds into efficient second possessions. A lower scoring average could coexist with a more demanding and more valuable role if those actions hold up against EuroLeague frontcourts.

His years in Israel now read as part of a development route rather than a finished evaluation. Exposure to several tactical environments gave Bingham repeated work in switch-heavy line-ups and in systems that asked the centre to cover ground behind the ball. UNICS then gave him the volume to prove that the athletic profile could support sustained production. Fenerbahçe are paying for the combination: Israeli experience, a breakout season and physical tools that remain scarce even at EuroLeague level.

The contract rewards what Bingham has already become while leaving room for another jump. He is no longer being assessed as an intriguing project, yet he has never played a EuroLeague minute. Fenerbahçe’s two-year commitment gives both parties time to absorb that transition. The first measure will not be whether he reproduces 15.6 points immediately; it will be whether his defence, screening and rim pressure survive the competition’s tighter margins often enough to earn closing-line-up trust.
