body: Hapoel Eilat have signed American forward Aaron Wheeler as they rebuild for their return to the Israeli Basketball Premier League. Wheeler stays in the competition after spending 2025/26 with Hapoel HaEmek, giving the promoted club a player already familiar with the league’s pace, travel and foreign-player match-ups rather than another newcomer facing a full period of adjustment.

The league’s official record lists Wheeler at 2.05 metres and shows 14 appearances last season. He averaged 7.9 points and 5.0 rebounds in 19.6 minutes, made 52.4% of his two-point attempts and converted 38.6% from three. He also recorded 1.3 steals and 1.4 blocks per game, unusually active defensive numbers for a forward working in fewer than 20 minutes a night.

Those figures point towards a complementary role. Wheeler does not arrive as a high-volume creator who requires an offence to be reorganised around him. His value is in possessions that connect a line-up: running the floor, finishing after the defence has shifted, contesting from the weak side and keeping the paint available by making enough open threes. The 17 successful three-pointers came from 44 attempts, a useful rate but still a modest sample.

Eilat earned promotion in April with an 84–70 victory over Elitzur Ashkelon. That result secured top position after 26 wins in 27 games and returned the southern club to the first division following a two-season absence. It was an emphatic campaign, built on week-to-week superiority rather than one successful playoff sequence.

The promotion record is a foundation, not a forecast. Dominating the National League and surviving in the Premier League are different assignments because the size and speed of opposing rotations change immediately. Eilat must add top-flight athleticism without weakening the ball movement, defensive discipline and competitive stability that made last season so consistent.

Wheeler addresses several of those needs in one place. His rebounding can help finish defensive possessions, while the combination of steals and blocks suggests he can disrupt passing lanes and protect behind an initial rotation. Eilat will still have to decide whether he is best deployed as a mobile power forward or in smaller units at centre. That choice will depend on the size and shooting around him.

The signing also carries a sensible limit. Fourteen games are enough to demonstrate that Wheeler can contribute in Israel, not enough to establish him as a guaranteed anchor across an entire season. Eilat’s coaching staff must turn efficiency in a restricted role into dependable availability and production over a longer schedule. If that transition holds, the club have found a two-way piece who can make the promoted roster more adaptable without demanding control of the ball.

title: Four appointments complete a generational change in Israeli basketball’s disciplinary court
dek: A year-long handover has replaced four long-serving judges with a salaried panel, while the association’s rules preserve the court’s formal independence and route of appeal.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: הרפורמה נמשכת: מונו ארבעה דיינים חדשים
source.author: ONE Sports Desk

verificationSources.label: Israel Basketball Association current disciplinary regulations

body: The Israel Basketball Association has completed a major change in its disciplinary court, appointing attorneys Gadi Zilberberg, Lior Boner, Amir Pavve and Yishai Zilberberg to replace four judges who have finished their terms. The incoming group will serve on a salaried basis after a handover that the association says was prepared over the course of a year.

The outgoing judges are Tagar Amiel, Tzvika Roizen, Eli Levin and Ezra Hausner. Their departure is substantial because the disciplinary court deals with the incidents that sit between competition administration and legal process: player and coach conduct, club responsibility, crowd offences and alleged breaches of the association’s rules. Its decisions can alter fines, suspensions and the conditions under which games are staged.

The association’s current disciplinary regulations describe the court as independent and sovereign in its decision-making. Judges are instructed to rule according to the association’s statutes, regulations and their own conscience, while appeals proceed to a separate supreme court. The constitution further requires a panel of three to five legally qualified judges appointed personally by the general assembly.

That framework makes the method of renewal as important as the names. A salaried panel may give the association more predictable availability and faster case management, but payment cannot be allowed to blur the institutional distance between the court and the body whose rules it interprets. The formal safeguards already exist in the regulations; credibility will be built through consistent reasoning and publication of decisions.

The transition has not begun from a standing start. Gadi Zilberberg appears in the association’s published decisions from the 2025/26 season, evidence that at least part of the handover was operating before the announcement of the completed panel. The association has also moved some hearings online and revised regulations during the wider reform process.

Remote hearings can reduce travel and scheduling friction in a national competition system, particularly for clubs outside the centre of the country. They also require careful procedure. Participants must be able to hear the case against them, present their response and understand which materials the judge considered. Convenience is useful only if the record remains complete and the process remains intelligible.

Association chairman Amos Frishman has presented the appointments as a continuation of institutional reform and thanked the outgoing judges for their service. The more meaningful test will come in ordinary cases rather than in the announcement: comparable offences should receive comparable treatment, written reasoning should make distinctions clear and appeal outcomes should feed back into future decisions.

Israeli basketball’s disciplinary court rarely attracts attention when it works well. Yet its rulings shape competitive fairness, supporter sanctions and the relationship between clubs and the governing body. Replacing four judges at once creates a genuine break with the previous era. The new panel inherits both authority and a public record against which its independence, speed and consistency can be measured.

body: Beitar Jerusalem have been ordered to pay M.S. Ashdod ₪450,000 in training and development compensation for Noam Mocha. The player-status ruling supplies the figure that remained unresolved after the midfielder committed his future to Beitar, turning an open acquisition cost into a defined obligation between the two clubs.

The distinction inside the decision matters. This is compensation for Ashdod’s role in training and developing the player, not a conventional transfer fee negotiated as part of a sale. The award recognises work performed before the move rather than assigning Ashdod a price for selling an active contract.

Mocha reached the end of his contractual route with Ashdod and was able to agree his next employment, but that did not automatically erase the originating club’s claim under the player-development system. Freedom to choose the next club and an obligation to compensate the developing club can therefore exist at the same time.

Beitar formally announced Mocha on a three-year contract in March. The club described him then as a young midfielder arriving from Ashdod and the youth national-team environment. A later pre-season update placed him among the new arrivals beginning work for 2026/27, so the sporting move was already in operation while the clubs awaited a financial determination.

That sequence separates two processes that are often compressed into the word ‘signing’. Beitar and Mocha settled the employment relationship first: length, start date and the player’s place in the new squad. The compensation question concerned Beitar and Ashdod. Thursday’s ruling closes that inter-club valuation without changing the three-season term publicly attached to the player.

For squad planning, certainty is more useful than a headline argument about which side won the case. Beitar can now place ₪450,000 against the cost of completing Mocha’s move, rather than carrying an unpriced liability into the season. The ruling converts uncertainty into a known acquisition expense.

That amount should not be confused with Mocha’s salary, bonuses or the annual first-team budget; none of those figures are established by the decision. Nor does the award become extra sporting revenue earmarked for Ashdod’s next signing. It is one specific payment between clubs, with separate employment and operating costs sitting outside it.

Ashdod, meanwhile, receive a concrete return for the development work recognised by the committee. The ruling does not assign a market value to every part of Mocha’s future career, nor does it predict what he may eventually contribute in Jerusalem. Its function is narrower and more institutional: to decide what one club owes another when a developed player moves after the relevant contract period.

The football question now belongs entirely to Mocha and Beitar’s staff. A three-year commitment gives the club time to develop him, but the compensation payment offers no guarantee of minutes or status. It simply removes the last documented financial uncertainty around the move. Beitar know the cost, Ashdod know the award, and Mocha can enter the season with the dispute no longer sitting beside his place in the squad.

body: Radinio Balker has extended his Huddersfield Town contract through 2028, closing the immediate route that could have taken the centre-back to Maccabi Haifa. Huddersfield published the extension on Thursday, converting what had been an advanced Israeli recruitment possibility into a firm commitment to the English club for the next two seasons.

The distinction between interest and a completed move matters here. Haifa had explored Balker as part of their search for a foreign central defender, but neither Israeli club nor English club had announced a transfer agreement. The authoritative event is the new Huddersfield contract. It means Haifa cannot treat the player as an available signing without a fresh negotiation with a club that has just lengthened its control of him.

Balker is not an unknown development player being retained for depth. Huddersfield’s first-team records list him as the number 12 and show him starting in central defence during the 2025/26 League One season. The club also identifies him as a Suriname international. He made his senior international debut in September 2025 and scored his first goal for the national team in a World Cup qualifier away to El Salvador the following month.

Those details explain the attraction for Haifa. Balker offers senior European league experience, current international football and a profile built around central defending rather than a positional conversion. But they also explain Huddersfield’s decision to secure him. A defender already integrated into the starting structure is more valuable under a longer contract than as a player approaching a point at which his negotiating leverage might shift.

For Haifa, the result should be read as a recruitment reset rather than a failed signing announcement. No completed transfer has been reversed because no completed transfer was made public. The practical consequence is still significant: one of the clearest centre-back options is no longer available on the terms that made an Israeli move plausible, and the club must decide whether to redirect its search or test Huddersfield’s resolve with a different proposal.

That decision cannot be separated from squad construction. Haifa need enough reliability at centre-back to support an aggressive defensive line and to survive a season in which availability rarely remains constant. Chasing a player who has just renewed can consume time and budget without improving the squad. Moving quickly to the next verified option may now be more valuable than preserving a negotiation whose economics have changed.

Huddersfield, meanwhile, receive clarity before the English season. Balker can prepare as a retained first-team defender rather than a player balancing two possible destinations, and the club holds a stronger contractual position if interest returns later. Haifa’s task is equally clear: the need has not disappeared simply because this route has. The next move must solve the defensive requirement rather than merely replace Balker’s name on the shortlist.

body: US President Donald Trump will attend Sunday’s World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at New York New Jersey Stadium, placing the head of state of the tournament’s largest host nation inside the venue for the concluding match. The White House announced the visit on Thursday, three days before the 15:00 local kick-off in East Rutherford.

The trip begins before matchday. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Trump will travel to New York City on Friday for a FIFA reception at Trump Tower and then appear at the final on Sunday. That sequence links the political hosting operation to FIFA’s own closing programme without changing the competitive terms of the match itself.

Argentina and Spain arrive with sharply different historical targets. Argentina are the defending champions and are seeking a fourth title, which would also make them the first country since Brazil in 1962 to retain the World Cup. Spain are attempting to add a second championship to the one won in 2010. The fixture is match 104 of the first 48-team men’s World Cup.

FIFA’s event plan turns Sunday into a long stadium operation. Gates are scheduled to open at 11:00, the closing ceremony begins at 13:30 and kick-off follows 90 minutes later. Jennifer Hudson is due to perform the United States national anthem, while the broader ceremony is designed to close a tournament staged across the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Presidential attendance adds another layer to an operation already built around federal, state and tournament coordination. The White House’s World Cup task force says its interagency framework covers transportation, tourism, safety and security across the 11 US host cities. New York New Jersey is the final stop for that system as well as the site of the trophy match.

There is also a direct stadium precedent. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump attended the 2025 Club World Cup final at the same East Rutherford venue, and official White House records show the president participating in the post-match ceremony alongside FIFA president Gianni Infantino. That history makes Sunday’s visit part of an established relationship between the administration and FIFA rather than an isolated late addition.

Any role beyond attendance should still be treated separately until the final ceremony plan is fixed. The durable facts are the White House confirmation, the Friday reception itinerary and the president’s planned presence on Sunday. On the field, the final remains the collision the tournament produced: Argentina’s 19-goal attack against a Spain side that have conceded only once. The head of state will be in the building, but the title will still be decided by the teams.

title: Yehezkel made Maccabi’s width a Super Cup weapon
dek: Three assists told the story, but the more important lesson was how one wide outlet kept changing the point of attack—even after Maccabi Tel Aviv went down to ten men.

source.name: Walla Sport
source.originalTitle: וזוהי רק ההתחלה: מכבי תל אביב זכתה בתואר אלוף האלופים
source.author: Walla Sport

body: Sagiv Yehezkel’s three assists in Maccabi Tel Aviv’s 3–1 Super Cup win are easy to treat as a spectacular individual line. The more useful conclusion is structural. Maccabi always had a route out of pressure because Yehezkel could receive wide, move the attack across the pitch and deliver before Hapoel Be’er Sheva’s defensive line had reset. He was not simply the last passer three times; he was the mechanism that stopped possession becoming predictable.

The opening goal established the pattern. Itamar Noy’s pass released Yehezkel into the right channel, and the ball across goal left Saied Abu Farchi with a simple finish in the 10th minute. The move began with Be’er Sheva unable to secure their defensive possession, but Maccabi still needed to turn that error into an uncontested shot. Width did the conversion: Yehezkel stretched the recovery run, Abu Farchi held the central lane and the final pass arrived before the cover could close.

The second assist was different enough to matter. Yehezkel supplied Dor Peretz from the left side in the 58th minute, and the captain placed his finish rather than overpowering Ofir Marciano. Later, Yehezkel created another headed chance for Peretz. That movement across the attack made him harder to contain than a winger fixed to one touchline. Be’er Sheva could identify the danger, but not a single zone in which to trap it.

Roy Revivo’s dismissal in the 66th minute should have changed the match’s geometry. Ten-man teams normally sacrifice their highest wide outlet, narrow the distances between defenders and accept longer periods without the ball. Maccabi did not abandon the threat. Six minutes after the red card, Yehezkel delivered the third assist and Abu Farchi completed his brace. The goal was tactical insurance: Be’er Sheva could not commit everybody forward while the best supplier on the pitch still had space to attack.

That is the sharpest criticism of the champions’ response. Kings Kangwa had already shown the value of varied movement by equalising with a backheel and later helped Be’er Sheva take control before half-time. Once they gained the extra player, however, their possession did not consistently force Maccabi’s reduced block to turn. Too many attacks met the defence in front of it, while the space left behind became more dangerous than the numerical advantage was productive.

Maccabi’s own performance was not without risk. Their pressure helped produce early openings, yet the match also contained enough loose transitions to warn against reading one July trophy as a finished model. Revivo’s second yellow created an avoidable emergency, and Be’er Sheva struck the frame before the interval. A system that gives Yehezkel freedom must still protect the spaces he leaves when an attack breaks down.

The encouraging part for Kenny Miller is that the width did not depend on sterile crossing volume. Yehezkel’s first assist followed a timed release behind the line, the second came after he appeared on the opposite side, and the third punished a team chasing the game. Those are three different match states. Maccabi used the same player to solve each one without demanding the same move repeatedly.

European qualifying will test whether that outlet survives against opponents who press the receiver earlier and recover with greater discipline. Maccabi will not always be able to create an empty goal or let Peretz arrive untracked. But the Super Cup offered a credible principle to carry forward: keep one wide player capable of receiving under pressure, crossing early and changing sides, and the whole attack has somewhere to breathe.

Abu Farchi’s brace and Peretz’s finish won the trophy; Yehezkel’s choices connected them. That distinction is why the performance deserves more than a celebration of three assists. Maccabi’s best attacking idea was portable across scorelines, sides of the pitch and even a red card. On the first competitive night of the season, that adaptability was the strongest evidence that the cup holders have more than a result to build on.

body: Or Blorian completed 75 minutes on his Major League Soccer debut as Sporting Kansas City lost 3–2 to St. Louis CITY SC at Energizer Park. The Israel centre-back started on the left side of Sporting’s central defence and helped his new team recover from two goals down, but Eduard Löwen’s late penalty decided a five-goal return from the World Cup break.

St. Louis built their advantage in eight first-half minutes. Jeong Sang-Bin converted from close range in the 28th minute before Marcel Hartel finished Simon Becher’s transition pass in the 36th. Sporting answered before the interval when Capita struck from outside the area in the 42nd minute, cutting the deficit to 2–1 and changing the second half from damage limitation into a genuine chase.

Blorian’s first assignment was demanding because St. Louis played with two forwards close enough to occupy both centre-backs while Hartel attacked the space behind them. The 26-year-old remained in the starting back line alongside Jansen Miller, with Jayden Reid and Ian James completing the defence in front of goalkeeper Stefan Cleveland. It was his first senior appearance for Sporting after joining from Hapoel Be’er Sheva this summer.

The debut ended after an injury delay in the 74th minute. Blorian received treatment on the pitch and Ethan Bartlow replaced him in the 75th, with no diagnosis or recovery timetable announced. Sporting equalised almost immediately: Dejan Joveljić met Manu García’s pass in the 76th minute and finished left-footed to make it 2–2.

The comeback did not survive the final phase. Löwen converted a penalty in the 85th minute to restore St. Louis’s lead, placing the kick beyond Cleveland for the winning goal. Sporting pushed through nine minutes of stoppage time but could not find a third response. St. Louis goalkeeper Benjamin Lundt and midfielder Daniel Edelman were booked late; Capita received Sporting’s only yellow card in the 78th minute. No player was sent off.

For Blorian, the most significant fact is that his first MLS appearance began as a start rather than a late introduction. Sporting trusted him in an away rivalry fixture immediately after the long league pause. His 75 minutes supplied a first measure of the speed, spacing and transition volume he will face in the competition, even if the treatment that preceded his substitution leaves his short-term availability to be clarified.

Sporting had signed the Israeli international to a contract running through the 2028/29 season, with club options beyond it. He arrived after winning the Israeli Premier League and Super Cup with Be’er Sheva and after breaking into the senior Israel squad. The move therefore carries an expectation that he can compete for a regular place rather than serve only as defensive depth.

The result belongs to St. Louis, whose two-goal opening and late penalty survived Sporting’s response. Blorian’s debut belongs in a different category: an incomplete individual night within a complete team defeat. He started, played 75 minutes and left with the score still 2–1; Sporting levelled after his departure and then conceded the winner. The next useful evidence will be whether he is available to continue building minutes in the following round.

title: Maccabi Haifa tie teenage striker Adrian Ballout to a new three-year deal
dek: The 2010-born forward from the Galilee village of Mi'ilya — credited with 103 goals in three junior seasons — has signed until 2029 after one championship-winning year in the academy.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: אדריאן בלוט חתם על חוזה ל-3 שנים במכבי חיפה

verificationSources.label: Maccabi Haifa youth department official signing announcement (Facebook, 17 Jul 2026)

body: Maccabi Haifa have moved to keep one of the most prolific junior goalscorers in northern Israel, announcing on Friday that Adrian Ballout, a striker born in 2010, has signed a three-year contract with the club's youth department. The deal, reported to run until 2029, arrives only one season after the teenager left M.K. Mi'ilya, the tiny Galilee village club where his scoring record first brought Haifa's scouts north.

"Ballout continues in green," the youth department wrote in its announcement, confirming that the forward will begin his second season in the academy after winning the league championship with the club's under-16 side last term.

Ballout was on the fringes of the squad that coach Eliezer Ben Aharon guided to the under-16 title — the top national division for his age group — and contributed five goals across all competitions, according to Israeli reporting on the deal. Those are modest numbers for a player signed as a pure finisher, which makes the length of the new commitment the real story: Haifa are paying for a trajectory, not for last season's output, and have chosen to secure the years in which that trajectory will be decided.

His background is unusual even by the standards of Israeli academy recruitment. Mi'ilya, perched in the hills of the western Galilee, has around 3,300 residents, almost all of them Melkite Greek Catholic Christians, and its youth club was founded barely a decade ago. Ballout only began organised football in the 2022-23 season, starting out at a football school in the neighbouring village of Fassuta before joining Mi'ilya's youth section at 13.

What happened next is why Haifa acted. Across three seasons at Mi'ilya he scored 103 goals in 69 appearances, according to ONE, which profiled him when he made the move last summer. In his final year he finished as the northern district's leading scorer in the under-16 league despite playing a year above his age group — 48 league goals for a side that placed fourth while fielding mostly 2010-born boys against older opposition. Andrei Fran, who founded Mi'ilya's youth department and coached him there, said at the time that Haifa had needed only two training sessions before deciding to sign him.

The new contract also has a defensive logic. The Galilee's Arab and Christian villages have long supplied talent to rival academies — earlier Mi'ilya products reached senior top-flight football after moving through Bnei Sakhnin's youth system — and a productive village striker who has already banked a championship season with Haifa would not have lacked suitors. Tying Ballout down until 2029 keeps every forthcoming pathway decision inside the club.

Those decisions come quickly now. The deal covers the under-17 and under-19 years, the stage at which Israeli academies separate genuine professional prospects from strong junior scorers, and the first call is whether Ballout continues with his own 2010 cohort or is pushed up an age group again, as Mi'ilya did with him. His first Haifa season suggested the step up in defensive quality is a real adjustment; the contract says the club believes the goals will follow.

For Mi'ilya, a village that had no youth club at all until the middle of the last decade, a second contract at the academy of one of the country's biggest clubs is a measurable return on a very small footballing economy — and a reason for Haifa's scouts to keep driving north.

title: Police detail strict entry rules for Beitar Jerusalem's Netanya meeting with Hapoel Tel Aviv

body: Israel Police say their preparations are complete for Saturday evening's meeting between Beitar Jerusalem and Hapoel Tel Aviv at the Miriam Stadium in Netanya, publishing a detailed set of instructions for supporters ahead of the 20:30 kick-off. From early afternoon, according to the announcement reported by ONE, hundreds of officers, stewards and security guards will be deployed around the ground and in the surrounding streets.

Entry will be tightly controlled. Gates open at 18:30 and everyone arriving will pass through what the force describes as rigorous screening, with supporters urged to come early and follow instructions. Access to the stadium area is restricted to ticket holders, and no tickets will be sold on the day. Weapons are barred outright, with no facility to deposit them at the gates; alcohol may not be brought in, anyone judged to be under its influence will be refused entry, and flying drones during the match is prohibited.

The sharpest warnings concern pyrotechnics. Supporter displays require prior approval from the police and fire service, while flares and similar devices are banned altogether — the police statement calls them a danger to life, warning that setting them off can bring a 3,000-shekel fine and criminal proceedings, and that throwing or igniting anything towards the pitch is an offence that could halt the game.
A separate instruction bars balaclavas, neck gaiters or any garment that obscures identification, on pain of a 500-shekel fine and refusal at the turnstiles.

Traffic around the stadium will be reorganised from the afternoon. The eastern and southern car parks close entirely and the western car park is reserved for invited guests, with supporters directed instead to parking at Cinema City, Gan Tzipor, the HaTzoran car parks and the Naimi Mall. HaYahalomim Boulevard will be shut in both directions from Rami Levy Square to the corner of HaEtztadion Street and Lantos Boulevard, and drivers coming from HaTzoran Street will not be able to turn left towards the ground.

The security posture reflects both the pairing and the moment. Meetings between Beitar and Hapoel Tel Aviv are among the most heavily policed in Israeli football, with the two support bases occupying opposite poles of the domestic game's culture. This one, staged at a neutral venue and listed by fixture services under the Toto Cup programme — the source itself does not name the competition — doubles as a final competitive outing before both clubs open their UEFA Conference League second-round qualifiers on 23 July, Beitar against AEK Larnaca of Cyprus.

The clubs will not be strangers for long either way: the fixture list published in June sends them straight back into each other's company on the opening day of the Ligat ha'Al season on 22 August. For now, the police message is plainer. The force closed its announcement by urging supporters to obey officers and stewards, avoid physical or verbal violence, and preserve, in its words, "a sporting atmosphere and an enjoyable experience for everyone".

Hours before kick-off, the operation produced its first arrests. Five suspects — one minor and four adults, residents of the centre of the country and Jerusalem — were detained by officers of the Netanya station during preparations around the ground, according to the police account as reported. Two were found carrying a substance suspected to be a dangerous drug, while the other three were held over suspected involvement in a violent incident. All five were taken for questioning at the Netanya station. Neither weapons nor pyrotechnics featured in the account of the arrests.

body: A 12-year-old from Herzliya stood on the top step of an international dance podium in Thessaloniki this week, an Israeli flag around her shoulders. Emily Elkobi, a pupil of the Dance Factory studio, won her solo category with a routine titled 'Cat Women', according to the report of her result published on Friday afternoon.

The competition that brought her to Greece is run by All Dance International, whose own records show its Intercontinental & Europe 2026 championship taking place at the TIF Helexpo exhibition grounds in Thessaloniki from 12 to 19 July. The Hebrew-language report describes the gathering as one of the biggest occasions in competitive dance and says entrants travelled from ten countries.

A note of precision is owed on the title itself. The Israeli report crowns Elkobi a world champion; the organiser's published structure lists Thessaloniki as its combined Intercontinental and European championship, one rung of a pyramid whose world finals proper are scheduled for Orlando, Florida, from 19 to 23 November. Category winners at each tier carry official All Dance titles, but which precise wording appears on her trophy could not be independently confirmed by the time of writing.

What is not in doubt in the account of the week is the scale of the double. Beyond her solo gold, Elkobi competed with Outrage, a crew from the same studio, which also finished first in its category. The group's coach, named in the report as Eyal Levi, came away with a Golden Ticket — an invitation to compete in Orlando, which tallies with the organiser's November world finals at the city's Hilton resort.

The routine that won the solo prize was built with choreographer and coach Irina Freidin. Behind it sat a training load that would make older athletes wince: five sessions a week through the year, rising in the final months before the championship to daily work of three to five hours, seven days a week.

Dance Factory Herzliya, directed by Tal Malka, is an established name on this circuit. Israeli coverage of the studio's earlier trips to world-level events records podium finishes for its crews, including category wins at a world dance championship in Portugal attended by delegations from dozens of countries.

The report does not state which age division Elkobi entered. Under All Dance's published rules, a 12-year-old falls within the Pre-Youth bracket for dancers aged 11 to 14, with solo, duo, trio and group subdivisions contested at each level.

The image the report dwells on is the flag. Receiving her trophy wrapped in it, the account notes, carried particular weight for an Israeli delegation competing abroad at present — a 12-year-old's small, deliberate gesture at the end of a very long season.

body: The last realistic route to a World Championship place now runs through a single match. Israel's under-20 handball side were beaten 35:23 by Iceland at the M20 EHF EURO in Romania on Friday lunchtime, a placement-round defeat at the Turda Arena that leaves Sunday's fixture — against the loser of Croatia's meeting with hosts Romania — as the one remaining chance to secure 15th place, the finishing position that Israeli reports say carries qualification for the age group's World Championship.

Israel arrived at the game severely under-strength. According to the Hebrew-language coverage, four squad members were unavailable: the first-choice goalkeeper and a centre back through injury, a third player suspended for the remainder of the tournament, and a fourth who has been sidelined since the opening match of the championship. Against opponents of Iceland's pedigree, the shortfall in the squad — known domestically as the reserve national team — told quickly.

It did not begin badly. Iceland squandered two penalties in the opening minutes — they would finish the afternoon nought from three from the seven-metre line, according to the official match sheet — and Israel edged 2:0 in front. The lead proved a mirage. Iceland moved 4:2 ahead and the gap widened relentlessly, through 16:6 to 20:9 at the interval, with Israel's attack repeatedly breaking down against a well-drilled defence and goalkeeping that ended the day on 20 saves from 43 Israeli attempts.

The second half was played out with the result beyond doubt. Israel's coaching staff used the closing period to hand court time to players who had featured only sparingly across the tournament, while Iceland kept scoring through a strikingly even spread: ten different Icelandic players found the net. Just 78 spectators were recorded at the Turda Arena for the midday throw-off.

Ben Gross led Israel's scoring with five goals, Yonatan Pelach added four, and Liam Madar and Idan Mena contributed three apiece. In goal, Yehonatan Benshitrit was kept busy, credited with ten saves from 36 shots faced.

The defeat caps a bruising fortnight. Official tournament records show Israel finished third in Group F after losing 42:33 to Sweden and 39:31 to Romania either side of a 43:33 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina, then lost 30:35 to Czechia in the rankings phase before producing their best result of the trip, a 39:31 victory over Poland. Thursday's 33:31 loss to the Faroe Islands routed them into Friday's meeting with Iceland.

Everything now rests on Sunday. Beat whichever of Croatia or Romania loses their placement tie, and this depleted group will have salvaged a World Championship ticket from a difficult campaign; lose, and the tournament ends in Turda with nothing to show for it but hard lessons.

body: Maccabi Tel Aviv's youth department has taken on two boys from the 2012 age group, with Liroy Oretzki and Marom Kadosh arriving from Nahalal Yizrael, the young Jezreel Valley club, ahead of the 2026/27 season. According to a report published on Friday by the Hebrew-language outlet ONE, the pair will be registered with the under-14 side — nearim gimel, in Israeli age-grade terms — based at the club's Kiryat Shalom training complex in south Tel Aviv. This is academy recruitment, not a senior transfer: both players are several years away from professional football.

Oretzki is described in the report as a centre-back who can also sit in front of the defence as a holding midfielder, while Kadosh is an out-and-out striker. The two spent last season together in Nahalal Yizrael's under-13 team, which competed in a regional Kids A division alongside the junior sides of Maccabi Tel Aviv North, Maccabi Petah Tikva North and Hapoel Tel Aviv North.

Kadosh's numbers stand out even at this level. The report credits him with 40 per cent of Nahalal Yizrael's goals last season — a striking share for any forward, whatever the age group. He began his football education in Hapoel Gilboa's youth setup, where he spent three consecutive seasons before making the short move across the valley.

Oretzki followed a similar path, joining Nahalal Yizrael after four straight seasons at Hapoel Gilboa. The report describes him as a fixture of the team's defensive spine and notes that he contributed six goals from the back — an unusual return for a player in his position.

Their team's collective record helps explain Maccabi's interest. Nahalal Yizrael finished third in the division with an 81 per cent success rate, conceding just 22 goals — the second-meanest defence in the league behind Maccabi Tel Aviv North, who topped the table at 95 per cent. Those figures come from the report itself; the Israel Football Association's registry could not be independently checked for this age group at the time of writing.

Nahalal Yizrael is a genuine grassroots success story. Relaunched under new ownership in the summer of 2023, on grounds where Maccabi Haifa previously ran youth activity, the club now works with more than 200 children from the Jezreel Valley and beyond, and fields league teams across most junior age groups at the top regional tier.

The move was brokered by Play It, the Israeli agency owned by Oren Sterling, a former Hapoel Haifa youth department director and chief executive, who attended the signing according to the report. Agency involvement in a deal for players this young reflects how early representation now begins in Israeli football's talent pipeline.

For Maccabi Tel Aviv, whose academy at Kiryat Shalom has supplied the first team for decades, the recruitment is routine business with a notable footprint: reaching into a two-year-old valley club for players who impressed against its own northern junior sides. For the two boys, it is the biggest step of their short careers — though at this age, nothing about the path ahead is guaranteed.

body: Hapoel Petah Tikva have turned to a familiar face ahead of the new Israeli Premier League season, announcing on Friday that French forward Franck Rivollier is returning to the club on a one-year contract with an option for two further seasons. The 25-year-old comes back barely a year after leaving, and the news arrived while the squad was working through its pre-season camp in Pravets, Bulgaria.

The signing carries an edge that goes beyond routine squad-building. Rivollier spent last season with Maccabi Petah Tikva, Hapoel's neighbours and rivals, and Hebrew-language coverage reached for the city's well-worn shorthand for such transfers: crossing the road. Having made the journey once already, from Hapoel to Maccabi last summer, the striker is now making it in reverse.

His first spell in blue was brief but well-timed. Rivollier arrived in January 2025 from Bulgarian side Spartak Varna and slotted into a team chasing promotion under head coach Omer Peretz. He scored four goals in 19 appearances as Hapoel sealed their return to the top flight at the end of that campaign, before his contract ran down and he moved across the city.

At Maccabi he managed six goals over the course of last season — steady rather than prolific — but the return will inevitably be read through the prism of local rivalry. Direct switches between the two Petah Tikva clubs are uncommon enough to sting, and Rivollier has now made one in each direction inside twelve months.

The player, for his part, leaned into the reunion rather than the rivalry. "I am excited to pull on the Hapoel Petah Tikva shirt again," he said in remarks released through the club. "My connection with Omer and with the crowd was something exceptional in my previous spell, and I am thrilled to open my second chapter at the club, in the top flight. I will do my utmost to prove myself and help the team meet its goals."

Born in Saint-Étienne and standing 1.92 metres, Rivollier came through in France with Lyon's reserves and Stade Rennais' B side, taking in a loan at Stade Briochin before a spell with Olympic Charleroi in Belgium. He first arrived in Israel in 2023, and his 11 goals for Hapoel Afula in 2023-24 remain his most productive season; a half-year detour to Spartak Varna followed before Petah Tikva, in both of its footballing colours, became home.

One detail is worth flagging: while one of the two reports stated flatly that the striker has signed, the fuller account described an agreement with the formal signature still to come, after which Rivollier is expected to link up with the squad during the Bulgaria camp. Neither suggested any obstacle remains.

For Peretz, the logic is straightforward. Hapoel go into the 2026-27 top-flight campaign wanting more physical presence and depth up front, and Rivollier offers both, along with an existing relationship with the coach and a dressing room he already knows. For the player, returning to the club where his promotion cameo made his local name is a chance to establish himself in the Israeli Premier League properly — this time from the first day of pre-season rather than a January arrival.

body: One flight of barriers into her continental championships, Hila Varsano already owns a faster Israeli under-18 record. The 17-year-old from Maccabi Tel Aviv clocked 1:00.02 for the 400m hurdles in Friday's opening round of the European U18 Championships in Rieti, finishing third in her heat at the Stadio Raul Guidobaldi and moving into Saturday's semi-finals.

The run trimmed 0.13 seconds from the national age-group best of 1:00.15 she set in Tel Aviv on 4 July, a mark World Athletics already lists as the Israeli U18 record. The senior national record — Irina Lenskiy's 56.09, which has stood since June 2000 — remains in another realm, but Varsano, born in April 2009, now has a sub-minute clocking squarely in view.

Rieti is staging the fifth edition of the biennial under-18 championships from 16 to 19 July, and Israel's day extended beyond the hurdles. Ido Noam and Aviv Ochman both came through the 2,000m steeplechase heats, in 5:53.23 and 5:53.63 respectively, to reach Sunday's final — and neither had a clean race. Ochman, of Leader Jerusalem, stumbled at the final water jump yet held on to qualify; Noam, who trains with Hapoel Emek Hefer and the excellence academy at the Wingate Institute, clipped one of the standard barriers in the second heat and likewise recovered.

Itay Magidi, the Israel Athletics Association's professional director and still the national record holder over the distance, made clear he would be happy to see that record go. Both runners, he said in comments carried by Israeli media, had come through their mishaps to qualify, and he believes each is capable of a top-eight finish on Sunday if they recover well in time.

The hurdles record was not Varsano's first of the summer: in May she ran in the quartet that set an Israeli U18 4x100m relay best of 47.49, according to her World Athletics profile. Her semi-final follows on Saturday, and her trajectory this month — 1:00.15 to 1:00.02 inside a fortnight — suggests the new figure may not survive the weekend either.

body: Daniel Worko is poised to make his first competitive appearance for Beitar Jerusalem on Saturday evening, with the 21-year-old midfielder pencilled into the projected line-up for the Toto Cup quarter-final against Hapoel Tel Aviv in Netanya. Yarden Shua's involvement, by contrast, hangs on a fitness verdict the club will not deliver until matchday.

Worko joined on 1 July from Hapoel Ramat Gan on a three-year contract running to June 2029, and the coaching staff have wasted little time in trusting him: the Israel youth international, comfortable in either holding midfield role, is expected to start alongside Boris Enow in the centre of the pitch. International databases register him under his given name, Degats, though the club announced his signing as Daniel Worko.

Shua's situation is less straightforward. The forward sat out the final training session with a virus and remained at home to rest, and a decision on whether he is fit to feature will only be taken on the day. Losing him would strip the attack of one of its most experienced options at the end of a week in which the treatment room has been busy.

There is better news elsewhere: Shon Weissman is also in line for his own first appearance in yellow and black, and Omer Atzili is expected to be handed carefully managed minutes as he continues a gradual return to full fitness.

Carabalí's enforced absence comes with a considerable consolation. A separate report on Friday afternoon indicated that the Colombian centre-back, whose representatives had spent recent weeks canvassing offers from abroad, has decided to stay in Jerusalem and extend his contract by a further two to three seasons. The defender, who arrived from AD Pasto in 2025 and quickly became a fixture of the back line, had a year remaining on terms worth roughly €200,000 annually; the new agreement is expected to carry a significant rise and to be finalised shortly.

The same report noted that owner Barak Abramov intends to handle contract talks with Gadrani personally once the Georgian returns to fitness. Gadrani earns around €250,000 a year, holds an option for an additional season, and is pressing for a substantial improvement of his own.

The tie itself kicks off at 20:30 on Saturday 18 July in Netanya, under the police matchday arrangements already reported in these pages. With both clubs opening their Conference League qualifying campaigns next week, squad management is as much a part of the evening as the result — a balancing act that falls to Almog Cohen in his first competitive weeks since stepping out of the sporting director's office and onto the touchline.

Taken together, the two threads point the same way: a projected eleven leaning on new arrivals, and a club moving to lock down the defenders it wants to keep. How much of that projection survives contact with Saturday — starting with Shua's fitness — should be clear within twenty-four hours.

title: France's World Cup Replay Petition Passes 50,000 Signatures as FIFA Backs Referee
dek: Fans claim Lamine Yamal handled the ball before the penalty that set Spain's 2-0 semi-final win in motion, but no formal French protest has been lodged and FIFA insists Iván Barton's appointment was fully justified.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: בצרפת דורשים לשחק מחדש את חצי הגמר מול ספרד
source.author: ONE editorial team

body: More than 50,000 people have signed an online petition in France demanding that Tuesday's World Cup semi-final defeat to Spain be replayed, escalating a refereeing row that has followed Les Bleus out of the tournament and into the build-up to Sunday's final in New Jersey.

Spain won the semi-final 2-0 in Arlington, Texas, on 14 July, taking the lead through Mikel Oyarzabal's first-half penalty before Pedro Porro added a second in the 58th minute to send La Roja through to face Argentina. It is the penalty, awarded by Salvadoran referee Iván Barton, that sits at the heart of the French grievance.

The sequence began with a loose ball in the Spanish attacking phase inside France's defensive third of the area, where Lucas Digne swung at the ball and instead caught Lamine Yamal, prompting Barton to point to the spot. French supporters argue the move should have been dead before the contact ever happened, because the ball had brushed Yamal's arm moments earlier. The petition puts it bluntly: during the penalty awarded to Spain, it states, Yamal touches the ball with his hand, France should not have conceded a first goal that changed the entire complexion of the match, and sport must be played by rules that, on the night, were not respected.

It is worth being precise about who is demanding what. The replay campaign is a fan-driven petition, not a formal challenge: the French Football Federation has lodged no protest or appeal with FIFA, and none is expected. World football's governing body has never granted a replay on the basis of a referee's judgement call, whose decisions on matters of fact are final under the laws of the game, and there is no procedural route by which a petition, however large, could overturn a completed semi-final.

The closest thing to an official French complaint came from the touchline. Didier Deschamps, whose final tournament as national coach ended with the defeat, pointedly asked reporters whether the referee was "up to the task of officiating a semi-final", adding that the penalty was not the only issue and that it "adds to everything else". His irritation also covered a 43rd-minute decision in which Barton awarded France a free-kick on the edge of the box for Fabián Ruiz's challenge on Ousmane Dembélé, then reversed his own call after consulting an assistant. Deschamps did, however, concede that his players' own errors had contributed to the loss.

FIFA's response was unequivocal. Pierluigi Collina, the governing body's director of refereeing and himself a World Cup final referee, was asked directly whether Barton had been up to the occasion. "Yes, absolutely," he said, insisting FIFA's referees are "world class". The video assistant referee reviewed the full penalty sequence during the match and supported the on-field award.

The technical case for the decision is also stronger than the petition allows. Under the current handball law, an offence requires the arm to make the body unnaturally bigger, and analysts who reviewed the footage noted that Yamal's arm stayed close to his side, with former FIFA-listed referee and broadcast rules analyst Christina Unkel observing that the contact came on the sleeve, which is not considered part of the arm for handball purposes.

There is an uncomfortable echo for France in the precedent, too. When Thierry Henry's unpunished handball set up the goal that denied the Republic of Ireland a place at the 2010 World Cup, FIFA flatly refused Irish requests for a replay. The same wall now stands in front of the French petition, whatever its signature count.

Spain, meanwhile, are preparing for Sunday's final against Argentina at MetLife Stadium, where Slovenia's Slavko Vinčić will become the first referee from his country to take charge of a World Cup final. The row over Arlington will rumble on in France, but the result — and Spain's place in the final — will stand.

body: Maccabi Haifa's summer-long pursuit of Omri Glazer has come down to a single number. Red Star Belgrade are demanding roughly €250,000 — close to a million shekels — before they release the Israel goalkeeper from his contract, according to a report published by the Israeli outlet Sport1 on Friday afternoon.

By the report's account, the fee is the last obstacle standing. Glazer has already agreed personal terms on a return to the club where he spent five seasons and is set to become one of the highest earners in the squad. What remains open is what, if anything, Haifa must pay the Serbian champions to walk him out of the door.

Red Star's leverage sits in the paperwork. Transfermarkt lists Glazer's contract in Belgrade as running to June 2027, and Friday's report describes his terms there as exceptionally high. The Serbian club are said to accept that the goalkeeper is heading home, and to have squared their own financial obligations to him, yet they are still pressing for additional compensation, currently pitched at around a million shekels. Sources cited in the report expect the matter to be settled shortly, at which point Glazer would sign.

Glazer, 30, left Israeli football three years ago as Hapoel Be'er Sheva's State Cup-winning goalkeeper and would return as one of the country's most decorated exports. Signed by Red Star in the summer of 2023 for a reported €1.5m, he has since collected three consecutive Serbian league titles and produced the defining night of his career in the Champions League, when he was credited with 13 saves — reported at the time as a group-stage record — in a defeat away to Manchester City. He has 23 caps for Israel.

For Haifa, the move would be a reunion rather than a gamble. Glazer first came through the door in 2016 and was part of the squad that won the 2020-21 championship — a spell he has himself previously described as a complicated one — before rebuilding his standing at Be'er Sheva and then abroad.

The urgency is structural. Friday's report suggests the club's hierarchy do not expect either of the goalkeepers currently on the books to carry the position this season and want the matter resolved quickly. The same report claims Haifa are in advanced negotiations to sell one of those keepers to Ukrainian side Metalist Kharkiv for a little over €3m — a sum that would dwarf the compensation in dispute with Belgrade.

Friday night added a pointed footnote in Belgrade. In Red Star's 5-0 league win over Mačva Šabac, the champions started a 17-year-old, Savo Radnović, in goal, with Glazer left out of the matchday goalkeeping picture altogether. Israeli coverage framed the selection as a question — a possible declaration of intent about a keeper the club is prepared to lose — rather than a confirmed step in the negotiation; no new fee, agreement or timetable was reported alongside it.

It caps a busy week of squad-building in any case. Haifa announced on Thursday that they had reached an agreement with Andrija Novakovich, the American-born striker who spent last season with Reggiana in Italy's second tier; he is expected in Israel in the coming days for a medical before signing. A first-choice goalkeeper is the loudest remaining item on a list that, per Friday's report, also stretches to a central defender and cover at left-back.

The calendar supplies its own deadline. Haifa open their Toto Cup campaign against city rivals Hapoel Haifa at the end of the month, and earlier Israeli reporting suggested the club hoped to have their new goalkeeper in place by then. Until the compensation question is answered, nothing is signed — but on Friday's evidence, nobody involved expects the answer to be no.

By Saturday morning the number had moved — upwards, and towards resolution. A further Israeli report put the sum Haifa will pay Belgrade at an estimated €300,000, framing it as the price of closing the deal rather than a demand still on the table, with Glazer expected to land in Israel within days. The same report said his personal terms are settled at roughly €400,000 a season before bonuses, and that, having trained with Red Star throughout, he should be match-fit for the Toto Cup opener next weekend. It also named the goalkeeper bound for Metalist Kharkiv as Heorhiy Yermakov, with Haifa said to retain a percentage of any future sale. Nothing has been formally announced by either club.

title: Liam Hermesh Agrees Move to Austrian Bundesliga Side Grazer AK
dek: Out of contract at Maccabi Haifa and fresh from a Moldovan Cup-winning loan at Sheriff Tiraspol, the 22-year-old defensive midfielder is set to join GAK on a free transfer, with an unveiling expected within days.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: ליגיונר חדש: ליאם חרמש סיכם בגראצר א.ק

body: Liam Hermesh is poised to become the latest Israeli footballer to take his career into the Austrian Bundesliga, with reports in Israel and Austria on Friday indicating that the 22-year-old defensive midfielder has agreed to join Grazer AK after the expiry of his contract at Maccabi Haifa.

The deal is agreed rather than formally completed. Israeli reports say terms are in place for a free transfer and that an official presentation is expected within days, while the Austrian outlet laola1 reported the same afternoon that Hermesh had already been spotted at GAK's Weinzödl training centre in Graz. The club themselves have not yet announced the signing.

Born in Ramat Gan in March 2004, Hermesh has been without a club since 1 July, when his Maccabi Haifa contract ran down. Haifa chose not to take up an option to extend his stay when he returned from a season away, leaving one of Israel's more promising holding midfielders available for nothing.

That season away is precisely what put him on Austrian radars. Loaned to Sheriff Tiraspol for 2025-26, Hermesh made 15 competitive appearances as the Moldovan side finished runners-up in the league and lifted the national cup, beating Zimbru 2-0 in May's final in Chisinau — a match in which Israeli reports credit him with the winner. Playing regular football in a title race, and doing so abroad at 21, marked him out from peers still waiting for minutes at home.

According to the reporting in Israel, several domestic clubs explored bringing him back into the Israeli Premier League this summer, but the player and his agents, Adam Kidan and Gilad Katzev, prioritised a second spell in Europe. Haifa are also said to have secured a percentage of any future sale, meaning the club that developed him would still profit from a successful stint in Graz.

GAK are a club with history and a point to prove. Austrian champions in 2004 before financial collapse sent them tumbling through the divisions, they returned to the top flight in 2024 and have been assembling a squad to consolidate there. Austrian coverage of the deal framed Hermesh as the answer to a specific gap — a specialist screening midfielder to sit in front of the back line at the Merkur Arena — rather than a speculative punt.

The Austrian Bundesliga has become a genuinely useful middle rung for players of Hermesh's profile: a 12-team league, split into championship and relegation groups after 22 rounds, that offers European qualification places, competitive intensity and heavy scouting traffic from Germany. For a defensive midfielder valued by Transfermarkt at a modest €200,000, it is a stage where a good season changes a career trajectory quickly.

There is a practical wrinkle in his favour, too. Austrian reports describe Hermesh as holding Portuguese citizenship alongside his Israeli passport, which would simplify his registration and remove any non-EU quota questions for GAK — and would do the same for any bigger European club that comes calling later.

For Israeli football, the pattern is a familiar and healthy one: a young player squeezed for minutes at a top domestic club goes via a smaller European league, wins something, and earns a move up. If the paperwork is completed as expected, Hermesh will be presented in Graz within days, with the new Austrian season only weeks away.

title: Police announce further arrest over grenade attacks on Beitar owner's Japanika chain
dek: A suspect accused of throwing a grenade at a Kiryat Ono branch of Barak Abramov's restaurant chain has been remanded for 12 days, as police widen an investigation rooted in a feud between crime families.

source.originalTitle: המשטרה הודיעה: עצור נוסף בפרשת ג'פניקה

body: Israeli police have announced a further arrest in the investigation into the wave of grenade attacks on the Japanika restaurant chain, the sushi business owned by Beitar Jerusalem proprietor Barak Abramov. The suspect is accused of throwing a grenade at the chain's branch in Kiryat Ono, east of Tel Aviv, and a Tel Aviv court has extended his remand by 12 days while detectives from the district's central investigative unit continue their inquiries, according to Friday's announcement.

The suspect has not been named in Israeli coverage, and he is not identified here for that reason. The Jerusalem Post reported that a man arrested over the same Kiryat Ono attack is an 18-year-old from Bat Yam, and quoted police as saying the grenades used in the campaign were stolen army ordnance. Four further suspects have had their remands extended until 19 July.
All of the detentions remain at the investigative stage: no indictments have been reported, and every suspect is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

The affair itself is a sustained campaign of violence against Abramov's business interests. Roughly 15 grenade and shooting incidents were recorded within a single week in mid-July, with Japanika branches struck in Tel Aviv, Givatayim, Herzliya, Ramat Gan, Netanya, Afula, Kiryat Ono and, most recently, Rosh Pina. One person was lightly hurt in south Tel Aviv; other blasts damaged shopfronts and shook nearby homes.

Police believe the attacks stem from a feud between the Musli and Jarushi crime families, with Abramov's restaurants targeted as a means of inflicting economic pain on him. The businessman, who is reported to have once been close to the Musli brothers before developing ties to figures associated with the Jarushi family, is not a suspect in any wrongdoing and has given testimony to investigators as an injured party.

Earlier in the inquiry, detectives arrested Yossi Musli, the alleged head of a criminal organisation that police say is worth more than half a billion shekels and is suspected of involvement in murders, extortion and illegal gambling. Those are allegations only; he has not been convicted of any offence connected to this investigation.

The football dimension is what has kept Israeli supporters watching the case closely. Abramov bought Beitar Jerusalem in 2022, and under his ownership the club lifted the State Cup for the first time since 2009. He has publicly insisted that the violence surrounding his restaurant empire, a chain of some 20 branches he acquired outright in 2015, will not affect the club.

Update, 19 July: police have made a further arrest in the affair, this time over arson rather than a grenade. A 28-year-old man from Kiryat Ata is suspected of setting fire last week to the Japanika branch in Haifa's Carmel Center; he was detained on Saturday and a court extended his remand until Monday, 20 July. Police said advanced investigative means led them to identify his suspected involvement. The suspect has not been named in Israeli coverage, no indictment has been reported, and he, like every detainee in the inquiry, retains the presumption of innocence.

Update, 19 July: National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has publicly confirmed that he contacted Abramov after the grenade attacks on his restaurant chain, while insisting he plays no part in the police inquiry. Speaking on Radio 103FM, Ben Gvir dismissed criticism of the contact: "You fell on the wrong minister. From six in the morning I spoke with at least 26 citizens — that's my job," he said, adding that he understood police "didn't handle it properly initially." In a separate broadcast interview the same day, the minister, himself a Beitar Jerusalem supporter, said: "I am not involved in the investigation, I did not call the investigators and I did not tell them anything." Abramov had earlier said publicly that Ben Gvir initiated the contact.

Police attribute the attacks to a feud between the Musli and Jarushi crime families; chain owner Barak Abramov is not a suspect and has given testimony to investigators as an injured party.
Yossi Musli, the alleged head of a criminal organisation, was arrested earlier in the investigation; he has not been convicted of any offence in this affair.
Abramov has owned Beitar Jerusalem since 2022, and the club won the State Cup under his ownership, its first since 2009.

title: Kanyuk sets seven-day deadline as Hapoel Ramat Gan claim swells to 350,000 shekels
dek: Through his lawyer, the midfielder has sent the newly promoted club a formal warning letter demanding 350,000 shekels within seven days — citing unpaid bonuses, unlawful termination and missing pension contributions — before a lawsuit is filed.

body: The afterglow of Hapoel Ramat Gan's return to the Israeli top flight has been cut short by a pay dispute, with midfielder Gidi Kanyuk saying he is days away from suing the newly promoted club over 140,000 shekels in bonuses and compensation he insists were promised and never paid.

Kanyuk, a 33-year-old attacking midfielder who was part of the squad that sealed promotion in May, set out his grievance in remarks to Sport 5's Raz Zahavi. He said he had approached chief executive Moshe Barkat "countless times" about a promotion bonus and further payments he believes he is owed, "but I was not given any satisfactory answer". He added: "I contacted a lawyer yesterday, and in the coming days I intend to file a lawsuit."

According to the report, the 140,000-shekel figure — which the player states as a net amount — comprises three elements: a bonus for winning promotion, bonuses tied to his goal involvements, and an agreed compensation payment said to be triggered because his contract was not taken up for a further season. No contracts or documents were published, and the sums remain the player's own account of what he is owed.

For all his frustration, Kanyuk stopped short of blaming Barkat personally, describing the chief executive — a retired senior police commander who took charge of the club's day-to-day running — as the last person he would level accusations at. His complaint, as he framed it, is with a club that has not paid what he says it undertook to pay.

Nor is he alone. Ezekiel Henty, the Nigerian centre-forward who arrived in January for the second half of the promotion campaign, went public first, airing his grievances in a social-media post; according to the report, he is claiming 45,000 shekels net. It was Henty's post that prompted Kanyuk to take his own complaint to a lawyer.

Hapoel Ramat Gan responded on Friday evening with a statement disputing the framing rather than the obligations. "Since the new ownership arrived, the club's management has been working in an orderly and responsible way to settle the commitments relating to last season," the club said. "Contrary to what has been claimed, these are not payments whose due date has passed or commitments the club has breached. The club is committed to meeting its obligations in full, and the handling of the open matters is expected to be completed in the coming weeks."

The dispute may extend beyond the two players who have gone public. Israeli reporting on the club's response also lists claims from two further members of last season's squad, of 40,000 and 35,000 shekels respectively, suggesting the bonus question touches a wider group of the promotion-winning dressing room.

Both players have already moved on. Transfermarkt records show Kanyuk joining Bnei Eilat on 1 July, with Henty signing for Hapoel Rishon LeZion the same day — departures consistent with Kanyuk's assertion that his deal was not extended into the new season.

The dispute lands at an awkward moment for the Ramat Gan club, who ended a 13-year absence from the top division in May and have spent the summer assembling a squad for their first Ligat ha'Al campaign since 2013 — recruitment that has included the Brazilian forward Luan Campos. A public row with two members of the promotion-winning dressing room is not the backdrop they would have chosen.

End-of-season bonus rows are hardly unknown in Israeli football, where promotion clauses are a staple of second-tier contracts. Few, though, surface this quickly or this publicly. If Kanyuk follows through on his stated intention, a summer that began with long-awaited promotion will continue in front of lawyers.

The dispute escalated on Sunday, when Kanyuk's lawyer, Amir Cohen, sent Hapoel Ramat Gan a formal warning letter demanding immediate payment of 350,000 shekels in total — well beyond the 140,000 the player initially cited — and giving the club seven days before a lawsuit is filed without further notice. According to the letter, the claim now spans unpaid promotion and achievement bonuses, unlawful termination during a two-season contract without notice or a hearing, more than a year of missing or partial pension contributions, unlawful salary deductions and irregular vacation payments, conduct Cohen described as a systematic breach of the player's rights. The club had not responded to the letter at the time of the report.

title: Szoboszlai Commits His Prime to Liverpool With New Contract Until 2031
dek: The Hungary captain and reigning Player of the Season has signed a five-year extension at Anfield, ending months of negotiations three years before his previous deal was due to expire.

body: Dominik Szoboszlai has signed a new long-term contract with Liverpool, the club confirmed on Friday evening, with the agreement running until the summer of 2031 and binding one of Europe's most complete midfielders to Anfield through the heart of his career.

The five-year deal arrives with time to spare. Szoboszlai's previous contract, signed when he arrived from RB Leipzig in 2023, still had two years left to run, but negotiations that had rumbled on for several months accelerated sharply in recent weeks. The new terms are understood to lift the 25-year-old towards the top of the club's wage structure, with British reports placing his salary between £200,000 and £250,000 a week.

It is a renewal earned on the pitch rather than at the bargaining table. Since his £60 million move from Leipzig, Szoboszlai has made 147 appearances in all competitions, scoring 28 goals, and has grown from an energetic addition into a player around whom the side is increasingly organised.

Last season was his most productive yet: 13 goals and 12 assists across 53 matches, form that made him the club's Player of the Season. He was also nearly ever-present in the 2024-25 campaign that brought the Premier League title back to Anfield, having earlier collected a Carabao Cup winner's medal.

The Hungarian was unambiguous about his motivation. "I want to win everything that is possible in this country, also the Champions League," he said after signing, adding that he plays with "the feeling that it's never enough" — a restlessness his coaches have long regarded as his defining trait.

For Liverpool, the timing carries weight beyond the individual. After watching Trent Alexander-Arnold and Ibrahima Konaté leave on free transfers, the club has now secured two pillars of its midfield in quick succession, following Ryan Gravenberch's own long-term renewal in March. Szoboszlai will begin the 2026-27 season, his first under new head coach Andoni Iraola, as one of the dressing room's senior figures.

Hungary's captain will be 30 when the new deal expires, and the view inside the club is that his best years are still ahead of him. On Friday's evidence, Liverpool intend to make sure they happen in red.

body: Barcelona may look no further than their own academy for midfield cover this summer. Catalan daily Mundo Deportivo is reported to have identified Orian Goren, the 17-year-old Israeli in the club's youth ranks, as a candidate to help fill the gap left by Frenkie de Jong, who faces months on the sidelines after returning injured from the World Cup.

The Mundo Deportivo report, picked up by Israeli media on Friday, frames Goren as an internal option for Hansi Flick, who is said to prefer promoting from La Masia over spending in the market. The paper is reported to relay a view inside the club that the midfielder has more than enough potential to reach the first team, with those who work with him comparing his style to Pedri's. Every element of that projection remains reported rather than confirmed by the club.

De Jong's situation is the trigger. The Dutch midfielder played through pain in his right knee during the Netherlands' World Cup campaign, which ended with a penalty-shoot-out defeat to Morocco in the round of 32, and checks on his return to Barcelona found the joint unstable, with ligament damage feared. Spanish estimates of his absence have ranged from around four months, per early reporting, to as long as six, according to Diario AS.

Goren's own credentials are not in dispute. Born in Savyon on 15 March 2009, he came through Maccabi Petah Tikva's youth section before moving with his family to Catalonia and entering La Masia. He signed his first professional contract at 16, tying him to Barcelona until June 2028, and spent last season with the under-19s, the club's Juvenil A side.

The Catalan press has long been enthusiastic about him. Sport has described Goren as 'the most intelligent player in Barcelona's youth department', a technically polished midfielder with exceptional vision who can operate as an interior, push further forward, or even drop in as a pivot. Comparisons with Pedri and Andrés Iniesta have followed him through the age groups.

What is verifiable is his presence around the senior squad. Goren was among the academy players called into Barcelona's pre-season group when training resumed on 13 July, one of the youngest names involved, and the schedule ahead includes a first friendly against CE Europa on 24 July, two matches in Birmingham, a triangular tournament in Italy and the traditional Joan Gamper fixture.

The distinction between covering in pre-season and replacing De Jong competitively is worth keeping in view. Any minutes for Goren in the coming weeks would arrive in friendlies, and the Spanish reporting itself places other academy midfielders in the same conversation. A leap straight from Juvenil A to La Liga duty would be exceptional even by La Masia's standards, however highly the club rate him.

For Israeli football, the mere mention is notable. Goren, an Israel youth international who featured in under-17 European qualifying in March 2025, would become one of very few Israelis to train regularly with Barcelona's first team. The friendlies of late July should offer the first hard evidence of how seriously Flick intends to test the idea.

According to Mundo Deportivo, as relayed by Israeli reports, Goren is a candidate to provide internal midfield cover while Frenkie de Jong is injured, with Hansi Flick said to prefer academy solutions over signings.

Goren was included in Barcelona's pre-season training group that reconvened on 13 July 2026, with the first friendly scheduled against CE Europa on 24 July.

body: Deni Avdija's first summer as an NBA All-Star was supposed to be about consolidation. Instead, voices in Portland's own press corps are asking whether the Trail Blazers have spent it dismantling the very conditions that made his breakout possible.

The sharpest version of the argument comes from Rip City Project, a Portland-focused analysis site, where writer Reese Kunz contends the front office has failed to surround Avdija with complementary pieces. The Israeli forward thrived last season precisely because the offence ran through his hands, the piece argues, and the club's headline summer acquisition — Ja Morant — is another ball-dominant guard rather than the connective shooting Portland actually needed.

The transaction itself is not in dispute. On 29 June, Memphis sent Morant to Portland in exchange for Jerami Grant and Kris Murray, with the Grizzlies adding cash considerations — a deal that cost the Blazers no draft capital. Morant, the 2020 Rookie of the Year and a two-time All-Star, carries a career average of 22.4 points per game, but injuries and suspensions have limited him to 79 appearances across the past three seasons.

Fit, not price, is the objection. Morant "is at his best with the ball in his hands and can't effectively space the floor for Deni," Kunz writes — a genuine concern for a player who led the league in drives last season as Portland's primary initiator. The backcourt already houses Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday, and by Rip City Project's reckoning six players hold credible claims on five starting places, to the point that the site has floated bringing the newest arrival off the bench.

What the critics fear being disrupted is considerable. Avdija averaged 24.2 points — 14th in the league — with 6.9 rebounds and 6.7 assists in 2025-26, earned his first All-Star selection and carried Portland to a 42-40 record and a first playoff berth since 2021. The ledger had a debit side too: the Blazers were the league's worst turnover team, with Avdija's own giveaways inflated by his playmaking load — a price the Portland analysis considered worth paying to discover his best version.

There is a concession within the criticism. The first-round exit to San Antonio, in which the Spurs shaded Avdija off his right hand and sharply cut his assist production, showed he "can't be the 1a option on a contending roster," Kunz acknowledges. But the counter is that Portland's newcomers are not demonstrably better than him either — leaving, in this reading, a roster full of big names, muddled hierarchy and a capped ceiling rather than a clear structure built around or above its franchise player.

The riddle now passes to Micah Nori, appointed head coach on 23 June on a single guaranteed year with two team options, after interim coach Tiago Splitter parlayed his 42-40 season into the Chicago Bulls job. Nori, a long-serving Minnesota assistant, inherits an abundance of creators, thin spacing and a mandate to shrink the turnover count without shrinking Avdija.

For Israeli basketball the stakes are plain. Avdija is the country's flagship NBA presence, and his leap into stardom made Portland appointment viewing back home. Whether Morant's arrival complements that role or compresses it will be among the more consequential subplots of the Blazers' pre-season — and it says something that Portland's own observers are already flagging the danger in unusually blunt terms.

title: Andrija Novakovich: The Well-Travelled Striker Reuniting With Kenny Saief at Maccabi Haifa
dek: Eight years after sharing a United States camp with Kenny Saief, the Wisconsin-born target man arrives on the Carmel with a nomadic CV, a divisive goalscoring record and a friend already in the dressing room.

source.name: ONE
source.originalTitle: החבר של סייף: היכרות עם חלוץ הרכש של מכבי חיפה
source.author: ONE editorial team

Wikipedia — Kenny Saief (Paraguay first start, Maccabi Haifa move)
